items.title: Commercial build
items.text:
This page applies to the commercial o6 wheels distributed on PyPI. The AGPL build does not use o6 Credentials or Script Mode.

The commercial wheel contains the full Client and Server API. Without a valid o6-issued Credential, it runs in ten-minute Script Mode, which permits commercial use. Importing o6 starts a process-wide timer. When the timer expires, the process terminates with a failure status. A valid Credential removes this limit. On POSIX systems this is an immediate hard exit, so applications must not rely on shutdown handlers running when Script Mode expires.

items.title: Feature scope
items.text:
The full compiled API remains importable so documentation, annotations, and type discovery behave consistently. A valid Credential can separately enable client, server, and pubsub operations:

Feature Effect when omitted client Constructing o6.Client raises PermissionError. server Constructing o6.Server raises PermissionError. pubsub o6.pubsub operations raise PermissionError; Server instances contain no PubSub manager, information-model methods, or PubSub transports.

pubsub requires server, so a PubSub-enabled Credential contains both names. An empty Feature Scope enables every compiled feature. Unknown, duplicate, empty, or inconsistent scope entries make the Credential unusable and trigger the documented Script Mode fallback.

items.title: Credential location
items.text:
Set O6PYTHON_LICENSE_FILE to the Credential file's path:

export O6PYTHON_LICENSE_FILE=/path/to/o6python_license.json
python application.py

If O6PYTHON_LICENSE_FILE is unset, o6 checks only o6python_license.json in the process's current working directory. It does not search the user home directory, platform configuration directories, or the installed package.

If the default file is absent, o6 enters Script Mode and prints the normal Script Mode message without an additional missing-file warning. If O6PYTHON_LICENSE_FILE names a missing file, or a Credential is unreadable, malformed, incorrectly signed, not yet valid, or expired, o6 prints the specific reason to standard error and falls back to Script Mode. These warnings remain visible when O6PYTHON_SKIP_GREET suppresses the startup banner and routine valid-Credential information. The Script Mode notice and expiry message also always remain visible on standard error.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Python 3.11 – 3.14 (CPython) Platforms Linux x86_64 / aarch64, macOS x86_64 / arm64, Windows AMD64 / ARM64

Wheels bundle open62541 and OpenSSL, so no OPC UA stack or C toolchain is needed. Windows ARM64 wheels start at Python 3.11.

items.title: Install from PyPI
items.text:
pip install o6

Verify the installation:

python -c "import o6; print(o6.__version__)"

Info

PyPI ships the commercial build. Without a Credential, importing o6 starts ten-minute Script Mode, which permits commercial use — see Commercial build.

items.title: Build from the AGPL repository
items.text:
o6\Python may by used freely for public research and in education — no licence fee, no Credential, no evaluation timer counting down while you work. o6\Python is released under AGPL-3.0-or-later at o6-automation/o6-python-agpl.

Building it compiles open62541 from source and requires a C toolchain.

sudo apt install build-essential cmake pkg-config \
                 libssl-dev libjitterentropy3-dev libzstd-dev \
                 python3-dev python3-venv

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/o6-automation/o6-python-agpl.git
cd o6-python-agpl

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install . --no-build-isolation

Find out more on the official github page.

items.title: Manual
items.text: The manual is the reference narrative for o6\Python. It is written as a book: each chapter builds on the vocabulary introduced by the ones before it, so the examples grow shorter as those concepts become familiar. It therefore reads best from top to bottom, following the order of the navigation, through to Server.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
# Chapter What it gives you 1 OPC UA Fundamentals The specification's concepts — protocol, services, information modelling, datatypes, namespaces, nodesets. Independent of any SDK. 2 Node API The pythonic object model that the rest of the manual uses in nearly every example. 3 o6\Python SDK Fundamentals How the SDK maps the specification onto Python: built-in types, the namespace registry, writing and compiling nodesets. 4 Client The complete story of o6.Client — lifecycle, address space, subscriptions and history, raw services. 5 Server The complete story of o6.Server — lifecycle, building an address space, declared types, behaviour and callbacks, events, access control, operations.

If you already know OPC UA, chapter 1 is a refresher you can skim — chapters 2 and 3 are worth reading even then, as they establish the notation and the type vocabulary that the Client and Server chapters use without further comment.

Chapters 4 and 5 are written so that you can read either without knowing the other. if you only write clients, read Client and stop; if you only build servers, Server stands on its own after chapter 3.

items.title: Advanced topics
items.text:
The remaining two chapters are reference material rather than part of the reading path. Neither is required to use the SDK, their order carries no meaning, and each page stands alone and lists its own prerequisites.

  • Performance — end-to-end benchmarks against native open62541 C and asyncua, for both the client and the server role. Consult it when you need numbers, or when sizing a design's throughput budget.
  • Implementation details — how the binding itself works: memory management, variable callbacks, namespace matching, GIL and event-loop bridging, wire-format mapping. Consult it to diagnose a non-obvious failure, to extend the binding, or to judge whether an unusual use case is supported.

items.title: Release notes
items.text: The final chapter, Release Notes, lists new features, improvements, bug fixes, and breaking changes by release.

items.title: Node API
items.text:
o6\ gives you direct, pythonic access to OPC UA nodes and data types through the object model exposed by a connected client.

value = client.root.objects.MyVariable() # reads MyVariable on connected server

The Node API is more than a service-based wrapper. You can navigate an OPC UA server's address space — including both nodes and type definitions — using Python's regular attribute, subscript, and call operators. Those operators are translated into service requests like Browse, Read, Write, Call, letting you write expressions like the one above without ever constructing a request object.

items.title: A taste
items.text:
from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    print(client.objects.MyInteger())              # read
    client.objects.MyInteger(42)                   # write
    print(client.objects.TestMethods.Hello("o6")) # call

items.title: Motivation
items.text:
A service-based API is centered around OPC UA requests and response objects: building ReadRequests, sending them, and parsing the result. This is powerful and explicit, but it is also low-level and often very verbose.

The Node API is a higher-level, object-oriented layer on top of the OPC UA services.

Service API Node API client.serviceRead(...) client.root.objects.MyVariable.read() client.serviceWrite(...) client.root.objects.MyVariable(123) client.serviceCall(...) client.objects.MyMethod.call(...)

The . syntax in the Node API gives you canonical Python access to the server's actual UA objects, wrapped as Python node objects. This blends OPC UA's object-oriented model with Python's own object orientation so your code feels natural and easy to follow.

  • It reduces boilerplate compared to manually constructing service requests.
  • It makes address-space traversal readable and discoverable.
  • It preserves OPC UA semantics while fitting naturally into Python code.
  • It gives a smoother onboarding path for application developers who want the flexibility of OPC UA without leaving Python's object model.

The Node API is the bridge between OPC UA's object-oriented server model and Python's own object orientation.

items.title: Easy access to OPC UA nodes from a client
items.text:
Servers expose server.root, server.objects, server.types, server.views, and typed server[nodeId] lookup as local entry points into the same Node API. See Finding existing nodes for canonical server identity, lifecycle, and synchronous/asynchronous lookup.

When a client has connected, it exposes the server entry points as Python objects:

  • client.root
  • client.objects
  • client.types
  • client.views

These objects are live views into the server. The dotted attribute syntax represents the actual OPC UA nodes in the server address space, wrapped in Python node objects. Each path component is resolved on demand through a Browse request. Client handles cache child names and retry a cached miss with one fresh browse. Client node/reference mutations, BrowseName writes, reconnects, and updateRemoteNamespaces() invalidate navigation caches; a complete client.browse(node) invalidates that node's cache, including other handles for the same NodeId.

Changes made by another client or by the server do not automatically invalidate cached hits. Call client.invalidateNodeCache(node) to invalidate one parent's children, or client.invalidateNodeCache() for all existing handles. The next navigation browses again; async callers must await invalidation. Attribute reads and writes always go to the server.

from o6 import Client

client = Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840")
client.connect()

node = client.root.objects.MyVariable

# The node object supports call-style to access attributes
print(node())                     # read the node value
print(node(attr="BrowseName"))    # read a specific attribute by name
# or use the OPC UA AttributeId enum
# print(node(attr=o6.AttributeId.BROWSE_NAME))
node(123)                         # write a new value to the node

Expected output:

np.int32(42)
o6.QualifiedName('1:MyVariable')

In the example above, client.root.objects.MyVariable is a direct path into the server's object hierarchy. The node returned behaves like a Python object, while still representing the underlying UA node.

Important: a node object can be safely cached for later use, only when we are sure the server model remains unchanged and the node is not being removed or renamed on the server side.

items.title: Usage
items.text: This page is a hands-on tour of the Node API once a client is connected. It assumes you have an OPC UA server reachable at opc.tcp://localhost:4840.

items.title: Setting the stage
items.text:
A running example is the fastest way to learn. The snippets below assume a server that exposes an object with a few variables and a method, similar to the example server used by the tutorials:

Objects/
├── MyVariables      (Object)
│   ├── MyInteger    (Variable, Int32, read/write)
│   └── MyString     (Variable, String, read/write)
└── TestMethods      (Object)
    └── Hello        (Method, input: String, output: String)

The exact path is irrelevant — replace it with the structure of your own server. What matters is the three navigation patterns you'll see below: . to browse, [] to look up by path, () to act on a node.

items.title: Connecting
items.text:
A Node-API session is a regular Client session. The Node API is layered on top of an active client connection.

from o6 import Client

client = Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840")
client.connect()

Once client.connect() returns, the client has an active session and the entry-point nodes (client.root, client.objects, client.types, client.views) are live and ready to be navigated.

items.title: Browsing
items.text: Browsing is how you navigate from a node to its children. Two syntaxes are available: dotted attribute access for the common case, and bracket indexing for paths that are not safe as identifiers.

items.title: Entry points
items.text:
A connected Client exposes four top-level nodes that correspond to the four standard folders of the OPC UA address space:

Attribute NodeId What's inside client.root i=84 The address-space root. The three folders below are also reachable from here. client.objects i=85 The instance address space — your application's objects, variables, methods. client.types i=86 The type hierarchy — ObjectTypes, VariableTypes, ReferenceTypes, DataTypes. client.views i=87 Server-defined views over the address space, if any.

items.title: Dot syntax
items.text:
Every entry point is an ObjectNode that supports the same dot, bracket, and call syntaxes as any other node. Most user code starts from client.objects; the others are useful when you need to walk the type hierarchy or query a server-defined view.

. triggers a server-side Browse for the named child. Children are resolved lazily and cached on the parent node, so repeated access to the same child is free.

# A single step — resolve one child of Objects
parent = client.objects.MyVariables

# Chained steps — each `.` resolves one level
var = client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger

# We can continue from the cached parent
var = parent.MyInteger

Names are matched case-insensitively against BrowseName. The result is a Node subclass (VariableNode, ObjectNode, MethodNode, …) depending on the child's NodeClass.

In interactive shells, dir(node) and <TAB> completion both run a browse and list the children — see Interactive completion below.

items.title: Bracket syntax []
items.text:
The dot syntax fails when a BrowseName is ambiguous: if a node has more than one child with the same name (case-insensitively), node.child raises because the path does not pin it down to a single target. In these cases you have to use [], which returns a list of matching targets that you can disambiguate yourself.

# Two children both called "Status" → dot syntax can't pick one
nodes = client.objects["MyDevice/Status"]    # list of targets
status = nodes[0]                            # pick the right one

[] is translated server-side through TranslateBrowsePathsToNodeIds and handles the full range of the browse path syntax specified in the spcefication here.

items.title: Node access — the () operator
items.text: Once you have a node, the python call operator () handles every interaction: read, write, call. The distinction is by argument shape, not by a different method.

items.title: What () does
items.text:
Every Node subclass overloads __call__. Calling a node with no value is a read, calling it with a value is a write, and calling a MethodNode is a call. An optional attr= keyword selects which attribute to act on; None (the default) means the Value attribute for variables and the method invocation for methods.

# Read
node()

# Read a specific attribute
node(attr="BrowseName")
node(attr=o6.AttributeId.DISPLAY_NAME)

# Write
node(42)
node("hello")

# Call (method nodes only)
parent.MyMethod("arg1", "arg2")

The attr= keyword accepts either an o6.AttributeId member or a case-insensitive o6.AttributeId-like string such as "BrowseName", "NodeClass", "DisplayName", "Description", "DataType", "ValueRank", "AccessLevel", …

items.title: Reading values
items.text:
Call with no argument to read the current value of a variable:

value = client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger()
print(value)

Reading a different attribute:

name = client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger(attr="BrowseName")
print(name)             # QualifiedName('1:MyInteger')

class_ = client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger(attr="NodeClass")

items.title: Writing values
items.text:
Pass the new value as the first positional argument:

client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger(42)
client.objects.MyVariables.MyString("hello")

Writing a non-Value attribute: pass both value= and attr=:

client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger(value="NewName", attr="BrowseName")

This is equivalent to client.write(nodeid, value) on the high-level client API — but the node is reached through the address-space path, so no NodeId string is required.

items.title: Calling methods
items.text:
Method nodes are called by passing the input arguments positionally. When the method is reached through its parent object, the parent is picked up automatically:

result = client.objects.TestMethods.Hello("World")
print(result)           # (StatusCode.GOOD, "Hello, World!")

Typed Method calls return (StatusCode, *output_arguments) on success and raise o6.StatusCodeError for a failed method or service. This applies to local and remote handles. Remote handles now check method statuses explicitly. Use client.call() or server.call() to receive bad method statuses in the tuple; those APIs still raise for service failures.

The Object is part of an OPC UA Call; it is not intrinsic to Method identity. Dot lookup returns a lightweight bound Method containing both the Object used for that lookup and the Method node. A Method obtained directly by NodeId has no lookup context, so pass the Object explicitly with object=. It can be an Object node or a NodeId-like value:

method = client[helloMethodNodeId]
result = method("World", object=client.objects.TestMethods)

addReference only adds an address-space edge. It does not change which callback a Method uses or mutate the Method node. If the same Method is referenced from several Objects, every dot lookup receives its own binding and therefore calls it with the correct Object.

Methods that take no inputs are invoked with an empty call:

client.objects.TestMethods.GetCurrentTime()

items.title: Async — one rule covers everything
items.text:
In async tasks, calls on both client and server nodes are always awaitable, including local reads and writes that complete immediately. Sync and async share the same syntax — just add or drop the await:

import asyncio
from o6 import Client

async def main():
    client = Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840")
    await client.connect()

    # Read
    value = await client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger()

    # Write
    await client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger(42)

    # Call
    greeting = await client.objects.TestMethods.Hello("World")

    # Browse (also awaitable)
    node = await client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger

    await client.disconnect()

asyncio.run(main())

Under the hood, a sync call on a Client schedules a coroutine on the client's background loop and blocks the caller; an await on the same expression suspends until the result is available. The dot syntax, bracket syntax, and call syntax are identical in both modes — only the await keyword changes.

items.title: Firing events — the << operator (server-side)
items.text:
The three operators above work from a Client or a Server. A fourth, <<, is server-only: on an ObjectNode or ViewNode handle, it fires an event sourced at that node without going back to the owning Server object:

pump << o6.Event(server, message="Cavitation detected")
pump << {"message": "Cavitation detected", "severity": 400}   # a plain mapping works too

<< is only defined for Object and View nodes — the two NodeClasses OPC UA defines an EventNotifier attribute for — so using it on any other node class raises TypeError immediately, naming the reason. The same is true for a node obtained from a Client, since local event creation is a server-side operation.

This section is not the full picture — see Events for eventType inference, reusable event drafts, and the parentheses required when awaiting << on an externally-driven event loop.

items.title: Interactive completion
items.text:
The Node API is designed to be driven from a Python REPL (the standard >>> prompt, IPython, or any IDE / notebook that uses Jedi for completion):

  • client.objects.<TAB> shows the children of the Objects folder.
  • After a child is resolved, <TAB> on it shows its children, and so on.
  • dir(node) returns the same names explicitly.
  • Type hints on Node (via the bundled .pyi stubs) let your editor autocomplete the attr= keyword, the value= keyword for writes, and the available o6.AttributeId values.
>>> from o6 import Client
>>> client = Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840")
>>> client.connect()
>>> client.objects.<TAB>
# Lists the children of the Objects folder:
#   MyVariables  TestMethods  Server  ...
>>> client.objects.MyVariables.<TAB>
# Lists the children of the MyVariables object:
#   MyInteger  MyString  ...
>>> client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger.<TAB>
# Lists the Node API members on the resolved node:
#   nodeid  value  ...
>>> client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger(attr=<TAB>
# Lists the AttributeId enum members:
#   NODEID  NODECLASS  BROWSENAME  DISPLAYNAME  VALUE  ...

The dotted navigation fetches and caches child nodes on demand; the first <TAB> after connecting pays a single Browse round-trip, subsequent <TAB> presses on the same node are served from the cache.

dir(node) exposes Python aliases for child BrowseNames. Instance aliases use the same spelling rules as generated model members: My Variable becomes mySpaceVariable, My-Variable becomes myMinusVariable, 3DPosition becomes threeDPosition, and Class becomes class_. Type nodes keep class-style names, replacing punctuation with underscores, for example My Type becomes My_Type. Aliases that would start with _ receive a node prefix (Node for types), so they remain accessible without looking up private Python attributes. Unicode aliases are normalized to the identifier spelling Python uses in source code.

The original BrowseName is unchanged and remains usable through getattr or a namespace-qualified browse path (namespace index 1 in this example):

client.objects.mySpaceVariable()          # Read using the Python alias.
getattr(client.objects, "My Variable")()  # Read using the original BrowseName.
client.objects["/1:My Variable"][0]()      # Resolve by browse path and read.

Exact original names take precedence; otherwise lookup matches original names and aliases case-insensitively. Collisions, such as My Variable and MySpaceVariable both appearing as mySpaceVariable, raise AttributeError instead of selecting an arbitrary child. Use an exact original name or a browse path to disambiguate. Existing Python attributes retain normal precedence over child lookup; browse paths remain available when those attributes hide a child.

On the client's owning event loop, dir(node) lists cached children and Python attributes without making a remote request. Use await client.browse(...) for fresh discovery in that context.

Tip: dir(node) returns a list synchronously, even though the children are resolved from the server. It is implemented with asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe against the client's background loop, so it works in a regular interactive shell without await.

items.title: Putting it together
items.text:
from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    # browse (dot and bracket)
    var = client.objects.MyVariables.MyInteger
    method = client.objects["TestMethods/Hello"]

    # read
    print("before:", var())

    # write
    var(7)

    # read again
    print("after: ", var())

    # call
    greeting = method("o6")
    print("call:  ", greeting)

Expected output (values will differ):

before: 0
after:  7
call:   Hello, o6!

items.title: Quick reference
items.text:
Operation Node API Equivalent service call Browse by name node.child Browse Translate path node["a/b/c"] TranslateBrowsePathsToNodeIds Read value node() Read of Value Read attribute node(attr="BrowseName") Read of the given attribute Write value node(42) Write of Value Write attribute node(value=..., attr=...) Write of the given attribute Read via property var.value Read of Value Call method parent.MyMethod(arg1, arg2) Call Async variant await … (same syntax) — List children dir(node) / <TAB> Browse Fire an event (server-side) node << o6.Event(...) —

For the underlying service calls (when you need full control over the request payload), see the Client and Service API reference.

items.title: Performance
items.text:
The end-to-end benchmark compares native open62541 C, o6\Python, and asyncua as OPC UA clients and servers. Both roles are varied independently, so client-side and server-side cost can be attributed separately. Seven pairings are measured:

Client / server Purpose C / C Native baseline o6 / C and C / o6 Isolate the o6 client and server asyncua / C and C / asyncua Isolate the asyncua client and server o6 / o6 and asyncua / asyncua Complete Python applications on both sides

Each client is a separate process. All configurations access the same 100 writable Int32 variables using the same NodeId sequence and a common process barrier, one value per service call. Node objects are resolved before timing. Every figure below is the median aggregate throughput across five samples; every client performs 2,000 operations after 100 warm-up operations.

Async clients keep at most 32 application requests open independently. The total limits are therefore 32, 96, and 320 outstanding requests for one, three, and ten client processes.

All rates are OPC UA service calls per second. Larger is better.

items.title: Aggregate throughput
items.text:
Ten concurrent client processes, up to 32 requests in flight per client, reads, SecurityPolicy #None:

Role o6\Python asyncua Ratio Client, against a C server 113.2k 63.2k 1.8× Server, driven by C clients 45.1k 11.8k 3.8× Python client and server 36.0k 8.8k 4.1×

The native C pairing reaches 298.1k calls/s in the same configuration. The difference between the two Python stacks is larger in the server role than in the client role.

items.title: Effect of request pipelining
items.text:
Async throughput (32 requests outstanding) divided by sync throughput (1 outstanding), per pairing, at ten clients:

The native pairing's lower multiplier follows from its synchronous baseline, which is the highest sync figure in the matrix.

Server-side pairings gain least - effectively constant across a thirty-fold change in outstanding requests.

items.title: Scaling with client count
items.text: Both Python pairings peak at three clients and decline at ten. Ten client processes plus a server process on twelve logical CPUs is oversubscribed, and the ten-client samples scatter accordingly, the native pairing stays flat. At their respective peaks the two Python pairings differ by a factor of 4.2×.

items.title: Relative to the native baseline
items.text:
Each pairing divided by the native baseline (server and client implementation in C)

Role o6\Python asyncua Client, against a C server 38% 21% Server, driven by C clients 15% 4% Python client and server 12% 3%

items.text:
Recorded on 6 August 2026, 05:52 UTC with the following hardware:

Component Configuration Processor 13th Gen Intel Core i5-1345U, 12 logical processors Memory 16 GB (15.45 GiB reported) Operating system Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2, x86_64, glibc 2.39 Python CPython 3.12.3 Transport OPC UA TCP over loopback

items.title: Bug Fixes
items.text:
• The ten-minute Script Mode timeout now reports “Scripting Period ended” instead of “Trial period ended”.

  • dir(node) now exposes valid Python aliases for child names containing spaces, punctuation, leading digits, or keywords; the same aliases work with dot access.

  • Client and server browse() and browsePage() now return all reference fields by default; explicit result masks remain supported.

  • Local ExpandedNodeId values, including browse results, now display registered namespace shortnames and accept those strings when reconstructed.

items.title: New Features
items.text:
• Added bundled namespaces for CNC, DI package metadata, FDT, plastics dosing and foam cutting, surface cleaning and multi-stage systems, and unattended retail.

  • Client browsePage/browseNext and shared path-translation helpers match server browsing contracts.

  • Client addObject/addVariable return typed handles with server-style inputs; both conveniences accept parentReference and default to Organizes.

  • server.loop exposes the server's owning asyncio event loop as a read-only property.

  • Client.connect(createDefaultSubscription=False) opens a session without requiring subscription support or capacity.

  • Client.invalidateNodeCache(node) clears cached child navigation; omit node to invalidate all handles.

  • Servers expose typed server[nodeId] lookup and root, objects, types, and views folder handles, preserving node identity and application state; await indexing in async tasks.

  • Python history backends can serve pages through getHistoryPage, including token release and session validation.

items.title: Improvements
items.text:
• The Server SDK is now considered stable; removed the beta warning from startup banners and documentation.

  • Event-monitoring callback types and guides describe path-string payload keys, including nested fields.

  • MonitoredItem.requestedParams exposes the original creation settings; configuration snapshots also isolate nested filters.

  • Clarified value conversion, namespace mapping, and API behavior in the guides and examples, and repaired reference links.

items.title: Bug Fixes
items.text:
• Value-only client/server reads and callable nodes accept all Good-severity statuses; use valueOnly=False to inspect status and timestamps.

  • Scalar write(node, None) now matches batch null writes; callable local nodes return None when reading an accepted null value.

  • Variables added with historizing=True to a running server register for history immediately; failed registration removes the new node.

  • Variable creation accepts typed empty NumPy arrays and explicitly typed empty sequences, retaining the datatype and declared ValueRank.

  • Automatic datatype discovery preserves string, GUID, and opaque NodeIds, follows every browse page, and reports read failures.

  • Client child-navigation caches refresh after client mutations, reconnects, namespace updates, explicit browsing, and cached misses.

  • Callable local nodes preserve DataValue status and timestamp metadata, matching client nodes.

  • Client node creation and history failures preserve StatusCodeError.code; batch history errors identify the failed target in exception notes.

  • Node lookup validates service and attribute results; malformed responses raise RuntimeError.

  • Server.historize() and unhistorize() work in async code and restore node attributes when history configuration fails.

  • Calling Server.stop() from its worker loop no longer blocks shutdown; async worker callbacks can await the returned task.

  • Repeated Server.deleteMonitoredItem(handle) calls remain awaitable in async code.

  • Client monitored items retain accepted filters, discard policies, monitoring modes, and server-revised parameters across partial modifications.

  • Async client monitoring and subscription lifecycle callbacks now run on the client loop and log failures.

  • Monitoring rejects subscriptions owned by another client; triggering links reject foreign, uninitialized, or deleted items before sending requests.

  • Server now raises ValueError for incomplete or empty certificate/key pairs and for secureOnly=True without credentials.

  • Encrypted servers preserve the constructor's applicationUri in configuration and discovery responses.

  • deleteNode([]) returns [] without a deletion request on both client and server.

  • Client.deleteReference() now preserves the namespace URI and server index of ExpandedNodeId targets.

  • Client.addReference() and deleteReference() service failures now raise StatusCodeError instead of ValueError, preserving the status code.

  • Browsing attempts to release outstanding continuation points on failure or cancellation, including tokens returned during client cancellation.

  • Client.call() service failures now raise StatusCodeError with the original status available in .code.

  • Remote typed Method calls now raise StatusCodeError for failed method results, matching local calls and the documented behavior.

  • Server.read() now matches client read options, including raw DataValues and timestamp selection (SOURCE by default); explicit attributes use attr=.

  • Read service and value-only batch failures consistently raise StatusCodeError, preserving status codes and identifying failed batch entries.

  • Server-local monitored items report their actual target, mode, filter, and revised settings; ID-only handles explicitly report unavailable metadata.

  • Unsupported local modify(), setMonitoringMode(), and setTriggering() calls raise NotImplementedError without changing the item.

  • Server.write() with a DataValue now honors the requested attribute and rejects unsupported combinations without overwriting Value.

  • Awaiting server node creation from another event loop now returns a usable, fully configured handle and preserves creation errors.

  • Fixed crashes when awaiting Server.browse() with typed nodes; async calls now consistently require await for both Node and NodeId targets.

  • Synchronous server startup and asynchronous context entry wait for listening sockets and raise bind failures. Asynchronous callers of start() can await waitReady() before connecting clients.

  • Servers can restart after shutdown with active or pending TCP connections.

  • Namespace publication can be retried after a failure without recreating completed nodes or rerunning their initializers.

  • Role equality is consistent with hashing; name-only roles remain usable in permission APIs but are distinct from resolved roles.

  • Failed subscription and monitored-item deletions preserve retry handles; native deletion clears client handles, and subscription modifications retain accepted settings.

  • Server-local monitored-item handles become invalid after numeric deletion or server cleanup; foreign handles and out-of-range numeric IDs are rejected before deletion.

  • Repeated value encoding and decoding no longer leak datatype references, field names, or partially converted values.

  • Range reads retain error statuses in raw DataValues and raise on invalid or out-of-bounds value-only reads.

  • historyRead follows server-issued pages and releases unused continuation points on limits, failure, or cancellation.

  • Writes through node(value) now raise StatusCodeError when the server rejects them.

  • Node introspection no longer blocks its own event loop during interactive completion.

  • Client and server callback cycles are collected, including Python plugins and pending requests.

  • Cancelled client requests no longer raise errors when their responses arrive.

  • Namespace conversion preserves native values during callbacks and repeated datatype lookups.

  • Fixed Python 3.11 reference-count corruption during value conversion, DateTime comparisons, and timer callbacks.

  • DateTime comparisons with unrelated types now follow Python comparison semantics.

  • Empty union values no longer crash namespace conversion.

  • Deleting optional DataValue or DiagnosticInfo fields clears them safely; deleting required native properties raises AttributeError.

  • Client.read now honors timestampsToReturn.

  • Newly created subscriptions report the publishing interval, lifetime, and keepalive count revised by the server.

  • Fixed memory leaks during binary/JSON decoding, DataValue.value access, and structure formatting.

  • Non-type codec datatype arguments, oversized DateTime strings, invalid Guid byte lengths, and invalid string inputs are now rejected safely.

  • Async method, read, and write callbacks run on the server event loop and may suspend; shutdown cancels pending callbacks.

  • Fields declared with an abstract structured DataType accept concrete subtype values.

items.title: Breaking Changes
items.text:
• Commercial wheels without a valid Credential now use ten-minute Script Mode instead of the two-hour evaluation period; commercial use is permitted in Script Mode.

  • Async tasks must await local server creation, node calls, dynamic child lookups, reference mutations, reverse-connect, discovery, and dataset operations, even for immediate results; synchronous SDK callbacks retain their nonblocking behavior.

  • Client credentials no longer enable plaintext password tokens implicitly; configure encryption or explicitly set allowNonePolicyPassword=True.

  • Startup raises for pending history registrations without a configured database or when registration fails, retaining pending entries for retry.

  • Client.getEndpoints(), findServers(), and findServersOnNetwork() raise StatusCodeError for service failures instead of returning empty lists; raw discovery services still return full responses.

  • Non-Value writes require the attribute's expected datatype on client, server, and callable nodes; use LocalizedText for Description and numpy.uint8 for AccessLevel. Ordinary Value writes retain type inference.

  • Client non-Value writes reject DataValue status/timestamp metadata with BAD_WRITE_NOT_SUPPORTED instead of allowing it to be discarded.

  • Unknown client[nodeId] lookups raise StatusCodeError(BAD_NODE_ID_UNKNOWN) instead of KeyError, matching server lookup; local disconnected-client checks and malformed responses raise RuntimeError.

  • Client.deleteNode() and Server.deleteNode() return a list of per-target statuses for batch calls instead of one aggregate status; scalar calls return one StatusCode.

  • Rename the server deletion keyword deleteReferences to deleteTargetReferences, and await deleteNode() inside async tasks.

  • Client.deleteNode() service failures now raise StatusCodeError instead of ValueError.

  • addReference() and deleteReference() now use (source, reftype, target) and deleteBidirectional, return StatusCode, and require await in async tasks; use addReferenceLegacy() / deleteReferenceLegacy() to retain the old contract.

  • Server.browse() now returns a complete list of references, matching Client.browse(); remove .references access and move maxReferences= calls to Server.browsePage() for explicit pagination.

  • Client.browse() failures now raise StatusCodeError instead of ValueError; Server.browseNext() now raises StatusCodeError for failed page statuses.

  • Server.call() now returns (status, *outputs) for method failures, matching Client.call(); use status.check() to retain exception-based handling.

  • Server.write() now accepts parallel target/value lists or a mapping; replace broadcast calls with write(nodes, [value] * len(nodes)) and pass attributes with attr=.

  • Server.write() returns one status or an ordered list of statuses and continues batches after individual failures; check results with status.check() to retain exception-based handling.

  • Client.write() service failures now raise StatusCodeError instead of ValueError.

items.title: Known Issues
items.text: • Malformed binary union values can crash the underlying SDK decoder; an upstream fix is required.

items.title: New Features
items.text:
• Server.createEvent() emits immediately, matching the C SDK, with emitEvent() as an alias. Construct reusable drafts with o6.Event(server, ...) and emit them with trigger().

  • When eventType is omitted, emission uses the type of eventInstance if supplied; otherwise, the source's type definition is browsed for a GeneratesEvent reference, and that EventType is used.

server.addReference(
    source=o6.NodeId(PumpType),
    reftype=ns0.reftypes.GeneratesEvent,
    target=o6.NodeId(PumpFaultType),
)
pump = PumpType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="Pump1")

server.createEvent(source=pump, message="Cavitation detected")   # PumpFaultType

Without an event instance, a type declaring no GeneratesEvent target falls back to BaseEventType. A type declaring more than one, or a source with no type definition at all, raises ValueError. Passing eventType= explicitly selects the type argument. An Event draft resolves it at each trigger(). Field values retain C's precedence: explicit fields, instance properties, then emission defaults.

  • ObjectNode and ViewNode fire an event sourced at themselves with <<, without going back to the owning Server:
pump << o6.Event(server, message="Cavitation detected")
pump << {"message": "Cavitation detected", "severity": 400}
pump << eventInstance
pump << {"eventInstance": eventInstance}

An event instance must be an Object of BaseEventType or a subtype on the same server; emission reads its current fields without modifying the node.

  • Variable read and write callbacks may be async def, matching Method callbacks:
@o6.read
async def _read(self, **kwargs):
    return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, await self.device.readTemperature())

A coroutine that returns without awaiting completes synchronously. One that awaits leaves the operation pending and completes it when the coroutine finishes; server shutdown cancels it. This previously raised TypeError: Variable callbacks cannot be async.

  • @o6.enumtype supports declaring more than 255 members. This previously failed registration outright:
RuntimeError: UA_DataType_fromEnumDescription failed: BadEncodingLimitsExceeded

This unblocks o6.ns.bacnet, whose BACnetPropertyIdentifier declares 396.

  • Server-side historizing is added. historizing=True on addVariable used to only set the Historizing attribute; once server.config.setHistoryDatabase(...) is configured, it registers the Variable too:
server.config.setHistoryDatabase(capacity=100)
server.addVariable("Level", plant, 0.0, historizing=True)

historizing=o6.History(capacity=, strategy=, interval=) customizes capacity and sampling strategy per Variable; server.historize(target, ...) / unhistorize(target) do the same for a node this server didn't create.

  • Server and client application notifications are exposed as handler registries. Each server.on<Category>Notification — Lifecycle, SecureChannel, Session, Service, Subscription, MonitoredItem, DiscoveryRegisterServer, DiscoveryServerOnNetwork and Audit — is a list-like registry usable as a decorator, assignable as a whole, and changeable while the server runs:
@server.onSessionNotification
def _audit(notification):
    print(notification.type, notification.payload)

The client side offers onLifecycleNotification, onServiceNotification, and onGlobalNotification, which sees every notification the connection produces. A handler on either side receives an o6.Notification carrying type and payload, a read-only str -> Any mapping of that notification's fields.

  • Server.addSubscribedDataSet(name, metadata, targets) creates a native standalone subscribed DataSet, and removeSubscribedDataSet(dataSetId) removes it. This defines the dataset without creating or enabling a DataSetReader.

  • ServerConfig.maxSubscriptions and ServerConfig.maxSubscriptionsPerSession cap the number of subscriptions across all sessions and within one session:

server.config.maxSubscriptions = 50

items.title: Improvements
items.text:
• Server.createEventMonitoredItem raises ValueError when the effective EventFilter has no select clauses, instead of letting the server answer BadEventFilterInvalid.

  • The server manual gains a tutorial series covering type declaration, method implementations, variables with sources, callbacks, events and timers, access control, security policies, monitoring and history.

  • History reads now support continuation points for paging large result sets. Use client.serviceHistoryRead() with HistoryReadValueId.continuationPoint to resume reading from where the previous batch ended.

items.title: Bug Fixes
items.text:
• An OPC UA enumeration is a Python enum.IntEnum, an OptionSet an enum.IntFlag, chosen by the declaring decorator. An enumeration no longer drops a member valued zero, or one whose value is the sum of two others, from iteration, dir() and repr:
list(ApplicationType)   # all four members, not two

Members consequently compose as integers: A | B is a plain int rather than a member, and issubclass(SomeEnum, enum.Flag) is False. OptionSets are unchanged — in ns0, 48 enumerations change and 19 OptionSets do not.

  • An enumeration value outside the declared set decodes instead of raising, so one out-of-specification field no longer fails the read containing it. The value is preserved as sent, including a negative one:
BrowseResultMask(12).name   # None
int(BrowseResultMask(12))   # 12
  • value in SomeType now answers the same question on every supported interpreter, for both enumerations and OptionSets — including StatusCode. On 3.13+, an expression like 99 in SomeOptionSet used to answer True for every integer; it now discriminates. On 3.11, the same kind of expression used to raise TypeError; it now answers instead:
999999 in AccessLevelType   # False, not True (3.13+) or TypeError (3.11)

  • A notification payload no longer reports a corrupted namespace index for the node it concerns. The conversion borrowed the native namespace index rather than copying it, so a monitored NodeId could surface under the wrong namespace once the native value was released.

  • A default DisplayName derived from a BrowseName no longer carries the namespace qualifier:

machine = Machine(server=server, parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="ns=plant;Machine")
machine(attr=o6.AttributeId.DISPLAY_NAME)   # "Machine", not "ns=plant;Machine"

An explicitly passed displayName is preserved unchanged.

  • Building from source on Windows no longer fails on a backslashed nodeset directory path handed to CMake.

items.title: New Features
items.text:
• @o6.optionsettype and o6.bitmask declare an integer-form OPC UA OptionSet. Members are bit masks, and base= names the unsigned integer the OptionSet subtypes — it carries the wire width and the HasSubtype parent, and is mandatory:
@o6.optionsettype(ns="plant", base=o6.Byte)
class AccessLevelType:
    CURRENT_READ = o6.bitmask(0x01 << 0, name="CurrentRead")
    HISTORY_WRITE = o6.bitmask(0x01 << 3, name="HistoryWrite")

Bit fields declared with @o6.enumtype should move to it; @o6.enumtype now rejects o6.bitmask members, and @o6.optionsettype rejects o6.enumfield.

  • o6.optionsetbit declares one bit of a structure-form OptionSet — an @o6.datatype subtyping the ns0 OptionSet. Reading a bit is three-valued (None when ValidBits says the bit means nothing); assigning writes Value and ValidBits together. Generated structure-form OptionSets now carry one accessor per declared bit instead of leaving the two ByteStrings to be hand-masked.

items.title: Improvements
items.text:
• The client's limit on concurrent service calls is now configurable through client.config.maxAsyncServiceCalls (default 32, 0 disables it). Like all client.config fields, it must be set before connect().
  • Reusing send buffer improves async throughput by ~25%

items.title: Bug Fixes
items.text:
• Synchronous client calls no longer hang forever when the event loop passed as Client(loop=...) is not being run; they are driven to completion inline. Callbacks (data change, event, state) are still only delivered while that loop runs.
  • OptionSet-typed structure fields now surface as their flag class on read-back, in every namespace including ns0.
  • del instance.member on a generated structure no longer crashes the interpreter; it raises AttributeError, since a structure member always has a value on the wire. instance.__dict__ and vars(instance) now answer with a dictionary instead of raising, so debuggers and generic introspection work on structure instances.
  • import o6.ns.<x>.datatypes no longer executes the module body twice.
  • Argument.dataType resolved to the wrong namespace in several regenerated packages; it now points at the specification the argument's namespace actually intends:
namespace was is additive_manufacturing, cutting_tool ns=dexpi;i=3006, ns=dexpi;i=3013 ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3006, ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3013 glass_flat_v2 ns=aml;i=3006, ns=aml;i=3013 ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3006, ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3013 machine_tool, shotblasting, surface_technology_plasma, woodworking ns=bacnet;i=3006, ns=bacnet;i=3013 ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3006, ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3013 machinery_jobs ns=amb;i=3006, ns=amb;i=3013 ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3006, ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3013 wire_harness ns=amb;i=3008, ns=amb;i=3010 ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3008, ns=isa95_jobcontrol_v2;i=3010 gms ns=amb;i=3005, ns=amb;i=3008 ns=machinery_result;i=3005, ns=machinery_result;i=3008 - Integer-form OptionSet member values are now masks, not bit positions. Applies to every integer-form OptionSet, including AccessLevelType, AttributeWriteMask and PermissionType. Ordinary @o6.enumtype enumerations are unaffected.

If a value relied on the previous bit position, drop the extra shift:

# before — double-shifted because members were bit positions
value = 1 << int(my_flag) | 1 << int(my_other_flag)

# after — members are masks
value = my_flag | my_other_flag
  • The wire format of five struct fields is now correct against conformant equipment. Sizes are in bytes, measured against the same NodeSet on each release:
field declared base v2.0.2 now safety.RequestSPDUDataType.inFlags Byte 4 1 safety.ResponseSPDUDataType.outFlags Byte 4 1 fx_ac.AggregatedHealthDataType.aggregatedDeviceHealth UInt16 4 2 fx_cm.ConnectionDiagnosticsDataType.lastActivity UInt16 4 2 machinery_jobs.OutputInformationDataType.outputInfo Byte 4 1
  • o6.AccessLevel, o6.WriteMask and o6.Permission are retired. They aliased generated NS0 OptionSet DataTypes; the generated types are now the only spelling.
before after o6.AccessLevel o6.ns.ns0.datatypes.AccessLevelType o6.WriteMask o6.ns.ns0.datatypes.AttributeWriteMask o6.Permission o6.ns.ns0.datatypes.PermissionType

items.title: Improvements
items.text:
• New documentation site at https://docs.o6-automation.com/o6-python/, with a restructured manual, client and server tutorials, a full API reference, and performance benchmarks.
  • The PyPI project page now renders the package documentation and links to the docs site.

items.title: Bug Fixes
items.text: • @o6.enumtype(isAbstract=True) no longer crashes on Python 3.11 (the abstract-enum path used a functional-API call shape that 3.12's enum.IntFlag accepts but 3.11 rejects).

items.title: Breaking Changes
items.text: • Generated type names starting with a digit are spelled out instead of _-prefixed: _3DVector becomes ThreeDVector, _3DFrameType becomes ThreeDFrameType, and so on for all _3D* types in ns0 and the companion specs. This matches the OPC UA type dictionary and open62541. Enum members are unaffected and keep their _16_BIT spelling.

items.title: Distribution
items.text:
• Public o6 wheels contain the full Client and Server API.
  • Without an issued Credential, the public wheel runs in the existing two-hour evaluation mode. Its process-wide timer starts when o6 is imported; a valid Credential removes the time limit. Expiry terminates the process with a failure exit status; POSIX expiry is an immediate signal-safe hard exit.
  • An unreadable, malformed, incorrectly signed, not-yet-valid, or expired Credential prints the reason and falls back to evaluation mode instead of failing import. Fallback warnings remain visible when routine startup output is suppressed, as do the Trial Mode and expiry notices.
  • Commercial builds use O6PYTHON_LICENSE_FILE when set; otherwise they check o6python_license.json in the current working directory. AGPL builds do not use Credentials or evaluation mode. A missing configured path warns; a missing default file proceeds directly to the Trial Mode message.
  • Credential Feature Scopes independently control client, server, and pubsub; PubSub requires Server. Compiled symbols remain importable, while unauthorized construction or PubSub operations raise PermissionError. PubSub-disabled Servers omit the native PubSub manager, information-model methods, and transports.
  • Standard GIL-enabled CPython 3.11–3.14 is supported on Linux and macOS x86_64/ARM64 and Windows AMD64/ARM64.
  • Linux wheels require glibc 2.28 or newer (manylinux_2_28).
  • macOS wheels require macOS 15 Sequoia or newer.
  • Windows AMD64 supports Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 and Windows Server 2022 or newer; Windows ARM64 supports Windows 11 or newer.
  • Supported NumPy versions are >=2.0,<3; the native extension targets the NumPy 2.0 C API and is tested with minimum and current NumPy 2.x releases.

items.title: API organization
items.text:
• Added explicit public exports for o6 and its public modules.
  • Moved subscription classes to the canonical o6.subscription module and callback protocols and contexts to o6.server; the previous paths have been removed.
  • Made declaration, decorator, reference, datatype-registration, and node backend implementation paths private without changing the supported root authoring helpers.
  • Standardized public methods, properties, parameters, and model members on lowerCamelCase (nodeId, browseName, addVariable, encodeJson). Types remain PascalCase and decorators remain lowercase compounds. Previous public spellings have been removed rather than retained as compatibility aliases.
  • Grouped companion-spec symbols under each namespace's datatypes, objtypes, vartypes, reftypes, and instances modules instead of flattening them onto the namespace object.
  • Standardized datatype-discovery result keys on lowerCamelCase (typeName, typeId, binaryEncodingId, typeKind, structureType, membersSize).

items.title: Breaking Changes
items.text:
• o6.ns.<ns>.datatypes.<X>() now instantiates the concrete datatype.

    returns o6.Int32() numpy.int32(0) o6.nsx.ns0.BaseDataType.Structure.Argument() o6.Argument

    To obtain the NodeId, use o6.NodeId(o6.ns.<ns>.datatypes.<X>). Abstract datatypes (e.g. BaseDataType, Number, Integer) will throw when tried to instantiate.

  • struct members caml vs. snake case.

    In order to be PEP8 compliant previous versions converted member names of UA Structs and DataTypes to snake case naming convention. For better clarity, we are dropping this conversion and replacing these member names with their official names from the UA Namespace 0 and companion specs. In order to adhere closer to PEP8 we allow a single exception to the UA naming convention: the first character may be lower case for class members of python classes, that represent UA DataTypes and Structs.

  • enum members are consequently converted to capitalized snake case

  • dir() on a node lists instance children in lowerCamelCase

    Browsing a node now surfaces its Object, Variable, Method and View children under the lowerCamelCase name derived from their BrowseName, so completion offers client.objects.server.serverStatus instead of ServerStatus — the same spelling that generated declarations already use for their members. Type children (ObjectType, VariableType, ReferenceType, DataType) keep their PascalCase BrowseName. Dot access remains case-insensitive, so client.objects.server.ServerStatus still resolves.

items.title: New Features
items.text:
• OPC UA Browser, now built in feature of the o6.Client available through client.browseInteractive
  • Cleaned up Client API
    • removed client.fully_connected, client.connected is now only true when there's a secure channel and a session
    • removed client.disconnect_secure_channel in favor of client.disconnect() parameters closeSession and deleteSubscriptions
    • added range parameter for client.read and client.write, that lets one read into a slice of an array variable with e.g. "1:10"
    • StatusCode is now a proper Python IntFlag with full bitwise support: 
      if o6.StatusCode.Bad in status_code:
    #...

my_status_code = o6.StatusCode.Good | o6.StatusCode.UncertainLastUsableValue
    • added support for browse continuation point, i.e. client.browse now guarantees to return the complete list of references
    • cleand up and simplified history access through the client
    • revised the client node-management function parameters and added useful defaults for
      • parentReference - o6.ns.ns0.hasComponent
      • typeDefinition - o6.ns.ns0.objtypes.BaseDataVariableType
    • added callbacks for subscriptions
      • onCreated - fires when this subscription was created on the server
      • onStatusChange - fires when the server reports a status change for this subscription (e.g. keepalive timeout exceeded, session transfer on reconnect), receives the new StatusCode
      • onDeleted - fires when this subscription was deleted on the server
    • added callbacks for monitored item
      • onCreated - fires when this monitored item was created on the server
      • onDeleted - fires when this monitored item was deleted on the server

items.title: Client
items.text: This chapter is the complete story of o6.Client. This page covers what a client is and how one API serves both synchronous and asynchronous code.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
# Section What it covers 1 Lifecycle Constructing a client, discovery, connecting and disconnecting, sessions and channels. 2 Working with the address space Reading, writing, calling, browsing, namespaces and NodeIds, and node management. 3 Subscriptions & historical data Monitored items, subscriptions, and history. 4 Raw services & errors The service-level interface and status-code handling. 5 Notification handler Observing the client's own connection notifications (lifecycle, service calls).

The tutorials walk through the same material task by task with a running example server. This page is the connected picture behind them.

items.title: The two layers
items.text:
OPC UA is specified in terms of service sets — groups of related operations such as SecureChannel and Session management, Discovery, Read/Write, Browse, Method Call, and Subscriptions. o6.Client exposes those services on two levels.

The raw service interface mirrors the specification one-to-one. Every method is named serviceX — serviceRead, serviceBrowse, serviceCall — takes a request object from the generated data types, and returns the full response object. Nothing is interpreted for you: you build the request, you inspect responseHeader.serviceResult, you unpack the results.

The high-level interface sits on top and covers the workflows applications actually need: connect, read, write, browse, call, subscribe. It builds the request objects, manages the SecureChannel and the Session, resolves NodeIds across namespaces, decodes results into Python values, and works identically from synchronous and asynchronous code. For the overwhelming majority of applications this is the layer to use; reach for the raw services only when you need a parameter the high-level call does not expose.

Both layers live on the same object, so you can mix them freely in one program.

items.title: One API, synchronous or asynchronous
items.text:
Every request-issuing method on the client — connect, read, write, browse, call, monitor, all the serviceX methods — has a single implementation that adapts to the calling context.

Called from ordinary synchronous code, the call blocks and returns the result:

value = client.read("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable")

Called from inside a coroutine, the very same call returns something awaitable:

value = await client.read("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable")

What makes this work is a private event loop plus a worker thread. When you do not pass loop=, the client creates its own loop, runs it on a daemon worker thread, and every synchronous call is dispatched onto that thread and waited for. When you do pass a loop, the client uses it and expects you to run it; calls made from that loop are returned as awaitables, calls made from another thread are scheduled onto it and block the caller. A synchronous call made while that loop is not running is driven inline with run_until_complete rather than blocking forever — enough for request/response, but callbacks still only arrive while the loop runs. IPython and Jupyter are detected specially: because the kernel's loop is already running and cannot be blocked, the client always gets its own loop there, and synchronous calls keep working in a notebook cell.

client.loop exposes the loop; it is fixed at construction time.

The practical rules that follow from this:

  • Do not await a call in synchronous code, and do not forget to await it in async code. The return value is the plain result in the first case and an awaitable in the second.
  • A client is bound to one loop for its whole life. To use one from several event loops, create one client per loop.
  • Callbacks (data changes, events, subscription lifecycle) are invoked on the client's loop thread. Keep them short and never block them; hand work off to a queue if it takes real time.
  • After disconnect() the worker thread is stopped. Calling a service method then raises RuntimeError("Client event loop is not running").

The Async client tutorial covers loop ownership in more depth.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• First steps tutorials — connect, browse, read/write, call, all against a running example server.
  • Node API — the object-oriented view of the address space.
  • Namespace mapping in o6 — how NodeIds, namespaces, and compiled nodesets fit together.
  • Server — the other half, for building the server this client talks to.
  • Performance — batching, buffer sizes, and what to expect from large arrays.
  • API Reference — the generated signature-level reference for every method mentioned here.

items.title: Reading attributes
items.text:
read() is the workhorse. In its simplest form it reads the Value attribute of one node and gives you a Python value:

value = client.read("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable")

The target is anything a NodeId can be built from: a NodeId string, an o6.NodeId, an ExpandedNodeId, a Node object, or a generated type class:

client.read(o6.NodeId(2255))                       # NamespaceArray
client.read(client["ns=1;s=IntegerVariable"])      # a Node object
client.read(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType, attr="browseName")

Passing a list reads all of them in a single Read request, which is the whole point — one round trip instead of n:

values = client.read([
    "ns=1;s=IntegerVariable",
    "ns=1;s=DoubleVariable",
])
# [np.int32(42), np.float64(3.14159)]

Numeric values come back as NumPy scalars and arrays, which preserves the exact OPC UA data type (Int32 stays 32 bit) and makes array data cheap to work with.

items.title: Choosing the attribute
items.text:
attr selects which attribute to read. It accepts an o6.AttributeId member or a name as a string, matched case-insensitively and ignoring separators:

client.read("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", attr=o6.AttributeId.NODE_CLASS)
client.read("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", attr="browseName")   # same as BROWSE_NAME
client.read("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", attr="access_level")

This is how you get at metadata: BROWSE_NAME, DISPLAY_NAME, DESCRIPTION, DATA_TYPE, VALUE_RANK, ARRAY_DIMENSIONS, ACCESS_LEVEL, HISTORIZING, DATA_TYPE_DEFINITION, and the rest of o6.AttributeId.

items.title: Values, or the whole DataValue
items.text:
By default read() returns the value for every Good-severity status, including informational codes and flags, and raises for Uncertain or Bad. Choosing valueOnly=True discards status and timestamps; use valueOnly=False to receive DataValues and interpret their quality yourself. Service failures still raise. The range-error handling described below also applies in this mode:

dv = client.read("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", valueOnly=False)
print(dv.value, dv.status, dv.sourceTimestamp, dv.serverTimestamp)

This is the form to use when you need status details, including information carried by a successful read, or timestamps.

timestampsToReturn selects SOURCE, SERVER, BOTH, or NEITHER from ns0.datatypes.TimestampsToReturn. Omitting it (or passing None) selects SOURCE on both client and server.

items.title: Index ranges
items.text:
range reads a slice of an array variable instead of the whole thing. It takes OPC UA's inclusive string syntax or Python slices, which are stop-exclusive as usual:

client.read("ns=1;s=ArrayVariable", range="1:3")            # elements 1,2,3
client.read("ns=1;s=ArrayVariable", range=slice(1, 4))      # identical
client.read("ns=1;s=ArrayVariable", range=(slice(1, 4),))   # identical
client.read("ns=1;s=Matrix", range="1:3,4:6")               # two dimensions
client.read("ns=1;s=Matrix", range=(slice(1, 4), slice(4, 7)))

Slices must have explicit non-negative bounds and no step — OPC UA's NumericRange cannot express anything else, and violations raise ValueError before a request is sent. With a list of targets you may pass a list of ranges, one per target. Invalid, out-of-bounds, and non-array ranges follow the ordinary read error policy below. With valueOnly=False, the returned DataValue retains its original error status; batch reads return one DataValue per target.

A scalar range broadcasts across a target list; a range list must have exactly one entry per target. None and "" request the entire attribute. A nonempty range on a non-Value attribute returns BAD_INDEX_RANGE_NO_DATA using the same raw/value-only error policy. Invalid range strings are OPC UA status failures; malformed Python slices raise TypeError or ValueError.

An empty target list returns [] without issuing a request, including when the client is disconnected. Options and range-list lengths are still validated. Unsupported Python argument types raise TypeError; unknown attribute names, invalid slices and mismatched range-list lengths raise ValueError. valueOnly must be a bool. Only a Python list selects batch mode.

items.title: What read raises
items.text:
Client and server reads share this error contract:

Situation Result Good severity, valueOnly=True returns the value, discarding status and timestamps Single target, Uncertain or Bad, valueOnly=True raises o6.StatusCodeError List of targets, any Uncertain or Bad, valueOnly=True raises o6.StatusCodeError with the failed index in __notes__ Any per-target status, valueOnly=False returns the DataValue; inspect DataValue.status Service itself failed raises o6.StatusCodeError; .code retains serviceResult Client not connected raises RuntimeError("Client is not connected")

Callable node() reads follow the value-only policy too. Write return values and StatusCode.check() are unchanged; check() still compares exact codes.

client.read("ns=1;s=DoesNotExist")
# o6.StatusCodeError: BAD_NODE_ID_UNKNOWN

items.title: Writing attributes
items.text:
write() mirrors read() and comes in three shapes.

One node, one value:

status = client.write("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", 42)

Parallel lists, when you want per-node index ranges:

statuses = client.write(
    ["ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", "ns=1;s=DoubleVariable"],
    [100, 2.7182],
)

Or a mapping, which is the most readable form for a batch:

statuses = client.write({
    "ns=1;s=IntegerVariable": 100,
    "ns=1;s=DoubleVariable": 2.7182,
})

Nonempty writes are sent as one Write request. The single-node form returns one o6.StatusCode; the list and mapping forms return a list of status codes in input order, including a one-element batch. Empty lists/mappings return [] without a service call. The value argument must be omitted for the mapping form, and must be a list of matching length for the list form — anything else raises ValueError before writing. Even explicit value=None conflicts with a mapping. A list value for one scalar target is an array. All targets are attempted despite per-target failures; writes do not provide rollback. Server.write uses these same argument shapes and result types with local administrative privileges.

Explicit None writes a null value in scalar, list, and mapping forms, just as o6.DataValue(value=None) does. Nullable targets such as String variables accept it; non-nullable numeric targets return BAD_TYPE_MISMATCH and keep their value. A typed empty array, such as numpy.array([], dtype=numpy.int32), is an array with zero elements, not a null value. Omitting the value in client.write(node) raises ValueError. For callable nodes, node() reads and node(None) writes a null, raising StatusCodeError if the target rejects it.

attr works exactly as in read(), so writes are not restricted to values:

client.write("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", o6.LocalizedText("Counter"), attr="displayName")

range accepts an inclusive string, a stop-exclusive slice or tuple of slices, a broadcast range, or a per-target list. None and "" mean the whole attribute. Nonempty ranges require the Value attribute. It is supported for the single-node and list forms (not the mapping form, which has nowhere to put it):

client.write("ns=1;s=ArrayVariable", [99, 98], range="1:2")

To supply a status code or timestamps along with the value, pass a DataValue instead of a bare Python value. The server must permit it — writing timestamps requires AccessLevelType.TIMESTAMP_WRITE, writing a status requires STATUS_WRITE, and without them the write comes back BAD_WRITE_NOT_SUPPORTED:

dv = o6.DataValue()
dv.value = o6.Int32(77)
client.write("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", dv)

Unlike read(), Client.write() never raises for a bad per-node status — the status code is the return value. Service-level failures raise o6.StatusCodeError with the actual .code; Python input errors raise TypeError or ValueError. Check results explicitly, either directly or with StatusCode.check(), which raises StatusCodeError for anything but GOOD:

status = client.write("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", "not an int")
print(status)                      # BAD_TYPE_MISMATCH
if o6.StatusCode.BAD in status:    # StatusCode is a full IntFlag
    ...
status.check()                     # raises o6.StatusCodeError

The node(value) shorthand checks the write result and raises StatusCodeError on rejection, in both synchronous and asynchronous code.

Client, server, and callable-node writes accept the same payloads. Ordinary Value writes retain type inference, so client.write(node, 123) remains valid when its inferred datatype matches the node. Use explicitly typed NumPy numbers when exact width or signedness matters.

Non-Value attributes require their expected datatype: use o6.LocalizedText("Description"), o6.QualifiedName("Name"), or numpy.uint8(3) for Description, BrowseName, or AccessLevel respectively. No attribute-specific coercion is applied. A value-only DataValue envelope is also accepted; explicit status or timestamp fields on non-Value attributes return BAD_WRITE_NOT_SUPPORTED, including an explicitly supplied GOOD status.

items.title: Calling methods
items.text:
call() invokes an OPC UA method. It needs the object that owns the method, the method itself, and the input arguments in declaration order:

status, greeting = client.call(
    "ns=1;s=TestMethods",
    "ns=1;s=MethodHelloString",
    ["World"],
)
# (StatusCode.GOOD, 'Hello World!')

The return value is always a tuple whose first element is the method's status code, followed by the decoded output arguments — so a method with no outputs returns a one-element tuple. Node objects inside inputArgs are converted to their NodeIds automatically, at any nesting depth, so you can pass nodes where a method expects a NodeId.

A failing service raises o6.StatusCodeError, with the original status in .code. A method that returns a bad status code does not raise; invalid method selection and argument validation also return status tuples. Available outputs are preserved, so inspect the status before using them. Python argument conversion failures remain Python exceptions such as TypeError. server.call() follows the same result contract with administrative privileges; remote calls check session permissions. BAD_INVALID_ARGUMENT almost always means the argument list does not match the method's InputArguments declaration in count, type, or value rank.

The Node API offers the same call in object syntax, which reads better when you already hold the node:

client.objects.testMethods.MethodHelloString("World")

Typed Method node calls check the method status and raise StatusCodeError on failure. Their successful tuple includes the status and outputs. Remote Method nodes now perform this check explicitly; use client.call() when a bad status should be returned as data. Both forms can be awaited from async code.

items.title: Browsing
items.text:
browse() follows references from a node and returns a flat list of ReferenceDescription objects. Continuation points are handled internally: the call issues BrowseNext as often as needed, so the list is always complete even when the server chunks its response, including empty intermediate pages. server.browse() accepts the same filters and returns the same list shape. Node and NodeId targets work in synchronous code; async tasks await the call. Service and per-result failures raise o6.StatusCodeError. On failure or cancellation, collection attempts to release the outstanding continuation point; a lost connection can prevent release.

For explicit client pagination, use serviceBrowse and serviceBrowseNext, checking response-header and per-result statuses yourself. Local server paging uses browsePage and browseNext; see explicit pages and migration.

references = client.browse("i=85")

There is one thing to know before using the result, and it catches everyone once: the default resultMask is empty, so the server only fills in the target nodeId and leaves browseName, displayName, nodeClass, referenceTypeId, isForward, and typeDefinition at their zero values. Ask for the fields you need:

from o6.ns import ns0

for ref in client.browse("i=85", resultMask=ns0.datatypes.BrowseResultMask.ALL):
    print(ref.browseName, ref.nodeClass, ref.nodeId, ref.typeDefinition)

The remaining parameters narrow the traversal:

references = client.browse(
    "ns=1;s=Plant",
    direction=ns0.datatypes.BrowseDirection.FORWARD,   # FORWARD, INVERSE, BOTH
    reftype=ns0.reftypes.HasComponent,                 # reference type to follow
    refsubtypes=True,                                  # include its subtypes
    nodeClassMask=ns0.datatypes.NodeClass.VARIABLE,    # only Variables
    resultMask=ns0.datatypes.BrowseResultMask.ALL,
)

reftype defaults to HierarchicalReferences with refsubtypes=True, which is the "show me the children" traversal. INVERSE walks to the parent. nodeClassMask defaults to UNSPECIFIED, meaning every node class.

To resolve a path rather than enumerate children, use the browse-path syntax on a node — that goes through TranslateBrowsePathsToNodeIds:

node, = client.objects["/1:Plant/1:IntegerVariable"]

items.title: Browsing interactively
items.text:
For exploring an unfamiliar server there is a fully interactive browser built into the client:

selected = client.browseInteractive()          # starts at Objects
selected = client.browseInteractive("i=85")    # or anywhere else

It needs curses (on Windows: pip install windows-curses, otherwise ImportError). Quitting with n or p returns the selected NodeId or browse path as a string so you can paste it straight into code; any other exit returns None.

items.title: Namespaces and NodeIds
items.text:
A NodeId string like "ns=1;s=IntegerVariable" is namespace-relative, and the index 1 means something different on every server. o6 resolves this for you, which is why connect() spends two of its steps on namespaces.

On connect, the client reads the server's ApplicationUri and registers it in the process-wide namespace table under the shortname <clientname>_ns1, scoped to the endpoint URL. Then updateRemoteNamespaces() reads the server's NamespaceArray and maps every remaining namespace URI onto a compiled namespace module, scoped to the client name. Where several compiled versions of the same URI exist, the client reads the server's NamespaceMetadata (its NamespaceVersion) and picks the matching one, falling back to the newest available and logging a warning if the server is newer than anything you have compiled.

The visible effect is that ns=1 in your code means "namespace 1 of the server this client is connected to", and NodeIds returned to you print with the resolved shortname:

print(client.read("ns=1;s=IntegerVariable", attr="browseName"))
# client1_ns1:IntegerVariable

info = o6.ns.client1_ns1
print(info.uri, info.scope, info.index)
# urn:open62541.unconfigured.application  opc.tcp://localhost:4840  129

If a connected server adds namespaces at runtime, call client.updateRemoteNamespaces() again. It builds the new mapping — Python namespace table, SecureChannel decoder mapping, and custom data type chain — and swaps it in as one snapshot; a failed refresh leaves the previous, working snapshot in place, and an unchanged one is not rebuilt.

To discover the structure definitions of a server's custom data types, use getRemoteDataTypes(). Automatic discovery follows every browse page and preserves numeric, string, GUID, and opaque NodeIds. References with a remote server index or namespace URI are skipped because they cannot be read as local NodeIds through this session. Failed browse/read services and attribute reads raise StatusCodeError; types without the optional DataTypeDefinition attribute are skipped:

for dt in client.getRemoteDataTypes():
    print(dt["typeName"], dt["typeId"], dt["structureType"], dt["membersSize"])

It walks the DataType hierarchy below Structure (i=22) and reads DataTypeDefinition and BrowseName for every node it finds, returning one dict per type with the keys typeName, typeId, binaryEncodingId, structureType, and membersSize. Only nodes that actually carry a StructureDefinition — structures, structures with optional fields, and unions — appear. Pass a list of DataType NodeIds to query just those instead of walking the tree; an empty list returns [] without contacting the server.

The namespace machinery itself is described in Namespace mapping in o6, and loading nodesets so that custom types decode into real Python classes is covered in Loading and using nodesets.

items.title: The Node API from a client
items.text:
Everything above addresses nodes by NodeId. The Node API lets you address them the way the server models them — as an object graph. A connected client exposes the four standard entry points as live nodes:

client.root       # i=84
client.objects    # i=85
client.types      # i=86
client.views      # i=87

Attribute access resolves a child by BrowseName through a Browse request and caches it; calling a node reads or writes it; indexing resolves a browse path:

client.objects.plant.integerVariable()            # read the Value
client.objects.plant.integerVariable(42)          # write the Value
client.objects.plant.integerVariable(attr="browseName")
client.objects.testMethods.MethodHelloString("World")

dir() on a node browses it and returns its children, so tab completion walks the live address space: type client.objects. in a REPL and the server's actual nodes are offered, one Browse request at a time. That is the fastest way to explore an unfamiliar server, and it is why the dotted form is worth using even when you already know the NodeId.

BrowseNames are not Python identifiers — sometimes you need []

A BrowseName is an arbitrary OPC UA string. A Python attribute name is an identifier. Dot syntax can only reach the children whose BrowseName happens to be a valid identifier, and dir() deliberately lists only those — so a child missing from tab completion is not missing from the server.

Within that subset, lookup matches the BrowseName exactly first and then case-insensitively, so ServerStatus and serverStatus both resolve. Completion offers the spelling the generated declarations use: instances (Objects, Variables, Methods, Views) with a lowercased first letter, type nodes (ObjectType, VariableType, ReferenceType, DataType) in their original PascalCase.
