server.write("ns=1;s=Temp", o6.LocalizedText("Kettle temperature"), attr="displayName")

Attribute names are matched case-insensitively and ignore separators, so "browseName", "BrowseName", and "browse_name" are the same attribute.

A list read returns values in input order. Writes accept a scalar target/value, equal-length target/value lists, or a target-to-value mapping:

values = server.read(["ns=1;s=Temp", "ns=1;s=Counter"])
statuses = server.write(["ns=1;s=Temp", "ns=1;s=Level"], [30.0, 31.0])
statuses = server.write({"ns=1;s=Temp": 30.0, "ns=1;s=Level": 31.0})
for status in statuses:
    status.check()

A scalar write returns one o6.StatusCode. Lists and mappings return a list in input order, including a one-element batch; empty batches return []. Per-target failures remain in the results, and later targets are still attempted. Local batches execute sequentially without rollback. Local writes have administrative privileges; remote session permissions can produce different statuses.

Explicit None writes a null value in scalar, list, and mapping forms, matching o6.DataValue(value=None). Nullable targets such as String variables accept it; non-nullable numeric targets return BAD_TYPE_MISMATCH without changing their value. A typed empty NumPy array remains a zero-element array. Omitting the value in server.write(node) raises ValueError; callable node() reads, while node(None) writes a null and raises StatusCodeError if rejected.

To migrate a server broadcast call, replace server.write(nodes, value) with server.write(nodes, [value] * len(nodes)), or use a mapping. A list value for a scalar target remains an array. Pass the attribute with attr=. There is no positional-attribute or implicit-broadcast compatibility form.

Input shapes are validated before writing: mismatched lists, a scalar value for a target list, a separate value argument for a mapping (including None), or ranges with a mapping raise ValueError. Ranges can broadcast or be supplied as a list aligned with targets. None and "" mean the entire attribute. An invalid Python range raises TypeError/ValueError; an invalid OPC UA range string is reported through the target's status.

range= reads or writes a slice of an array value, using OPC UA's inclusive string syntax or stop-exclusive Python slices. Writes restrict ranges to the Value attribute. Reads return BAD_INDEX_RANGE_NO_DATA for a nonempty range on another attribute; None and "" read the entire attribute:

server.read("ns=1;s=Samples", range="1:3")           # elements 1,2,3
server.read("ns=1;s=Samples", range=slice(1, 4))     # identical
server.write("ns=1;s=Samples", [99, 98], range="1:2")

server.read supports the same read contract as the client: attr, timestampsToReturn, valueOnly, and range are keyword-only. Scalar targets return scalars, lists return results in input order, and empty lists return []. Use attr= for existing positional attribute calls; there is no positional compatibility form.

from o6.ns import ns0

dv = server.read("ns=1;s=Temp", valueOnly=False,
                 timestampsToReturn=ns0.datatypes.TimestampsToReturn.BOTH)
print(dv.value, dv.status, dv.sourceTimestamp, dv.serverTimestamp)

Timestamp selection defaults to SOURCE; SERVER, BOTH, and NEITHER are also supported. Read callbacks receive includeSourceTimestamp=True for SOURCE and BOTH, including the default read; SERVER and NEITHER pass False. Raw DataValues retain per-target statuses and supported metadata, including failures. Value-only reads accept all Good-severity statuses and discard status and timestamps. They raise o6.StatusCodeError for Uncertain or Bad, with .code preserving the status and an exception note identifying the failed batch index. Service failures use the same exception family. Python input errors use TypeError or ValueError.

Local reads retain administrative privileges. Client reads still use the remote session's permissions, so differently authorized callers can receive different statuses. Local batches read targets sequentially and do not promise an atomic snapshot. Reads can also be awaited, including from another running event loop.

Passing an o6.DataValue to write for the Value attribute stores the value together with its explicit status and supported source timestamp metadata:

import datetime

dv = o6.DataValue()
dv.value = o6.Double(42.0)
dv.sourceTimestamp = o6.DateTime(datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc))
server.write("ns=1;s=Temp", dv)

For other attributes, the DataValue payload must have the attribute's OPC UA datatype. For example, Description requires o6.LocalizedText:

server.write(
    "ns=1;s=Temp",
    o6.DataValue(value=o6.LocalizedText("Kettle temperature")),
    attr=o6.AttributeId.DESCRIPTION,
)

An incorrectly typed DataValue payload returns a bad status without changing Value or the requested attribute. Non-Value attributes cannot store DataValue status or timestamp metadata; supplying any of it (including explicit Good) returns BadWriteNotSupported before changing that target on both client and server. Bare non-Value payloads must also have the exact attribute datatype: use o6.LocalizedText for Description and numpy.uint8 for AccessLevel. Attribute-specific coercion is not applied. Ordinary Value writes retain their existing type inference, including bare Python integers.

Both public write methods return MaybeAwaitable[StatusCode | list[StatusCode]]. Async tasks await the result, including from another running event loop. Service failures raise o6.StatusCodeError, preserving .code. To retain exception-based handling, check each returned status; typed node(value) calls already check write failures and continue to raise:

status = await server.write(temperature, 23.5)
status.check()

Value range writes preserve source timestamps and source picoseconds, and require the supplied status to match the stored status. Server timestamps on reads are generated by the server; they do not round-trip a supplied timestamp. As with bare values, range= on another attribute raises ValueError.

server.read and callable node() reads accept Good severity, including informational codes and flags, and raise o6.StatusCodeError for Uncertain or Bad. To inspect quality even on successful reads, choose server.read(..., valueOnly=False) and interpret the returned DataValue's status yourself. Write status handling and StatusCode.check() are unchanged. If you deliberately store an Uncertain status, expect a value-only read to raise:

uncertain = o6.DataValue()
uncertain.value = o6.Double(1.0)
uncertain.status = o6.StatusCode.UNCERTAIN_SENSOR_NOT_ACCURATE
server.write("ns=1;s=Temp", uncertain)
server.read("ns=1;s=Temp")     # raises StatusCodeError: UncertainSensorNotAccurate

items.title: Node handles
items.text:
The handle returned by every addX call is usually more convenient than a NodeId. Calling a Variable node with no argument reads it, calling it with one argument writes it, and _value is the property form of the same thing:

temperature()             # 22.5
temperature(23.5)         # write
temperature._value        # 23.5
temperature._value = 24.0
temperature(attr="browseName")

Attribute access browses to children by BrowseName, using the lowerCamelCase spelling for instances, and dir() lists them — which is what makes a REPL usable:

plantObject.temperature()   # the child Variable, read
plantObject.serial()
dir(plantObject)            # ['add', 'counter', 'level', 'samples', 'serial', 'temperature']

A Method reached through its Object is bound to that Object and can be called directly; the bare handle needs the Object passed explicitly:

plantObject.add(2.0, 3.0)                # (StatusCode.GOOD, 5.0)
method(2.0, 3.0, object=plantObject)     # same call, unbound handle

o6.NodeId(node) converts any handle back to its NodeId. The full syntax — including browse paths and the awaitable forms — is described in Node API.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
A Method callback receives the Object the Method was invoked on, followed by the input arguments in declaration order, and returns a tuple whose first element is a status code:

def divide(node, dividend, divisor):
    if divisor == 0:
        return (o6.StatusCode.BAD_INVALID_ARGUMENT,)
    return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, dividend / divisor)

A Bad status may be returned alone. A non-Bad status must be followed by exactly the number of outputs the Method declares. Callbacks may be async def; the positional arguments and the result tuple are identical either way. Per-call state belongs on node or in a closure — there is no callback context.

Invoking a Method from inside the server uses server.call, with the same result contract as client.call:

status, *outputs = server.call(plantObject, method, [10.0, 4.0])
status.check()
quotient = outputs[0]

Both return (statusCode, *output_arguments), including bad method statuses, invalid method selection, and argument-validation failures. Outputs reflect the actual method result; a result with no outputs is (statusCode,). Node handles are accepted for object and method IDs and normalized inside input arguments. Synchronous and asynchronous callbacks use the same result contract. Await the call from asynchronous code, including a separate caller loop.

Service or local submission failures raise o6.StatusCodeError, whose .code retains the original status. Python conversion errors remain Python exceptions, such as TypeError. Local calls use administrative privileges; remote calls check the session's permissions.

Migration: server.call previously raised for bad method statuses. Inspect the first tuple element, or call status.check() to retain exception handling:

try:
    status, *outputs = server.call(plantObject, method, [10.0, 0.0])
    status.check()
except o6.StatusCodeError as error:
    print(error.symbol)      # BadInvalidArgument

Typed Method node calls such as plantObject.divide(10.0, 4.0) check the method status and raise on failure, locally and remotely. Their successful result still includes the leading status.

Replacing a Method's behaviour later is server.implement, described in Implementing behaviour.

items.title: References and deletion
items.text:
from o6.ns import ns0

server.addReference(source=plantObject, reftype=ns0.reftypes.HasComponent, target=temperature)
server.deleteReference(source=plantObject, reftype=ns0.reftypes.HasComponent, target=temperature)
server.deleteNode(scratch)

Both reference APIs use (source, reftype, target) and return an individual StatusCode. Call .check() on a synchronous result to raise for a rejected mutation; inside an async task, await the operation first and then check its status. 

status = await server.addReference(source=plantObject, reftype="i=47", target=temperature)
status.check()
status = await server.deleteReference(source=plantObject, reftype="i=47", target=temperature)
status.check()

Client service failures raise StatusCodeError. Invalid Python arguments remain TypeError or ValueError.

forward=False creates or deletes an inverse edge. Deletion uses deleteBidirectional=True by default; False removes only the requested source-side edge. Both operations accept NodeId-like or ExpandedNodeId targets and preserve remote namespace URI and server index metadata. Creating an exact existing local edge returns BAD_DUPLICATE_REFERENCE_NOT_ALLOWED. Deleting an absent edge returns UNCERTAIN_REFERENCE_NOT_DELETED. The underlying server stores remote edges but omits them from browse results; repeated creation of an exact remote edge returns GOOD without adding another edge.

Local creation accepts the same metadata keywords as the client, but a nonempty targetServerUri returns BAD_NOT_IMPLEMENTED, and an explicit targetNodeClass other than UNSPECIFIED returns BAD_NOT_SUPPORTED without creating an edge. The client sends these fields to the remote server for validation.

The server positional order is a breaking change. Migrate server.addReference(source, target, referenceType) to server.addReference(source=source, reftype=referenceType, target=target); use the same keywords for deletion and rename bidirectional to deleteBidirectional. The canonical APIs do not guess argument order. addReferenceLegacy(source, target, referenceType, *, forward=True) and deleteReferenceLegacy(source, target, referenceType, *, forward=True, bidirectional=True) retain the old server order, keyword names, and None/StatusCodeError behavior. Both compatibility and canonical methods must be awaited inside async tasks, including tasks on the server's own loop.

items.title: Node deletion
items.text:
Both client and server use deleteNode(nodeId, deleteTargetReferences=True). Pass a Node, NodeId-like value, or list of targets. A scalar target returns one StatusCode; a list returns one status per target in input order, including one-element lists. Every target is attempted even after a failure. An empty list returns [] without a deletion request. Duplicate targets have separate results: after a successful deletion, deleting the same NodeId again returns BAD_NODE_ID_UNKNOWN.

statuses = server.deleteNode([firstNode, "ns=1;s=Missing", lastNode])
# [GOOD, BAD_NODE_ID_UNKNOWN, GOOD]; both existing nodes have been deleted
for status in statuses:
    status.check()

Inside async tasks, await deletion before inspecting the result:

status = await server.deleteNode(scratch, deleteTargetReferences=False)
status.check()

deleteTargetReferences=True removes incoming references from remaining nodes; False leaves dangling references to deleted targets. Browsing omits dangling edges, but they become visible if the NodeId is reused. The native stack can also delete hierarchical children that have no other parent, with either flag. Retained server handles and aliases become invalid on deletion; reusing a NodeId creates a distinct live handle and does not revive the old object.

Malformed Python arguments raise TypeError or ValueError before any target is deleted. Individual deletion failures are returned in their target's status; client service failures raise StatusCodeError. Server deletion uses local administrative privileges; client deletion remains subject to the remote session's authorization.

Migration: rename the old server keyword deleteReferences to deleteTargetReferences; the old keyword is no longer accepted. The flag can also be passed as the second positional argument, matching the client. Scalar server deletion returns a status instead of None and does not raise for individual failures. Batch deletion on both backends now returns a list instead of one aggregate status. Use status.check() on each result to retain exception handling, and await deletion in async tasks, including tasks on the server's own loop.

items.title: Browsing and address-space queries
items.text:
The server can walk its own address space. Both server.browse and client.browse return a complete flat list of ReferenceDescription objects, following continuation points internally.

references = server.browse(plantObject, resultMask=ns0.datatypes.BrowseResultMask.ALL)
for reference in references:
    print(reference.browseName, reference.nodeClass, reference.nodeId)

As on the client, the default resultMask is empty and fills in only the target NodeId — pass BrowseResultMask.ALL (or the specific bits you need) to get BrowseNames and node classes. direction=, reftype=, refsubtypes=, and nodeClassMask= narrow the traversal exactly as they do on the client. Async tasks await the call for both Node and NodeId targets.

For explicit pagination, use server.browsePage(..., maxReferences=...) and server.browseNext(releaseContinuationPoint, continuationPoint). Old callers that read .references from browse now use the list directly; old page-limit callers move to browsePage. See explicit pages and migration for continuation and release examples.

browseRecursive walks the whole subtree in one call and returns a flat list of ExpandedNodeId values:

everything = server.browseRecursive(server.objectsNode)

Browse paths resolve without constructing a request:

path = ns0.datatypes.BrowsePath()
path.startingNode = o6.NodeId(server.objectsNode)
path.relativePath = ns0.datatypes.RelativePath("/1:Plant/1:Temperature")

result = server.translateBrowsePathsToNodeIds(path)
print(result.statusCode, [str(t.targetId) for t in result.targets])

browseSimplifiedBrowsePaths(origin, [QualifiedName, ...]) does the same for a plain list of BrowseNames, and translateBrowsePaths(request) takes a full TranslateBrowsePathsToNodeIdsRequest when you need the service-level form.

Two more helpers round this out. forEachChildNode(nodeId, callback) invokes callback(childId, isInverse, referenceTypeId) for every reference on a node, including its parent edge and its HasTypeDefinition edge — it is a raw reference iterator, not a children-only browse. And findDataType(nodeId) returns the Python type registered for a DataType:

server.findDataType(o6.NodeId(o6.Double))    # <class 'numpy.float64'>

items.title: Implementing behaviour
items.text:
Declared types describe the interface; the behaviour lives in Python classes and callbacks that server.implement binds to them. The complete rules are in Server callbacks and Implementing Object Behavior; what follows is the server-side shape and the traps.

An implementation is an undecorated subclass of a declared type. Variable behaviour uses the @o6.read / @o6.write decorators, Method behaviour uses @o6.call:

import o6
import plant

class TemperatureImpl(plant.TemperatureType):
    reading = 19.5

    @o6.read
    def _read(self, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, self.reading)

    @o6.write
    def _write(self, value, *, range, session):
        if value.value < 0:
            return (o6.StatusCode.BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE,)
        self.reading = float(value.value)
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD,)

class MachineImpl(plant.MachineType):
    temperature: TemperatureImpl

    def __init__(self, *, tag="untagged", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.tag = tag

    @o6.call("ns=plant;Reset")
    def resetMachine(self, mode):
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, True)

The pair is registered on one server, after the namespace is published and before nodes of that type are created:

server = o6.Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(plant)                              # 1. publish the model
server.implement(plant.MachineType, MachineImpl)     # 2. bind the behaviour
server.implement(plant.TemperatureType, TemperatureImpl)
server.start()                                       # 3. serve

Getting that order wrong is a hard error, not a silent one: calling implement before ns.append raises KeyError with the type's NodeId, because the type node does not exist in the server's nodestore yet.

The @o6.call target deserves attention. A single-segment target is a qualified UA BrowseName — "Reset" means ns=0;Reset, so a Method declared in the plant namespace needs "ns=plant;Reset". A target containing a dot is a Python member path through the containing Object, such as "controller.reset". A target that matches nothing fails at registration with uses @o6.call for unknown UA Method.

items.title: The marker-versus-implementation trap
items.text:
server.implement(Type, Impl) governs nodes that enter through native type instantiation — a client's AddNodes request, a Mandatory member created as part of a larger instance, server.addObject(typeDefinition=...). It does not change what direct Python construction produces:

machine = plant.MachineType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="M-100")
type(machine).__name__          # 'MachineType__Live' — the generated class
machine.reset(o6.Int32(1))      # StatusCodeError: BadNotImplemented

machine = MachineImpl(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="M-101", tag="line-1")
type(machine).__name__          # 'MachineImpl__Live'
machine.reset(o6.Int32(1))      # (StatusCode.GOOD, True)
machine.tag                     # 'line-1'

Instantiate the implementation class when you construct nodes from Python. The server.implement binding is what makes externally created nodes come out as MachineImpl. Members do follow the binding either way: machine.temperature is a TemperatureImpl in both cases above, because it was created by type instantiation.

items.title: Runtime changes
items.text:
implement also replaces individual callback slots on concrete nodes, which is how you attach behaviour to imperatively created nodes:

computed = server.addVariable("Computed", server.objectsNode, 0.0)

server.implement(computed, read=lambda node, **kw: (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, 3.5))
computed()                       # 3.5 — the callback owns the value now
server.implement(computed, write=lambda node, value, **kw: (o6.StatusCode.GOOD,))

A read slot must exist before a write slot: open62541's callback value sources must be readable, so a write-only Variable is rejected. Once a Variable is callback-backed, the callbacks own its state and no shadow value is kept.

Positional forms reset behaviour. implement(node, None) repeats the construction-time resolution, and a positional value abandons the callbacks and installs that value in native storage:

server.implement(computed, o6.Double(11.0))     # back to native storage
computed()                                      # 11.0

Two edges are worth knowing because both surface as errors rather than surprises. implement(variable, None) on a Variable that was created with native storage raises TypeError telling you to pass a value instead — there is no construction-time callback to restore. And implement(method, None) on a Method created by addMethod clears the slot rather than restoring the original function, so subsequent calls return BadNotImplemented; re-install the callback with call= when you want it back.

Type-level changes never rewrite existing nodes:

server.implement(plant.TemperatureType, read=type_read)   # future Variables only
server.implement(plant.MachineType, None)                 # future Objects only

items.title: Server callbacks
items.text:
Server.implement installs server-local Python behavior. With a UA type and an implementation subclass it selects how future instances are constructed. With call=, read=, or write= it replaces a callback slot on a Method, Variable, or VariableType. Existing instances are never rewritten by a type-level change.

Every callback starts with the node being acted on. Variable callbacks additionally receive operation metadata as keyword arguments.

items.title: One resolution rule
items.text:
read, write, and call choose their callbacks in exactly the same way. When a node is created, o6 starts at its concrete Python implementation type and searches upwards through its base types. The first matching callback is copied onto the concrete Variable or Method node. Then the containing Objects finish from the inside out: every matching @o6.read("path"), @o6.write("path"), or @o6.call("path") replaces that concrete slot. An outer path therefore wins if several paths target the same node. A later Server.implement replaces or clears the same slot directly.

That is the entire precedence model: nearest type first, then path callbacks in finish order, then explicit runtime changes. Invocation never searches a type hierarchy or resolves a path; it calls the callback already stored on the concrete node. Passing None clears that slot and does not reveal or recompute an earlier callback. A runtime callback placed on a VariableType is a template for Variables created afterwards and does not modify existing Variables.

Read and write are separate slots on one Variable, whereas a Method has one call slot. This is the only resolution difference between the three.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
def divide(node, dividend, divisor):
    if divisor == 0:
        return (o6.StatusCode.BAD_INVALID_ARGUMENT,)
    return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, dividend / divisor)

server.implement(method, call=divide)

The callback signature is:

(node, *inputs) -> (o6.StatusCode, *outputs)

node is the Object on which the Method was invoked. Inputs and outputs follow the order of the Method's InputArguments and OutputArguments. A bad status may be returned alone. A non-Bad status must be followed by exactly the declared number of outputs. Application state belongs on node or in a closure; Methods have no callback context or registration context.

Method callbacks may be synchronous or async def; both forms have exactly the same positional arguments and result-tuple behavior.

OPC UA Call identifies both the Object and the Method. Callback ownership follows the Method node while node/self follows the individual invocation.

Pending async calls are represented by GC-tracked state owned by the server and referenced by the asyncio Task. Cancellation resolves the native output pointer against that server-owned state; there is no process-global callback registry.

items.title: Methods declared on ObjectTypes
items.text:
A Method declared by an ObjectType gets its Python behavior when its Object is created:

  • @o6.call(...) associates the qualified UA BrowseName with an ordinary Python instance method.
  • Object creation selects the implementation from the Object's concrete Python type and stores it on the copied Method node.
  • A subtype that does not override the Method inherits the nearest base implementation.
  • A subtype may repeat @o6.call(...) on a differently named Python method; that nearest association wins.
  • Per-object state belongs directly on the Object; it does not require a separate Method callback.

o6 configures open62541 to copy every Method declaration into each Object instance. Mandatory and selected Optional Methods therefore have an independent Method NodeId and callback slot. Construction checks the concrete Python class first and proceeds upwards through its base classes only on a miss. Invocation uses the callback already stored on the Method. There is one dispatcher and no UA type query or global callback registry.

A dotted target binds behavior from a containing Object to a nested Method:

class CellImpl(CellType):
    @o6.call("controller.reset")
    def resetController(self, mode):
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD,)

The target is a path of generated Python member names. It is resolved once when the containing Object finishes and stored directly on that instance's Method node together with its containing Object. Calls never browse the address space, and instances remain independent.

The same simple rule decides every read, write, and call callback during construction. First, search the concrete implementation type and then its base types; copy the first matching callback onto the concrete target node. Then apply dotted paths as containing Objects finish, replacing that slot. Nested Objects finish before their containers, so an outer path targeting the same node is applied last. Invocation performs no type or path lookup.

Optional Methods follow the same rule. Enabling one creates an independent Method node from its declaration. An ordinary server Method retains its construction Object and dot lookup through that Object returns the Method node itself. A parentless Method, or the same Method reached through an additional Server.addReference edge, uses a lightweight bound value for that call.

items.title: Method resolution
items.text:
Every Method node has at most one Python callback. There is no separate "override" and "default" callback:

  1. Search the Object's concrete Python type and then upwards through its base types; store the first matching @o6.call(...) implementation on the Method.
  2. Apply dotted paths as the instance tree finishes; each path replaces the callback on its concrete target Method.
  3. At invocation, call the stored callback or return BAD_NOT_IMPLEMENTED.

Server.implement(method, call=callback) sets the one callback on exactly the given Method node. Passing None clears it; class and path resolution are not repeated. Changing a class or ObjectType declaration affects future instances, not Method nodes already created.

class ConnectionManagerImpl(fx_cm.objtypes.ConnectionManagerType):
    @o6.call("ns=fx_cm;EditConnectionConfigurationSets")
    def edit_sets(self, action, sets):
        ...

class AuditedConnectionManagerImpl(ConnectionManagerImpl):
    @o6.call("ns=fx_cm;EditConnectionConfigurationSets")
    def edit_sets_with_audit(self, action, sets):
        ...

The second decorator deliberately changes the Python implementation name. If the name stays edit_sets, an ordinary undecorated Python override is enough. Two decorators on the same class may not target the same qualified UA Method; class creation reports both competing Python names. Misspelled targets are reported as unknown instead of becoming silently unreachable implementations.

items.title: Variables
items.text:
@o6.variabletype(ns="demo", nodeId="ns=demo;i=1001", dataType=o6.Double)
class TemperatureType(o6.ns.ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType):
    @o6.read
    def _read(self, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, self.device.currentTemperature)

    @o6.write
    def _write(self, value, *, range, session):
        if value.value < 0:
            return (o6.StatusCode.BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE,)
        self.device.currentTemperature = value.value
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD,)

A read callback has the signature (self, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp) -> (StatusCode, value). A Bad status is returned alone. A successful result has exactly one Python value, converted using the Variable's declared datatype, or an o6.DataValue when timestamps and picoseconds must be supplied explicitly.

A write callback has the signature (self, value, *, range, session) -> (StatusCode,). value is the requested o6.DataValue. Read and write callbacks may also be async def; they keep the same arguments and result tuples as synchronous callbacks.

An async call, read, or write callback runs in an asyncio Task from its initial state. o6\Python leaves the native operation pending until the Task finishes, including when the callback returns without awaiting. Use an ordinary def callback for immediate synchronous completion. Native cancellation, including server cleanup, cancels the Task and its current await.

Synchronous callback dispatch rejects recursion with BadInvalidState. A Variable cannot re-enter the same read or write callback, and a Method cannot re-enter the same concrete Method node. The invoking Object is irrelevant to this check. Any nested callback on the same Variable is rejected, including a read calling write or a write calling read. Independent nodes are unaffected. Suspended async callback execution is not guarded after the callback has returned to the native dispatcher.

The decorators return the original methods. A Python subtype overrides _read or _write normally and needs no second decorator. Application state belongs directly on the Variable; there is no callback registration context.

items.title: Implementing an existing companion type
items.text:
Generated companion modules describe the UA interface and remain unchanged. Define behavior in an undecorated subclass and bind the pair explicitly to one server:

from o6.ns.vendor.objtypes import MotorType
from o6.ns.vendor.vartypes import TemperatureType

class TemperatureImpl(TemperatureType):
    @o6.read
    def _read(self, **kwargs):
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, self.device.temperature)

class MotorImpl(MotorType):
    temperature: TemperatureImpl

    @o6.call("Start")
    def start(self):
        return self.backend.start()

server.ns.append(o6.ns.vendor)
server.implement(MotorType, MotorImpl)

The binding is stored on the MotorType node in that server's own nodestore. Since every server owns a distinct type node, the binding is naturally server-specific and needs no separate registry. Register it before accepting node creation. Objects subsequently created through Server.addObject, native APIs, or a client's AddNodes request are exposed as MotorImpl; the global node constructor applies its member annotations and decorators after native type instantiation has completed. Its early phase creates selected member implementations first; its normal phase runs __init__ once and installs callbacks after the complete Mandatory subtree exists.

The binding matches that exact UA TypeDefinition. Register companion subtypes explicitly with their own implementation classes. Passing None restores the declaration's own Python type for future instances without changing existing Objects or Variables:

server.implement(MotorType, None)

For direct Python construction, instantiate MotorImpl(...). Calling MotorType(...) explicitly retains the generated Python class; the server binding is for nodes entering through native type instantiation.

Member implementations stay scoped. The annotation above makes motor.temperature a TemperatureImpl, but an independently created TemperatureType uses its generated Python class. Bind that separately when global behavior is wanted:

server.implement(TemperatureType, TemperatureImpl)

The first argument must be a generated or decorated ObjectType/VariableType; the second must be its undecorated subclass. Repeating the same pair is harmless. A competing pair on the same server is rejected. The binding does not publish a UA subtype or change any companion metadata.

Normal Python __init__ is also called for nodes originating in native code or over AddNodes. The node is already complete before the initializer runs in both paths; super().__init__() only continues ordinary Python initializer inheritance. An AddNodes request carries no Python-only arguments, so a class registered with Server.implement must provide defaults for such arguments or obtain dependencies from server/node state.

An Object implementation can select a Python-only implementation class for an inherited Variable member:

class TemperatureImpl(TemperatureType):
    @o6.read
    def _read(self, **kwargs):
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, self.device.currentTemperature)

class MachineImpl(vendor.objtypes.MachineType):
    temperature: TemperatureImpl

This changes only the concrete Python class. The Variable keeps its standard UA TypeDefinition and all address-space metadata. The same annotation rule composes through nested Object implementations.

For an inherited Optional UA member, temperature: TemperatureImpl includes the member in every instance constructed as that implementation, whereas temperature: TemperatureImpl | None leaves it optional. The UA declaration and its ModellingRule remain unchanged.

A member-specific callback can instead be installed when an Object is constructed:

class MachineImpl(vendor.objtypes.MachineType):
    @o6.read("parameterSet.temperature")
    def _read_temperature(self, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, self.device.readTemperature(range))

    @o6.write("parameterSet.temperature")
    def _write_temperature(self, value, *, range, session):
        self.device.writeTemperature(value.value, range)
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD,)

The string uses Python member names. When the containing Object finishes, o6 resolves it once and stores the callable with its containing Object in that concrete Variable direction, replacing behavior copied from its VariableType. Nested Objects finish before their containers, so an outer path targeting the same Variable is applied last. Every operation keyword, including range, is forwarded unchanged; invocation does not traverse the path. Missing paths and non-Variable targets fail construction.

range is None for a complete value or a tuple of stop-exclusive Python slices. For example, OPC UA range 2:5 becomes (slice(2, 6),). session is an o6.Session for client operations and None for internal operations.

items.title: Runtime Variable overrides
items.text:
Read and write can be overridden independently on one Variable or for a VariableType and its subtypes:

server.implement(TemperatureType, read=type_read)
server.implement(machine.temperature, read=instance_read)

During construction, each direction is copied from the nearest server-local or Python VariableType implementation. A path decorator then replaces the same concrete slot during Object finish. Keyword arguments replace individual slots:

server.implement(machine.temperature, read=None)
server.implement(TemperatureType, read=None)

Removing the final callback from a concrete Variable needs an explicit whole-node choice. Positional None repeats construction-time resolution; a positional value switches to native storage without calling the old read callback:

server.implement(machine.temperature, None)
server.implement(machine.temperature, o6.Double(20))

Changing a VariableType callback affects future Variables only. Reset uses the type and containing-object behavior that apply when reset is requested.

The stored read and write slots select the value source together. If neither slot is present, the Variable uses its native stored value. If a read slot is present, the Variable uses Python callbacks; without a write slot it is read-only. A write slot without a read slot is rejected because open62541 callback value sources must be readable.

Variable call syntax uses exactly that resolved source. variable() performs a normal Value read and variable(value) performs a normal Value write; neither form bypasses callbacks to reach native storage.

Once a Variable becomes callback-backed, its callbacks own the value state; o6 does not keep a shadow value.

Native Variables with a concrete datatype always have a value. When none is provided during creation, open62541 supplies a zero-initialized scalar or a typed empty array. A truly empty value is legal only for BaseDataType (Variant), which is the datatype normally used by BaseVariableType.

items.title: ObjectType and VariableType initialization
items.text:
@o6.objecttype(ns="demo", nodeId="ns=demo;i=1001")
class MachineType(o6.ns.ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    def __init__(self, *, device, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.device = device

    def __del__(self):
        self.device.close()

Declared ObjectTypes and VariableTypes use ordinary Python construction. Their __new__ completes OPC UA node construction first, then invokes the application initializer on the fully usable node. super().__init__(...) is therefore only the normal cooperative Python initializer call; it performs no OPC UA work. Initializers inherit through the Python type hierarchy normally.

Python finalization is inherited normally as well. The server's nodestore reference keeps the Python object alive while the OPC UA node exists. After the node is removed, any remaining Python references may delay __del__, so use it for Python-owned resources rather than protocol actions that must occur at the exact instant of OPC UA deletion.

items.title: Calling the API from callbacks
items.text:
A synchronous SDK callback keeps immediate local results: value = node() works when the operation completes inline. If the operation needs more work on the same event loop, it returns an awaitable without blocking. A callback that needs that result before continuing must use async def and await. This rule also applies when a synchronous callback is invoked inside an async operation. Async callbacks and tasks started by callbacks always use the async contract; ordinary synchronous helpers called by an async task also use it.

async def read(node, **kwargs):
    value = await other_variable()
    return o6.StatusCode.GOOD, o6.DataValue(value=value)

Node creation helpers and dynamic child navigation follow the same async rule. Existing async code that used immediate local results must now add await. Metadata properties, Python constructors, and synchronous configuration APIs remain ordinary Python operations.

items.title: Declared types
items.text:
The declarative route describes the model once, as Python classes, and lets the server build the nodes. A namespace module is an ordinary Python module that calls o6.ns.namespace(...) at the top and defines decorated classes below it:

# plant.py
from typing import Optional

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace("plant", uri="http://example.org/Plant/", version="1.0")

@o6.enumtype(ns="plant", description="Machine state")
class MachineState:
    IDLE = 0
    RUNNING = 1
    FAULT = 2

@o6.variabletype(ns="plant", dataType=o6.Double, valueRank=o6.ValueRank.SCALAR)
class TemperatureType(ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType):
    engineeringUnits: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(dataType=str)
    )
    highLimit: Optional[ns0.vartypes.PropertyType] = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(dataType=float)
    )

@o6.objecttype(ns="plant", nodeId="ns=plant;i=1001", browseName="MachineType")
class MachineType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    state: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(dataType=MachineState)
    )
    temperature: TemperatureType = o6.hasComponent(TemperatureType())
    reset: o6.node.MethodNode = o6.hasComponent(
        o6.call(
            browseName="ns=plant;Reset",
            inputArgs=[ns0.datatypes.Argument(
                name="mode", dataType=o6.Int32, valueRank=o6.ValueRank.SCALAR)],
            outputArgs=[ns0.datatypes.Argument(
                name="ok", dataType=o6.Boolean, valueRank=o6.ValueRank.SCALAR)],
        )
    )

The server publishes it, and from then on the classes are the API:

import o6
import plant

server = o6.Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(plant)
server.start()

machine = plant.MachineType(
    parent=server.objectsNode,
    browseName="M-101",
    nodeId="ns=plant;i=5001",
    values={"state": int(plant.MachineState.RUNNING)},
)

machine.state()                    # 1
machine.temperature(23.5)
machine.temperature.engineeringUnits()

server.ns.append(module) registers every namespace the module declared (from its __NAMESPACES__ metadata) and then injects its decorated nodes. Appending the same module twice is a no-op. A module that mixes already-published namespace URIs with new ones is rejected, and when a URI is already published only the index alias is added — one address space holds one release of a given namespace URI. For a single-file script, server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__]) works, though a separate importable module is preferable because a client process can import the same module and decode the types.

The decorators themselves — @o6.datatype, @o6.enumtype, @o6.referencetype, @o6.variabletype, @o6.objecttype, field metadata, declaration order, NodeId allocation, and values= seeding — are the subject of Writing a Nodeset in Python. Packaged companion specifications (DI, IA, and friends) are appended the same way and are covered in Using Nodesets. The rest of this chapter covers the parts that belong to the server rather than to the model.

items.title: Declared type instance ownership
items.text:
Calling an @o6.objecttype or @o6.variabletype class creates either a live server node or an ordinary declaration instance. The optional server argument is resolved in this order:

  1. An explicit server=<Server> selects that server. An explicit server=None forces a declaration instance.
  2. A live parent node selects the server that owns that node. A conflicting explicit server is rejected.
  3. A declaration parent produces another declaration.
  4. Calls made while a registered Python namespace module is being evaluated remain declarations; server.ns.append(module) materializes them later.
  5. Otherwise, exactly one live server in the Python process is inferred.
  6. With no live server, the result is a declaration. With multiple live servers, construction is ambiguous and raises TypeError; pass server= explicitly.

A bare NodeId does not identify a server. It therefore relies on the unique live-server rule — and server.objectsNode is a NodeId, not a node handle:

import o6

server = o6.Server()

# The only live server is inferred even though objectsNode is a NodeId.
motor = MotorType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="Motor")

# Always a normal declaration instance, regardless of live servers.
declaration = MotorType(server=None)

With a second live server in the process, the same call fails with cannot infer server: multiple live servers exist; pass server=<server> or server=None explicitly. Pass server=server and it succeeds again.

Namespace declarations remain ordinary Python objects even if a server exists:

import sys

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(shortname="plant", uri="urn:example:plant")
motors = ns0.objtypes.FolderType(parent=ns0.instances.objects, browseName="Motors")
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])

items.title: Views
items.text:
Views are address-space instances, so they are declared with the o6.view factory rather than a class decorator:

productionView = o6.view(
    nodeId="ns=plant;i=5001",
    browseName="Production",
    containsNoLoops=True,
)

The default parent is the standard Views folder and the default reference is Organizes. Server selection follows the same rules as other declared instances: pass server= explicitly, let a live parent or the sole live server select it, or use server=None to retain the declaration for a later server.ns.append(module) call. references=[...] attaches existing declarations to the View, and the remaining arguments (displayName, description, eventNotifier, writeMask, rolePermissions, accessRestrictions) map onto the corresponding attributes.

For a View created at runtime rather than declared in a model, use server.addView.

items.title: Type child relationships
items.text:
Children of an @o6.variabletype or @o6.objecttype are defined as node instances first, then linked with one of two camel-case identity helpers:

_name = ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(dataType=o6.String, browseName="Name")
_controller = ControllerType()
_reset = o6.call()

@o6.objecttype(nodeId="ns=plant;i=1001", browseName="MachineType")
class MachineType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    name: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(_name)
    controller: ControllerType = o6.hasComponent(_controller)
    reset: o6.node.MethodNode = o6.hasComponent(_reset)

hasProperty and hasComponent each take exactly one existing instance and preserve its static type: an input of type T returns T. They work for Variables, Objects, Methods, and their subtypes.

Beyond those two, o6.organizes, o6.hasEventSource, o6.hasNotifier, o6.hasOrderedComponent, o6.hasAddIn, o6.hasInterface, o6.hasCondition, o6.generatesEvent, and o6.hasEncoding cover the remaining standard hierarchies. Each has an inverse form — o6.propertyOf, o6.componentOf, o6.organizedBy, o6.eventSourceOf, o6.notifierOf, o6.orderedComponentOf, o6.addInOf, o6.interfaceOf, o6.isConditionOf, o6.generatedBy — that points the reference the other way. For a custom ReferenceType, o6.reference(instance, SomeReferenceType) links through it, and the three-argument form o6.reference(source, SomeReferenceType, target) adds an edge between two live nodes immediately.

Optionality belongs to the relationship and is inferred exclusively from Optional[T]:

_componentName = ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(dataType=o6.LocalizedText)
componentName: Optional[ns0.vartypes.PropertyType] = o6.hasProperty(_componentName)

# The instance can also be left undefined.
documentation: Optional[ns0.vartypes.PropertyType] = o6.hasProperty(None)

Node constructors describe the node itself. They do not accept an optional argument.

items.title: Type interfaces
items.text:
An ObjectType or VariableType implements OPC UA InterfaceTypes through the decorator's interfaces argument:

@o6.objecttype(
    nodeId="ns=plant;i=1001",
    browseName="MachineType",
    interfaces=[IMaintainableType, ns0.objtypes.IOrderedObjectType],
)
class MachineType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    pass

Interface markers are abstract ObjectTypes derived from ns0.objtypes.BaseInterfaceType. Interfaces are OPC UA type metadata, not Python mixins: they do not enter the implementing class's MRO and their members are not copied into its class body. The server adds the HasInterface references after all types in the module exist. Mandatory interface members are then instantiated according to the normal OPC UA type-instantiation rules.

Properties owned directly by a DataType or EnumType are constructed before the type and passed through the decorator's children argument:

_enumStrings = ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
    browseName="EnumStrings",
    value=[o6.LocalizedText("OFF"), o6.LocalizedText("ON")],
    dataType=o6.LocalizedText,
    valueRank=1,
)

@o6.enumtype(ns="plant", nodeId="ns=plant;i=1200", browseName="Mode")
class Mode(ns0.datatypes.Enumeration):
    enumStrings: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(_enumStrings)
    OFF = 0
    ON = 1

The relationship is declared on the type class, like other type children. o6.hasProperty also keeps the linked node out of Python's enum member table. These children are injected beneath the DataType node; they are not emitted as free-standing instances with an explicit parent NodeId.

items.title: Events
items.text:
Emit immediately with server.createEvent(...) (also available as server.emitEvent(...)), or construct a reusable Python draft with o6.Event:

event = o6.Event(
    server,
    eventType=ns0.objtypes.BaseEventType,
    source=server.serverNode,
    message="Production started",
    severity=200,
)
event["/BatchId"] = "B-1042"
eventId = event.trigger()

Field keys are event-filter path strings such as /BatchId, or QualifiedName values when a default namespace is needed. Explicit fields use open62541's fast event-field map. An Event is a mutable mapping, so dict(event), len(event), del event[key], and iteration all work, and its eventType, source, message, severity, and fields attributes can be reassigned between triggers.

An existing object node can additionally supply the payload. Fields absent from the explicit map are then resolved from that instance:

event.eventInstance = machineEventInstance
event.trigger()

Resolution order is explicit event.fields, then eventInstance, then the standard BaseEventType defaults. trigger() returns the generated 16-byte EventId.

This follows C's field precedence even for EventType and SourceNode: a stored property, including a null NodeId on a newly created instance, wins over the corresponding emission argument. Populate these properties when preparing the instance, or override them in fields. If the properties are absent, the SDK uses the emission arguments. For example:

machineEventInstance.EventType(o6.NodeId(MyEventType))
machineEventInstance.SourceNode(o6.NodeId(pump))
pump << machineEventInstance

createEvent emits without a draft and returns the EventId, matching C's UA_Server_createEvent. emitEvent is an alias for the same operation:

eventId = server.createEvent(
    ns0.objtypes.BaseEventType,
    source=server.serverNode,
    message="Shutdown requested",
    severity=500,
)

Both validate severity against the OPC UA range and raise ValueError outside 1..1000. source defaults to the Server object, so server.createEvent(message="...") is a valid minimal call. To subscribe directly to a custom source, enable its EventNotifier SubscribeToEvents bit. Events also reach the standard Server object.

o6.Event(server, ...) constructs the draft directly without emitting or accessing the address space. createEvent, emitEvent, and trigger() return MaybeAwaitable[bytes]; callers on another asyncio loop must await the result.

items.title: Inferring the event type
items.text:
eventType defaults to None. The type argument passed to the SDK is selected in this order: explicit eventType, then eventInstance's HasTypeDefinition when supplied, otherwise source's declared GeneratesEvent target. Field resolution still follows the precedence described above.

When the source type has exactly one GeneratesEvent reference to an EventType, that EventType is used:

@o6.objecttype(ns="plant", browseName="PumpFaultType")
class PumpFaultType(ns0.objtypes.BaseEventType):
    pass

@o6.objecttype(ns="plant", browseName="CavitationFaultType")
class CavitationFaultType(ns0.objtypes.BaseEventType):
    pass

@o6.objecttype(ns="plant", browseName="PumpType")
class PumpType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    pass

server.addReference(
    source=o6.NodeId(PumpType),
    reftype=ns0.reftypes.GeneratesEvent,
    target=o6.NodeId(PumpFaultType),
)
pump = PumpType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="Pump1")

eventId = server.createEvent(source=pump, message="Cavitation detected")
# eventType resolved to PumpFaultType, no eventType= needed

A type that declares no GeneratesEvent target falls back to BaseEventType — the server.createEvent(message="...") example above resolves this way, since the Server object's own type declares none. A type that declares more than one GeneratesEvent target cannot be inferred and raises ValueError naming the ambiguity:

@o6.objecttype(ns="plant", browseName="ValveType")
class ValveType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    pass

server.addReference(
    source=o6.NodeId(ValveType),
    reftype=ns0.reftypes.GeneratesEvent,
    target=o6.NodeId(PumpFaultType),
)
server.addReference(
    source=o6.NodeId(ValveType),
    reftype=ns0.reftypes.GeneratesEvent,
    target=o6.NodeId(CavitationFaultType),
)
valve = ValveType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="Valve1")

server.emitEvent(source=valve, message="which fault?")
# ValueError: cannot infer eventType: type ... declares more than one
# GeneratesEvent target; pass eventType= explicitly

Without an explicit type or event instance, a source with no type definition at all raises ValueError too. For either error, pass eventType= explicitly — it wins regardless of what source's type declares.

Inference reads the live information model, so a GeneratesEvent reference added or removed at runtime takes effect on the very next createEvent/trigger(). A reusable Event draft resolves the type on every trigger, so reassigning eventInstance or source takes effect next time. Inference leaves the draft's eventType attribute as None.

items.title: Firing an event from a Node handle
items.text:
An Object or View node handle can fire an event sourced at itself with <<, without navigating back to the owning Server and passing source= explicitly:

pump << o6.Event(server, message="Cavitation detected")

<< also accepts a plain mapping in place of an Event draft, as shorthand for a one-off event:

pump << {"message": "Cavitation detected", "severity": 400}

An existing event instance can be passed directly, or as eventInstance in an argument mapping or draft:

pump << machineEventInstance
pump << {"eventInstance": machineEventInstance}
pump << o6.Event(server, eventInstance=machineEventInstance)

The instance must be an Object of BaseEventType or a subtype on the same server. Its current fields are read on every emission; the node is neither modified nor deleted. To override a field for one emission:

pump << {
    "eventInstance": machineEventInstance,
    "fields": {"/Message": o6.LocalizedText("Override for this emission")},
}

All forms emit from pump, identical to server.createEvent(source=pump, ...). A reusable Event draft's own source field is left unchanged by <<, so the same draft can be fired against a different node afterward. << is only defined for Object and View nodes — the only NodeClasses OPC UA defines an EventNotifier attribute for — so variable << o6.Event(...) raises TypeError immediately, naming the reason; a node handle obtained from a Client also raises TypeError, since local event creation is server-only.

<< returns a MaybeAwaitable[bytes] like emitEvent, so on a server running on an external asyncio loop it must be awaited with parentheses:

eventId = await (pump << o6.Event(server, message="Cavitation detected"))

Without the parentheses, await pump << o6.Event(...) parses as (await pump) << o6.Event(...), not await (pump << o6.Event(...)) — await binds to pump alone, since << sits outside the grammar rule await requires.

items.title: Server-local monitored items
items.text:
A server can subscribe to its own nodes without a client session. This is how you drive internal logic from value changes and how you observe your own events.

def onChange(monitoredItemId, nodeId, attributeId, dataValue, context):
    print(nodeId, dataValue.value)

item = server.createDataChangeMonitoredItem(
    "ns=1;s=Temp",
    onChange,
    samplingInterval=100.0,
    context={"tag": "temperature"},
)

The callback may be a plain function or async def. context is handed back unchanged on every notification, timestamps= selects which timestamps the DataValue carries (default SOURCE), and monitoringMode= sets the initial mode. The returned object is an o6.subscription.MonitoredItem whose id is the server-local identifier; delete it with either form:

server.deleteMonitoredItem(item)          # or server.deleteMonitoredItem(item.id)

item.itemToMonitor identifies the monitored node and attribute; item.mode reports the accepted initial mode. item.requestedParams retains the creation parameters, and item.params includes the backend's revised sampling interval and queue size. These properties return independent snapshots, including nested filters. Editing a snapshot does not reconfigure the item.

Keep the handle returned by creation to inspect its metadata. Constructing MonitoredItem(server=server, monitoredItemId=id) provides an alias for validity checks and deletion, but its configuration properties raise RuntimeError because creation metadata is unavailable. Deleting through any alias or numeric ID, or cleaning up the native server, invalidates retained handles.

Operation Local support Create and inspect Supported for data changes and events item.delete() / server.deleteMonitoredItem(...) Supported on the owning server item.modify(...) Raises NotImplementedError; no public local backend API item.setMonitoringMode(...) Raises NotImplementedError; no public local backend API item.setTriggering(...) Raises NotImplementedError; no public local backend API

Unsupported operations raise immediately, including in async code, before scheduling work or changing state. Delete and recreate the item to change its configuration. Local items have no client subscription or publishing interval. Creation and deletion can be awaited from the server's loop or another asyncio loop; synchronous callers receive the result directly.

Event monitoring needs a filter with at least one select clause; createEventMonitoredItem raises ValueError without one. The easiest way to build a filter is the query parser:

eventFilter = ns0.datatypes.EventFilter.parse("SELECT /Message, /Severity, /SourceName")

item = server.createEventMonitoredItem(
    server.serverNode,
    lambda monitoredItemId, fields, context: print(fields),
    selectClauses=list(eventFilter.selectClauses),
)

whereClause= adds a ContentFilter alongside selectClauses=. For full control — a complete EventFilter, plus queueSize, discardOldest, clientHandle, samplingInterval, and monitoringMode — pass eventFilter= instead (not together with selectClauses=/whereClause=; that raises TypeError):

item = server.createEventMonitoredItem(
    server.serverNode,
    onEvent,
    eventFilter=eventFilter,
    queueSize=10,
)

One of selectClauses= or eventFilter= is required; omitting both raises ValueError.

The callback receives (monitoredItemId, fields, context), where fields is a dict[str, Any] keyed by selected event-filter paths, such as "/Message" or "/ConditionName/Id". For example, read the message with fields["/Message"].

For event items, itemToMonitor.attributeId is EVENT_NOTIFIER and params.filter retains the event filter. Events are driven by emission: samplingInterval is retained and revised by the backend but does not set an event polling period. clientHandle is retained but does not route local callbacks. queueSize and discardOldest control local notification buffering; there is no remote Publish request or client publishing schedule.

items.title: Timers
items.text:
Periodic work belongs on the server's event loop, not on a thread of your own:

def poll():
    server.write("ns=1;s=Temp", read_sensor())

callbackId = server.addRepeatedCallback(poll, 500.0)      # every 500 ms
server.changeRepeatedCallbackInterval(callbackId, 1000.0)
server.removeCallback(callbackId)

The callback runs on the loop thread, so the same rule as everywhere else applies: keep it short. Intervals are milliseconds.

items.title: Creating and running a server
items.text:
A server is created, configured, filled with nodes, and started. Nodes may be added before or after start(); only the configuration has an ordering requirement.

import o6

server = o6.Server(port=4840)
server.start()
# ... serve ...
server.stop()

The full constructor signature:

Server(
    port=4840,                      # TCP port to listen on
    logger=None,                    # Python logger for all server output
    loop=None,                      # asyncio event loop to use
    *,
    certificate=None,               # path, Path, or DER/PEM bytes
    privateKey=None,
    trustList=None,                 # trusted client certificates
    issuerList=None,                # intermediate CA certificates
    revocationList=None,            # CRLs
    secureOnly=False,               # offer no unencrypted endpoint
    acceptAllCertificates=False,    # skip client certificate validation
    applicationUri=None,
    accessControl=None,             # o6.AccessControl subclass instance
    allowNonePolicyPassword=False,  # permit passwords on an open channel
    rbacForAnonymous=False,         # enforce role permissions for anonymous sessions
)

server.running reports whether the networking layer is up, and server.endpointUrl gives the URL clients connect to:

print(server.running)        # False before start()
print(server.endpointUrl)    # opc.tcp://localhost:4840

Both start() and stop() are idempotent — calling start() on a running server or stop() on a stopped one does nothing. A stopped server can be started again.

The context-manager form is the one to prefer, because it stops the server even when the body raises:

with o6.Server(port=4840) as server:
    temperature = server.addVariable("Temperature", server.objectsNode, 22.5)
    print(temperature())

Synchronous start() and both context managers wait until the network listeners are ready and raise bind errors, for example if the port is occupied. On the server's running asyncio loop, start() schedules listener creation; use await server.waitReady() afterwards, or prefer async with server. Cancelling the readiness wait shuts down startup and closes its listeners.

server.loop exposes the owning asyncio.AbstractEventLoop as a read-only property, like client.loop. It is the loop supplied to the constructor, the running loop detected there, or a newly created loop when neither is available. Supplied and detected loops remain caller-owned; a loop created by the server is managed by the server and must not be closed directly by application code. Stopping the server does not replace the loop.

import asyncio

async def serve():
    server = o6.Server(port=4840)
    assert server.loop is asyncio.get_running_loop()
    server.start()
    try:
        await server.waitReady()  # must run on server.loop
        await asyncio.Event().wait()
    finally:
        server.stop()

stop() normally completes synchronously. A callback running on a background server's own worker loop starts shutdown without blocking and receives a Task; an async callback can use await server.stop() to wait for cleanup. The worker exits after that task completes. Restart from outside the worker after shutdown.

If a server is garbage-collected while still running, __del__ stops it and releases the native resources. That is a safety net, not a plan: hold the server in a variable for as long as it should serve, and stop it explicitly.

items.title: Well-known entry points
items.text:
Three properties return the NodeIds every address space starts from:

server.objectsNode    # i=85, the Objects folder — the usual parent
server.typesNode      # i=86, the Types folder
server.serverNode     # i=2253, the Server object — the default event source

They are o6.NodeId values, not node handles. That distinction matters exactly once, in Declared type instance ownership.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
server.config is the live configuration object. Most of it must be set before start(); the security-related setters and the history database explicitly raise RuntimeError if the server is already running.

The application identity is what a client sees in GetEndpoints and FindServers:

server.config.applicationUri = "urn:example:plant-server"

description = server.config.applicationDescription
description.applicationName = o6.LocalizedText("en-US", "Plant Server")
server.config.applicationDescription = description

applicationDescription returns a copy, so the read–modify–write above is the correct shape; mutating the returned object alone changes nothing.

server.config.logger is write-only and redirects all server log output to a Python logger. The same logger can be passed as Server(logger=...).

items.title: Security
items.text:
Certificates are passed to the constructor as file paths, Path objects, or raw DER/PEM bytes. Supplying both a certificate and a private key enables the encrypting security policies; the trust list decides which client certificates are accepted.

The certificate and private key must be supplied together and must not be empty. secureOnly=True requires both; invalid combinations raise ValueError during construction. The explicit applicationUri is preserved when encryption is configured and should match the URI in the server certificate.

from o6.util import createSelfSignedCertificate

key, cert = createSelfSignedCertificate(
    appUri="urn:example:plant-server",
    commonName="PlantServer@localhost",
)

server = o6.Server(
    port=4840,
    certificate=cert,
    privateKey=key,
    trustList=[client_cert],
    applicationUri="urn:example:plant-server",
)

With that configuration the server advertises a None endpoint plus Sign and SignAndEncrypt endpoints for every policy its build supports — typically Basic256Sha256, Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep, and Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss. A client that presents a trusted certificate can then pick any of them:

client = o6.Client(
    "opc.tcp://localhost:4840",
    certificate=client_cert,
    privateKey=client_key,
    trustList=[cert],
    securityMode=o6.SecurityMode.SIGN_AND_ENCRYPT,
    securityPolicy=o6.SecurityPolicy.BASIC256SHA256,
    applicationUri="urn:example:secure-client",
)

Log lines such as Could not add SecurityPolicy#EccNistP256_AesGcm with error code BadCertificateInvalid on startup are expected with an RSA certificate: the elliptic-curve policies need an EC key and are skipped.

acceptAllCertificates=True accepts every client certificate without validation. It exists for development and interop testing, and it defeats the purpose of the trust list — do not ship it.

Warning

secureOnly=True removes the None endpoint entirely. In the current build no client can then connect — including a correctly configured secure o6.Client — because endpoint discovery is performed over the None endpoint before the secure channel is opened; every attempt fails with BadSecurityPolicyRejected. Leave secureOnly at its default and restrict access through access control instead until this is resolved.

allowNonePolicyPassword=True permits UserNameIdentityToken authentication on an unencrypted endpoint. It is deliberately separate from access control, because it is a transport decision: without it the stack strips the username/password UserTokenPolicy from an insecure endpoint and logs a warning that the password would travel in the clear. Enable it for local testing only.

Neither access control nor these transport settings can be replaced after the server starts.

items.title: Lifecycle notes
items.text:
A few practical details for long-running processes.

Configuration is not hot-swappable. Security settings, access control, and the history database all raise RuntimeError once the server is running. Address space changes, by contrast, are fine at any time — adding and deleting nodes while clients are connected is normal operation.

Node handles keep their Python object alive through the server's nodestore reference for as long as the OPC UA node exists. After a node is deleted, remaining Python references may delay __del__, so use __del__ for Python-owned resources rather than protocol actions that must happen at the instant of deletion.

Server names are assigned internally as server0, server1, … and are reserved: a Client(name="server1") is rejected. The live-server registry that declarative construction consults holds weak references, so a server becomes invisible to inference as soon as your last reference goes away — which is another reason to keep it in a variable.

Stopping a server keeps its event loop alive so that later synchronous configuration calls still work; the loop is closed when the object is finalized. A stopped server can be restarted with start().

To observe start() and stop() from inside Python rather than waiting for the next call site to check server.running, register a handler on server.onLifecycleNotification — see Notification handler for the worked example. Handlers can also be added and removed while the server is running.

items.title: Notification handler
items.text:
open62541 exposes server-side application notifications — typed callbacks the C library fires at well-defined points during a server's life: when it starts, when a client opens a secure channel, when a session is created or activated, when a service call begins or ends, when a subscription or monitored item is added, when discovery registers another server, when an audit-worthy action occurs.

o6 exposes those points as a list-like, decorator-friendly registry directly on the server: server.on<category>Notification is a category of handlers you can read, call, decorate, replace, and clear.

items.title: Adding, removing, and clearing handlers
items.text:
A category is a list-like registry. There are four ways to add a handler:

@server.onLifecycleNotification             # decorator (most common)
def a(n): ...

def b(n): ...                               # declare function to be added as callback later, like:

server.onLifecycleNotification(b)           # call form
server.onLifecycleNotification = [a, b]     # wholesale replacement
server.onLifecycleNotification = [a]        # clears b, keeps a

And three ways to remove:

server.onLifecycleNotification.remove(a)  # remove one, raises if unknown
server.onLifecycleNotification.clear()    # remove all
server.onLifecycleNotification = []       # also remove all

Handlers fire in registration order. Multiple handlers per category are supported, which is useful when an application library wants to subscribe to a notification alongside user code without coordinating registration.

The category is a regular list for iteration too:

for handler in server.onLifecycleNotification:
    print("registered:", handler)

print(bool(server.onLifecycleNotification))     # False when no handlers
print(len(server.onLifecycleNotification))      # 0 when no handlers

items.title: Hot-swap
items.text:
Handlers can be added, removed, and replaced at any time — before start(), while the server is running, and after stop():

server = o6.Server(port=4840)
server.start()

# Register a handler while running
@server.onLifecycleNotification
def runtime_watcher(n):
    log.info("lifecycle: %s", n.lifecycle)

# Replace the whole list at any time
server.onLifecycleNotification = [runtime_watcher, another_handler]

# Or clear
server.onLifecycleNotification.clear()

server.stop()

A server with no registered handlers pays nothing for the mechanism.

items.title: Synchronous and asynchronous handlers
items.text:
A handler may be a plain function or async def. Async results are scheduled on the server's event loop, so the server never blocks waiting on a coroutine:

@server.onLifecycleNotification
async def on_stopped(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    log.info("lifecycle: %s", n.lifecycle)

Returning a coroutine object is enough — no await is performed by the server. Failures inside a coroutine are caught and logged the same way synchronous failures are.

items.title: Errors don't crash the server
items.text: An exception raised inside a handler is caught, logged, and swallowed — the same pattern other server-side callbacks (Method, Variable, MonitoredItem, access control) follow. The notification that triggered the failure is dropped, the surrounding handlers still run, and the server and the operation that triggered the notification continue.

items.title: Server Notifications
items.text: The categories below are the notifications a server currently exposes. Each one is registered the same way, via its own server.on<category>Notification registry.

items.title: Reading the payload
items.text:
Every notification the handler receives is an o6.Notification. Besides type and lifecycle, it carries payload — a read-only str -> Any mapping of that category's fields, keyed exactly as documented in each section below (e.g. "session-id", "subscription-id"). Access it like any mapping; a key documented for the category is always present, so a plain subscript is fine:

@server.onSessionNotification
def on_session(notification):
    session_id = notification.payload["session-id"]
    print(notification.type, session_id)

Values are already converted to the matching Python/o6 type — a NodeId stays an o6.NodeId, a RegisteredServer stays an o6.ns.ns0.datatypes.RegisteredServer, and so on — so no manual decoding is needed.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
Fires when the server starts and when it stops. The lifecycle category has no payload; the notification's lifecycle field names which point occurred: "started", "shutdown", "stopping", or "stopped". A normal run fires "started" once, and "stopping"/"stopped" once each on stop() — a deferred shutdown path may also fire "shutdown".

server = o6.Server(port=4840)

@server.onLifecycleNotification
def on_lifecycle(notification):
    ...

The handler runs on the server's event loop thread — blocking inside it blocks the whole server, so offload slow work to a queue or a thread pool.

Calling back into the server needs an async def handler. On the server's own loop server.emitEvent(...), server.browse(...), and every other MaybeAwaitable method return an awaitable; a plain def handler never awaits it, so the call does nothing beyond a RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited.

@server.onSessionNotification
async def on_session(notification):
    await server.emitEvent(message=f"session {notification.payload['session-id']}")

items.title: Secure Channel
items.text:
Fires once when a client opens a secure channel and once when it closes. Both calls carry the same securechannel-id, remote-address, and security-policy-url, since they describe the same channel at two points in its life. notification.lifecycle is None here — use notification.type (NotificationType.SECURECHANNEL_OPENED or SECURECHANNEL_CLOSED) to tell open from close.

server = o6.Server(port=4840)

@server.onSecureChannelNotification
def on_secure_channel(notification):
    ...

The payload:

Key Meaning securechannel-id The channel's numeric identifier. connection-manager-name Name of the underlying connection manager (e.g. "tcp-source"). connection-id The connection manager's own connection identifier. remote-address The remote peer's address, as reported by the network layer. protocol-version Negotiated OPC UA TCP protocol version. recv-buffer-size / send-buffer-size Negotiated chunk buffer sizes. recv-max-message-size / send-max-message-size Negotiated maximum message sizes. recv-max-chunk-count / send-max-chunk-count Negotiated maximum chunk counts. endpoint-url The endpoint URL the client connected to. security-mode The channel's MessageSecurityMode. security-policy-url The channel's security policy URI. certificate-type-id NodeId of the certificate type, if any. remote-certificate The remote peer's certificate bytes, if any.

items.title: Session
items.text:
Fires as a session moves through its lifecycle: created, activated, deactivated (unbound from its secure channel), and closed. A plain client connect/disconnect round-trip fires all four, in that order. notification.lifecycle is None here — use notification.type to tell created/activated/deactivated/closed apart.

server = o6.Server(port=4840)

@server.onSessionNotification
def on_session(notification):
    ...

The payload:

Key Meaning session-id The session's NodeId, matching Session.id as seen by an AccessControl hook on the same session. securechannel-id The owning secure channel's numeric identifier, 0 once the session has been deactivated. session-name The client-supplied session name. client-description The client's ApplicationDescription. client-user-id The authenticated user id of the session. locale-ids The client's requested locale ids.

items.title: Service
items.text:
Fires around every individual service request the server processes (e.g. Browse, Read, Write) — once when processing begins, once when it ends. A single call fires the handler twice: once with NotificationType.SERVICE_BEGIN, once with NotificationType.SERVICE_END, both carrying the same request-id. notification.lifecycle is None here.

This category fires at a much higher frequency than lifecycle, secure channel, or session — once per service call rather than once per connection — but a server with no handlers registered pays nothing for it.

server = o6.Server(port=4840)

@server.onServiceNotification
def on_service(notification):
    ...

The payload:

Key Meaning securechannel-id The secure channel the request arrived on. session-id The requesting session's NodeId, or the null NodeId if no session is bound to the channel. request-id Identifies the request/response pair — the same value on both the begin and end notification for a call. service-type NodeId of the request's DataType, e.g. o6.NodeId(o6.ns.ns0.datatypes.BrowseRequest).

items.title: Subscription
items.text:
Fires when a real client creates, modifies, or deletes a subscription. notification.type tells the points apart (NotificationType.SUBSCRIPTION_CREATED, _MODIFIED, _PUBLISHINGMODE, _TRANSFERRED, _DELETED); notification.lifecycle is None here.

server = o6.Server(port=4840)

@server.onSubscriptionNotification
def on_subscription(notification):
    ...

Note that Client.connect() creates its own internal subscription as part of connection setup, so a handler sees that subscription's created/deleted notifications too, alongside any subscription the application creates explicitly. Use subscription-id to tell them apart.

The payload:

Key Meaning session-id The owning session's NodeId, or the null NodeId if the subscription isn't bound to a session. subscription-id The subscription's identifier, unique within its session. publishing-interval Negotiated publishing interval in milliseconds. lifetime-count Publishing intervals without a Publish request before the subscription is deleted. max-keepalive-count Publishing intervals without notifications before a keepalive is sent. max-notifications-per-publish Cap on notifications per Publish response. priority Publishing priority relative to other subscriptions. publishing-enabled Whether the subscription currently publishes.
