o6 exposes the live state of a client's connection as a 3-tuple: (SecureChannelState, SessionState, StatusCode). The client.state property returns it on demand — there's no separate "callback registration" API, you poll it. For a dashboard that's running its own event loop, polling once per UI frame is enough; for a long-running service, a dedicated thread or asyncio task polling on a timer is the typical shape.

This page walks through state callback primitives:

  • Read client.state and understand what each field means.
  • Drive an asyncio task off the state tuple to react to drops.
  • Distinguish "channel renegotiated" from "session reactivated" from "totally lost".

Info

This tutorial expects the example server running in the background, and assumes you know how to create and connect a client, how to browse the address space, how to secure the connection, and how to name your client in Application description. The snippets use the distillery's DistillingSystem at ns=1;i=1000 to demonstrate the state transitions.

items.title: Read client.state
items.text:
client.state returns a tuple[SecureChannelState, SessionState, StatusCode]. The two *State fields are enums, and the third is the most recent status code the worker thread saw. If you followed the other tutorials to this point, the channel shoud be open and the session activated:

from o6 import Client, SecureChannelState, SessionState

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    channel, session, status = client.state
    print("channel :", channel)   # e.g. SecureChannelState.OPEN
    print("session :", session)   # e.g. SessionState.ACTIVATED
    print("status  :", status)

The interesting values for a connected client are:

  • SecureChannelState.OPEN — the secure channel is up and messages can flow.
  • SessionState.ACTIVATED — the OPC UA session is active and the server has accepted our user_identity_token.

client.connected is a convenience for "channel OPEN and session ACTIVATED":

print(client.connected)   # True

The full state machine has more values, but the common ones a dashboard cares about are:

SecureChannelState Meaning CLOSED No channel. Default before connect(). CONNECTING TCP / handshake in progress. OPEN Channel up. CLOSING Channel tearing down. SessionState Meaning CLOSED No session. Default before connect(). CREATED CreateSession request sent / acknowledged. ACTIVATED ActivateSession accepted — fully usable. CLOSING Session tearing down.

Anything other than OPEN and ACTIVATED means the client is not in a usable state.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    channel, session, status = client.state
    print(f"channel={channel.name}  session={session.name}  status={status}")
    print(f"connected: {client.connected}")

items.title: React to state changes in an asyncio task
items.text:
For a long-running service, a single asyncio task that polls client.state is the standard shape. When the session drops, log it; when it comes back, resume work. Let's look at the state of pur control loop of the distillery — make sure the client isn't "disconnected" and send a notification the moment the state moves off ACTIVATED.

import asyncio
from o6 import Client, SessionState

async def watch_state(client):
    last = None
    while True:
        _, session, status = client.state
        if session != last:
            print(f"session: {last} -> {session} (status={status})")
            last = session
        if session == SessionState.CLOSED:
            print("connection lost — stopping work")
            return
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    asyncio.run(watch_state(client))

If the distillery server restarts mid-run, the session goes ACTIVATED -> CLOSING -> CLOSED. If the network drops, the channel will hit a BadCommunicationError and the status code on the state tuple will record it. The watcher only has to compare against the last value and log the transitions.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import asyncio
from o6 import Client, SessionState

async def watch(client):
    last = None
    while True:
        _, session, status = client.state
        if session != last:
            print(f"{last} -> {session}  ({status})")
            last = session
        if session == SessionState.CLOSED:
            break
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    asyncio.run(watch(client))

items.title: Distinguish "channel renegotiated" from "session lost"
items.text:
SecureChannelState and SessionState move independently, which is useful when you're debugging connection issues. A common pattern:

  • channel changed but session is still ACTIVATED: the channel was renegotiated (cert renewal, transport refresh) and the session was kept alive across it. Nothing to do.
  • session dropped but channel is still OPEN: the OPC UA session expired or was closed by the server. You can still try to client.connect() again to reactivate it (the underlying channel survives).
  • Both CLOSED: the connection is fully gone. Reconnect from scratch.

For the distillery, if the server is restarting while the client is running, you'll see the session field transition through CLOSING -> CLOSED while the channel field lingers on OPEN for a moment, then itself goes CLOSING -> CLOSED. Catching the session drop first is the right place to surface "reconnecting…" in the UI.

import asyncio
from o6 import Client, SecureChannelState, SessionState

async def watch_both(client):
    last_ch, last_se = None, None
    while True:
        ch, se, status = client.state
        if ch != last_ch:
            print(f"channel: {last_ch} -> {ch}")
            last_ch = ch
        if se != last_se:
            print(f"session: {last_se} -> {se}  ({status})")
            last_se = se
        if ch == SecureChannelState.CLOSED and se == SessionState.CLOSED:
            print("fully disconnected — stopping watch")
            return
        await asyncio.sleep(0.25)

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    asyncio.run(watch_both(client))

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import asyncio
from o6 import Client, SecureChannelState, SessionState

async def watch(client):
    last_ch, last_se = None, None
    while True:
        ch, se, status = client.state
        if ch != last_ch or se != last_se:
            print(f"channel={ch.name}  session={se.name}  status={status}")
            last_ch, last_se = ch, se
        if ch == SecureChannelState.CLOSED and se == SessionState.CLOSED:
            return
        await asyncio.sleep(0.25)

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    asyncio.run(watch(client))

items.title: What's next?
items.text: • Load packaged companion specs — make o6.ns.di, o6.ns.ia, and the other bundled companion-spec types available on a client, so the type tree in the distillery's address space can be navigated from Python.

items.title: Load packaged companion specs
items.text:
The distillery's connections are stable now — the channel stays open, the session stays activated, the watchers log only the transitions you expect. Time to start using the types the server publishes, not just the values. The distillery's Kettle.Temperature is a Double, but the OPC UA type system also defines EUInformation, Range, ServerStatus, and many other standard types that an address space may reference. To use domain-specific types from Python, you load the matching companion spec into your client.

o6\Python includes packaged companion models under o6.ns.<shortname> (o6.ns.di, o6.ns.ia, …). Use print(o6.ns) to inspect the installed names and versions; import a module to access its declarations.

This page walks through three steps:

  • Import a bundled companion spec.
  • See what is registered in the process-wide namespace table.
  • Use the types and address nodes by their namespace URI.

Info

This tutorial expects the example server running in the background, and assumes you know how to create and connect a client, how to browse the address space, and how to secure the connection. The distillery itself doesn't use any companion-spec types directly, but the snippets use o6.ns.di (the Devices companion spec) as the example, since it's the closest match to "industrial equipment" and ships with o6 by default.

items.title: What are namespaces and companion specs useful for?
items.text:
OPC UA defines a fixed set of base types in ns0 — the namespace the spec itself publishes (http://opcfoundation.org/UA/, index 0 on every server). That covers the basics: Boolean, Double, String, the standard services (ReadRequest, WriteRequest, CallRequest), the standard event types (BaseEventType), the standard reference types (HasComponent, HasProperty, Organizes), and so on. But "industrial equipment" is broader than that: a vendor's pump exposes operating hours and motor current, a PLC exposes program organization units (POUs) and tag tables, an analyser exposes calibration certificates, and so on.

A companion spec is a nodeset published by an industry group or standards body that defines those domain-specific types in its own namespace. The OPC Foundation publishes a family of them — DI (Devices), IA (Industry Automation), I4AAS (Asset Administration Shell), Machinery, Robotics, Safety, … — each one a self-contained *.NodeSet2.xml file. o6\Python compiles the ones it ships into importable Python modules. The distillery is a simple example, so it doesn't use any of these, but a real industrial deployment almost always loads at least one.

In Python, two things matter:

  • The types become importable. Generated declarations are grouped by kind under o6.ns.<shortname>.datatypes, .objtypes, .vartypes, .reftypes, and .instances. You can construct datatype values, instantiate declared types, and pass them to the server — o6 does the encoding.
  • The nodes become addressable by shortname. The matching NodeIds — ns=di;i=..., ns=ia;i=..., … — work without hard-coding the server's numeric namespace index. Use nsu=<full-uri>;... when carrying a full namespace URI.

The catch is that a companion spec must be known to both sides for the type definitions to agree. A server that publishes ns=di;i=15889 as a TransferResultDataDataType only makes sense to a client that has the DI nodeset registered and knows how to decode that type. Importing it on the client is enough to encode values; reading values of that type from a server that does not publish the DI nodeset returns an opaque ExtensionObject instead of the decoded structure.

items.title: Import a bundled companion spec
items.text:
Each shipped companion spec is a module. Importing it registers the namespace in the process-wide table and makes its types available:

import o6
import o6.ns.di    # register the Devices companion spec

Info

Importing o6 pre-registers every shipped namespace. Accessing o6.ns.di lazily loads its generated category modules and declarations.

Unlike the retired XML-loading workflow, there is no per-client "append" step: registration is process-wide, and when a client connects it automatically maps the server's namespace indices to the registered URIs (see NodeIds and namespace info).

items.title: See what is registered
items.text:
The process-wide registry is the o6.ns singleton. Printing it shows every registered namespace with its shortname, URI, scope, version, and global index:

import o6
import o6.ns.di

print(o6.ns)
# o6.ns (count=...):
#   name   uri                               scope    version  pub_date  index
#   ns0    http://opcfoundation.org/UA/      ::global 1.05.06            0
#   di     http://opcfoundation.org/UA/DI/   ::global 1.05.0             2
#   ...

To iterate the entries programmatically, use filter(), which returns matching NamespaceModule singletons:

for namespace in o6.ns.filter():
    print(namespace.index, namespace.shortname, namespace.uri)

items.title: Use the types and address nodes
items.text:
Once the module is imported, declarations are available through their category modules:

import o6
import o6.ns.di
from o6 import Client

tr = o6.ns.di.datatypes.TransferResultDataDataType
print(tr)
i = tr()                        # create an instance of this type
print(i)                        # {sequenceNumber=0, endOfResults=False, parameterDefs=[]}
i.sequenceNumber = 42

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    # NodeIds addressed by URI/shortname work once connected — the server's
    # index for `di` is mapped automatically on connect.
    nid = o6.NodeId("ns=di;i=15889")
    print(nid.ns.shortname)     # "di"

In a Python REPL, category modules provide focused completion: for example, o6.ns.di.datatypes.<TAB> lists DI datatypes.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
• Load nodeset files — same shape, but for nodesets that aren't bundled (vendor specs, your own models).
  • NodeIds and namespace info — shortname → index resolution and reading namespace metadata off any NodeId.
  • Semantic discovery — navigate the distillery's address space by BrowseName rather than by NodeId, with the dotted client.objects.DistillingSystem.Kettle.Temperature() style.

items.title: Load nodeset files
items.text:
Companion specs that aren't bundled with o6\Python (vendor specs, your own models, …) come as *.NodeSet2.xml files. o6 does not parse nodeset XML at runtime — instead you compile the nodeset once into a Python module, then import that module exactly like a bundled companion spec.

This page walks through three steps:

  • Compile a nodeset XML file into a Python module.
  • Import the module to register it in the process-wide table.
  • Use the loaded namespace's types and NodeIds.

Info

This tutorial requires you to know how to create and connect a client and how namespaces work. It assumes a server is running on localhost as described in Set the Stage. Note the distillery server does not itself publish a custom nodeset — this page is about the general workflow for any server that does.

items.title: Compile a nodeset into a Python module
items.text:
The compiler lives in the source repository under tools/nodeset_compiler/ (it is not part of the PyPI wheel). Point it at the *.NodeSet2.xml, bind the base OPC UA namespace with --existing, give the namespace a shortname (the stable handle you'll use everywhere afterwards), and write the generated package with --out:

python -m tools.nodeset_compiler.backend_python path/to/MyCustom.NodeSet2.xml \
    --existing ns0=deps/UA-Nodeset/Schema/Opc.Ua.NodeSet2.Services.xml \
    --shortname custom \
    --out mycustom

The generated mycustom/ package follows the same shape as the bundled o6.ns.di / o6.ns.ia packages: it registers its namespace on import and defines one decorated class per type definition, split into datatypes, objtypes, vartypes, reftypes and instances.

If the nodeset builds on another one (most vendor specs depend on DI), declare each dependency with another --existing SHORTNAME=FILE so cross-namespace parents resolve:

python -m tools.nodeset_compiler.backend_python path/to/MyCustom.NodeSet2.xml \
    --existing ns0=deps/UA-Nodeset/Schema/Opc.Ua.NodeSet2.Services.xml \
    --existing di=deps/UA-Nodeset/DI/Opc.Ua.Di.NodeSet2.xml \
    --shortname custom \
    --out mycustom

Info

The legacy runtime-loading path (o6.ns.load("…​.NodeSet2.xml") / server.ns.load(...)) has been retired. Namespaces are declared by importing a compiled module, not by parsing XML at runtime. See Compiling Nodesets for the full workflow, including dependency chains and the batch pipeline.

items.title: Import the module
items.text:
Importing the generated module registers its namespace in the process-wide o6.ns registry and makes its declarations available — exactly like importing a bundled companion spec:

import o6
import mycustom          # your generated module

client = o6.Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840")

# Registered in the global table; addressable by shortname.
print(o6.NodeId("ns=custom;i=1").ns.shortname)   # "custom"

If you drop the generated directory into the o6/ns/ package as o6/ns/custom/, it also becomes reachable as o6.ns.custom with no import of your own — the same attribute style as the bundled specs. Otherwise import it by whatever module path you saved it under; the ns=custom;... resolution works either way once the module has been loaded.

As with bundled specs, there is no per-client "append" step: registration is process-wide, and a client maps the server's namespace indices automatically when it connects (see NodeIds and namespace info).

items.title: Use the types and NodeIds
items.text:
The generated module exposes its declarations, and the shortname works in any NodeId:

import o6
import mycustom
from mycustom import datatypes, objtypes, vartypes     # one per OPC UA type family
from o6 import Client

dt = datatypes.MyDataType          # the generated type class
value = dt()                       # construct an instance

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    nid = o6.NodeId("ns=custom;s=SomeNode")

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
• Load packaged companion specs — the bundled o6.ns.di / o6.ns.ia.
  • NodeIds and namespace info — shortname → index resolution and reading namespace metadata off any NodeId.
  • Loading & Using Nodesets — the full reference for the Namespace machinery.
  • Compiling Nodesets — every compiler flag, dependency chains, and the batch pipeline.

items.title: NodeIds and namespace info
items.text:
Every OPC UA node is identified by a NodeId. o6.NodeId accepts the standard i=, s=, and g= identifier forms. It also accepts ns=<shortname>;... for a registered shortname and nsu=<full-uri>;... for a full namespace URI.

A NodeId is really two things glued together: a namespace (which authority the identifier belongs to) and an identifier (the actual i=..., s=..., or g=... value inside that namespace). The same identifier string — i=2253 — means the same thing on every server, because it's defined in ns0, the OPC UA namespace that the spec itself defines. An identifier like i=1302 means different things on different servers, because that one belongs to the server-local namespace (ns=1), which carries the distillery's own nodes. The namespace is what gives the identifier its stable meaning across servers; the integer index is just a server-local slot.

This page walks through three steps:

  1. Build a NodeId in any of the supported string forms.
  2. Read namespace info (URI, version, index, …) off any NodeId.
  3. Use NodeIds with the high-level and Node APIs.

Info

For the bigger picture — what a namespace is, how URIs and indices relate, and why ns0 is fixed — see Namespaces. The short version is: ns0 is the namespace defined by the OPC UA specification itself, its index is always 0 on every server, and it carries the standard types and services (NodeId, ReadRequest, BaseEventType, DataChangeFilter, …) the protocol is built on.

items.title: Build a NodeId in any of the supported string forms
items.text:
The OPC UA spec defines three identifier types for NodeId:

  • i=... — numeric, e.g. "i=2253" for the Server object. Numeric identifiers in ns0 are assigned by the spec; numeric identifiers elsewhere are vendor- or server-assigned.
  • s=... — string, e.g. "ns=1;s=MyVariables.MyInteger". Useful for human-readable names that survive rebuilds of the address space.
  • g=... — GUID, e.g. "ns=1;g=ABC123...". Globally unique by construction; rare in practice.

Each is namespaced by an integer (ns=2;...), by an o6 shortname (ns=di;...), or by a full URI (nsu=http://opcfoundation.org/UA/DI/;...). The integer index is just a slot in the server's namespace array — what makes a NodeId portable across servers is the URI behind the index, not the index itself:

n0 = o6.NodeId("i=84")  # Root, in ns0 (the default when ns= is omitted)

The ns= parameter may be left, in this case ns=0 is assumed. i=84 is Root, the standard top of the address space, defined by the spec itself — every OPC UA server exposes it at the same NodeId because it lives in ns0.

n1 = o6.NodeId("ns=1;s=MyVariables.MyInteger")

ns=1 is also a special case. It's the server-local namespace — the distillery's own nodes live here — reserved for "this server" by Part 5, §6.3.1. For a server-local NodeId, n1.ns is just the integer index (1); it has no .uri, .version, or other metadata. To find the URI behind the server's ns=1, read it off the server's ApplicationDescription (see Application Description) — there is no other way to get it from a NodeId alone. For other registered namespaces, o6\Python lets ns= accept a shortname:

n2 = o6.NodeId("ns=di;i=15889")    # a DI type, looked up via the DI nodeset's shortname

The ns=<shortname> form resolves through o6.ns. Use nsu=<full-uri> when the full URI itself is the portable identifier. Numeric indices are server-local.

Tip

Hard-coded numeric indices can break when a server rebuilds and shifts DI, IA, or vendor namespaces. Use ns=di;... with a registered shortname or nsu=<full-uri>;... instead.

items.title: Read namespace info off any NodeId
items.text:
A NodeId doesn't just carry its own identifier — it also carries the resolved namespace. The .ns attribute returns the namespace's NamespaceModule singleton, not a separate metadata wrapper:

import o6
import o6.ns.di

n = o6.NodeId("ns=di;i=15889")
ns = n.ns
print(ns.shortname)         # "di"
print(ns.uri)               # "http://opcfoundation.org/UA/DI/"
print(ns.index)             # global numeric index, e.g. 7
print(ns.version)           # "1.05.0"
print(ns.scope)             # "::global"
print(ns.publicationDate)   # "" if the nodeset recorded none

The attributes come straight from the compiled namespace module. shortname is the registered handle ("di", "ia", "ns0", "custom", …); uri is the stable identity; index is the cached global slot (the same value on every server); scope marks where the namespace is valid; and version and publicationDate carry source metadata.

Note

ns.index is a cached slot that o6 allocates when the namespace registers, not a live read from a particular server. The number is stable across processes, but it's not guaranteed to match the index the server assigned (e.g. an admin who reordered the server's namespace array). For a stable, server-portable identifier, use ns.uri.

For ns0, the same call gives you the spec-defined namespace directly:

n0 = o6.NodeId("i=2253")           # the Server object, in ns0
print(n0.ns.shortname)             # "ns0"
print(n0.ns.uri)                   # "http://opcfoundation.org/UA/"
print(n0.ns.index)                 # 0 (always, on every server)
print(n0.ns.version)               # the spec version o6 was built against, e.g. "1.05.07"
print(n0.ns.publicationDate)       # the build date, e.g. "2026-07-30T00:00:00Z"

ns0 is special: its index is always 0 on every server, and the URI is always http://opcfoundation.org/UA/. The metadata you read back (version, publication date) is the version of the OPC UA spec that o6 was built against, not anything the server publishes.

items.title: Use NodeId's with the high-level and Node APIs
items.text:
Anywhere a NodeId is expected — client.read, client.write, client.call, client.monitor, … — you can pass a string, a parsed NodeId, or an o6.ns.<shortname>.<type> reference that resolves to one:

import o6
import o6.ns.di          # register DI so its type symbols are importable
from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    # String form — works for ns0 (default) and ns=1; everything else
    # benefits from a registered shortname or full namespace URI.
    v1 = client.read("ns=1;i=1204")   # Status.Setpoint

    # Parsed NodeId
    nid = o6.NodeId("ns=1;i=1204")
    v2 = client.read(nid)

    # ns0 type reference (ns0 is auto-loaded with `import o6`)
    event_type = o6.ns.ns0.objtypes.BaseEventType

    # Companion-spec type reference (the matching module must be
    # imported — `import o6.ns.di` is what registered it above).
    transfer_dt = o6.ns.di.datatypes.TransferResultDataDataType

Info

Most of the bundled companion specs (o6.ns.di, o6.ns.ia, …) are auto-loaded with import o6, so o6.NodeId("ns=di;...") works without an extra import o6.ns.di. Some smaller or vendor specs are deliberately not auto-loaded — for those, import o6.ns.<shortname> is required before ns=<shortname>;... will resolve. o6.ns lists what's currently registered.

The same NodeIds work as targets for the Node API when you navigate the address space with . or [].

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
• Load packaged companion specs — what o6.ns.di / o6.ns.ia give you out of the box.
  • Loading & Using Nodesets — the full reference for the Namespace object.
  • Namespaces — the spec-level story: URIs vs indices, the namespace array, why ns0 is fixed.

items.title: Semantic Discovery
items.text:
Picking up from Load packaged companion specs: you've been carrying NodeId strings around the distillery code — "ns=1;i=1302" for Kettle.Temperature, "ns=1;i=1204" for Status.Setpoint. Those NodeIds are correct, but they make the code brittle: if the server is rebuilt and the namespace indices shift, every NodeId literal has to be updated by hand. The last piece of the user story is to replace those literals with a semantic lookup — navigate the address space by BrowseName, with the dotted client.objects.DistillingSystem.Kettle.Temperature() style, and let o6 resolve the NodeId at the moment of the call.

This is the same operation Browse does — traverse the address space looking for a child — but exposed as a Python expression rather than a list of ReferenceDescription. The Node object you get back can be read, written, or called with (); the underlying NodeId is hidden.

This page walks through three steps:

  1. Navigate the distillery by BrowseName with client.objects.DistillingSystem.Kettle.Temperature.
  2. Read, write, and call on the resulting Node with the () syntax.
  3. Use [] for ambiguous BrowseNames and dir(...) for REPL discovery.

Info

This tutorial expects the example server running in the background, and assumes you know how to create and connect a client, how to browse the address space, and how to load packaged companion specs. The snippets use the distillery's DistillingSystem (ns=1;i=1000), Kettle (ns=1;i=1300), and Status (ns=1;i=1200) sub-objects as the running example.

items.title: Navigate by BrowseName
items.text:
The distillery's address space has a stable shape: under Objects you find DistillingSystem, and under DistillingSystem you find Kettle, Status, Identification, Distillate, Actuators, Events. The Node API exposes that as a dotted path:

from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    objects = client.objects                           # the Objects folder
    distilling = objects.DistillingSystem              # ns=1;i=1000
    kettle = distilling.Kettle                          # ns=1;i=1300
    temperature = kettle.Temperature                   # ns=1;i=1302

Names are matched case-insensitively against BrowseName — kettle, KETTLE, and Kettle all resolve to the same child. Each . triggers a server-side Browse for the named child on the current node. The result is a Node subclass (VariableNode, ObjectNode, MethodNode, …) depending on the child's NodeClass.

The Node API hides the NodeId — temperature.nodeId is the underlying integer/string, but you rarely need to touch it. Read, write, and call are all done on the Node object itself.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    temperature = client.objects.DistillingSystem.Kettle.Temperature
    print(temperature)                # ns=client1_ns1;i=1302
    print(type(temperature).__name__) # VariableNode

items.title: Read, write, and call on the resulting Node
items.text:
The () operator handles every interaction. The distinction is by argument shape, not by method.

Reading a variable value becomes a call with no arguments:

temperature = client.objects.DistillingSystem.Kettle.Temperature
print(temperature())               # e.g. 20.0

Writing the variable is a call with a single positional argument:

setpoint = client.objects.DistillingSystem.Status.Setpoint
setpoint(90.0)                     # writes the Value attribute

Reading a non-Value attribute uses the attr= keyword:

print(temperature(attr="BrowseName"))  # "Temperature"
print(temperature(attr="NodeClass"))   # "VARIABLE"

Writing a non-Value attribute uses both value= and attr=:

temperature(value="KettleTemp", attr="BrowseName")

Calling a method on an object is also () — pass the input arguments positionally. The parent object is picked up automatically:

distilling = client.objects.DistillingSystem
status, = distilling.Start()       # StatusCode, then any output args

The distillery's Start and Shutdown take no inputs and produce no outputs, so the destructure is just status, = .... The first element of the tuple is the StatusCode (see Call a method for the full shape).

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import o6
from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    # Read
    temperature = client.objects.DistillingSystem.Kettle.Temperature
    print("temperature:", temperature())

    # Write
    setpoint = client.objects.DistillingSystem.Status.Setpoint
    setpoint(90.0)

    print("browse name:", temperature(attr="BrowseName"))
    print("node class:", temperature(attr="NodeClass"))

    # Call a method
    distilling = client.objects.DistillingSystem
    status, = distilling.Start()
    print("start status:", status == o6.StatusCode.GOOD)

items.title: Disambiguate with [] and explore with dir(...)
items.text:
Two situations don't fit the dotted path cleanly:

  • Ambiguous BrowseNames. If more than one child of the same node has the same BrowseName (case-insensitively), the dotted form can't pick a single target. Use [] with a browse path — a /-separated string of <namespace-index>:<BrowseName> segments (see Node API syntax) — and it returns all matching targets for you to pick from. The distillery doesn't have any actually-ambiguous names (both its Level variables — Kettle.Level at ns=1;i=1301 and Distillate.Level at ns=1;i=1401 — sit under different parents, so the path /1:Kettle/1:Level is already unambiguous), but the mechanism is the same either way — index into the returned list:
matches = client.objects.DistillingSystem["/1:Kettle/1:Level"]   # a list, even with one match
kettle_level = matches[0]                                        # pick the target
print(kettle_level())
  • REPL discovery. When you don't know what children a node has, dir(node) runs a Browse and returns a list of the child names. Combined with <TAB> completion, it's the same workflow as the interactive browser in Browse but inside a Python REPL:
>>> dir(client.objects.DistillingSystem)
['identification', 'status', 'kettle', 'distillate', 'actuators', 'events', 'start', 'shutdown']

The list is fetched lazily on the first dir(...) and cached afterwards, so subsequent dir() calls are free.

Tip

In a Python REPL, dir(...) plus <TAB> completion is the fastest way to explore a server you don't know yet. The first dir(node) triggers a Browse; once you know the names, the dotted path does the rest.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    # Browse path navigation via []
    matches = client.objects.DistillingSystem["/1:Kettle/1:Level"]
    print(f"{len(matches)} match(es):")
    for m in matches:
        print(f"  {m}  ({m()})")

    # REPL discovery 
    print("children of DistillingSystem:", dir(client.objects.DistillingSystem))

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
• Node API syntax — the same syntax you just learned, viewed from the language-feature angle: the three shapes (., [], ()) and how they map to the high-level client.read / client.write / client.call.
  • NodeIds and namespace info — when you do need the NodeId (for logging, error messages, or handing off to a different system), this page shows how to get it back out of a Node and how shortnames resolve to indices on the server.

items.title: Low-level service calls
items.text:
If you need full control over a request — fill in every optional field, override a default, or capture the raw response — every service the o6 client supports has a serviceX method that takes a pre-built request object and returns a pre-built response. The high-level methods (client.read, client.write, client.call, client.browse, …) are thin wrappers over the same calls.

This page walks through the low-level basics:

  • Build a request object.
  • Call the corresponding serviceX method.
  • Read fields off the response.

Info

This tutorials requires you to know how to create and connect a client and how to use the high-level API for read / write and call. We assume a server is running on localhost as described in Set the Stage.

items.title: Build a request object
items.text:
Each service has a paired request type that lives in o6.ns.ns0. The request has the same fields as the spec's request message — required fields set, optional fields left at their defaults:

from o6.ns.ns0.datatypes import ReadRequest, ReadValueId

req = ReadRequest()
req.nodesToRead = [ReadValueId("ns=1;i=1204")]

ReadValueId accepts a plain NodeId string directly in its constructor for the simple case of reading the Value attribute — you only need to build it up field-by-field (attributeId=, indexRange=, dataEncoding=) when you're after something other than Value. Request types themselves (ReadRequest, WriteRequest, …) take no constructor arguments — build one with Type() and set its fields by attribute, as above.

items.title: Call the corresponding serviceX method
items.text:
The suffix of a serviceX method is the OPC UA service name. Pass the request, get the response back:

from o6 import Client

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    response = client.serviceRead(req)

The complete list of serviceX methods on the client mirrors the OPC UA service sets:

  • Discovery: serviceFindServers, serviceFindServersOnNetwork, serviceGetEndpoints
  • Node management: serviceAddNodes, serviceDeleteNodes, serviceAddReferences, serviceDeleteReferences
  • View: serviceBrowse, serviceBrowseNext, serviceTranslateBrowsePathsToNodeIds, serviceRegisterNodes, serviceUnregisterNodes
  • Attribute: serviceRead, serviceHistoryRead, serviceWrite, serviceHistoryUpdate
  • Method: serviceCall

Every serviceX method returns a MaybeAwaitable to be readily used in both sync and async contexts — add await in async code:

async with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    response = await client.serviceRead(req)

items.title: Read fields off the response
items.text:
The response object mirrors the spec's response message. Read the fields you care about the same way you read any Python attribute:

with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
    req = ReadRequest()
    req.nodesToRead = [ReadValueId("ns=1;i=1204")]   # Status.Setpoint
    response = client.serviceRead(req)

    # First check the service-level result code
    print(response.responseHeader.serviceResult)   # StatusCode.GOOD

    # Then read the per-node results
    result = response.results[0]
    print(result.status)         # StatusCode.GOOD
    print(result.value)          # e.g. 90.0

A non-Good responseHeader.serviceResult means the whole service call failed (e.g. the secure channel is in a bad state). A non-Good per-node status means only that node failed. The serviceX methods do not raise on either — they hand you the raw response and let you decide.

Tip

Start with the high-level API (client.read, client.write, client.call, …). Drop down to serviceX only when you've outgrown the wrapper — typically because you need a header field, an unusual parameter combination, or to debug a low-level status code.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
• Read / write value and Call a method — the high-level wrappers.
  • The Client API reference — full surface of every serviceX method.

items.title: Async Clients
items.text:
Client in o6 is dual-mode: the same connect() / disconnect() calls work from plain synchronous code, from inside an async coroutine, or from a thread that owns its own event loop. The only thing that changes between those worlds is whether you await the call and which event loop the client uses behind the scenes. This page walks through the async side of that story.

This page assumes you have read Connect / disconnect first — the basic construction and connect/disconnect cycle is covered there, and only the async-specific bits live here.

items.title: Awaiting connect() and disconnect()
items.text:
In async code, connect() and disconnect() are coroutines. You call them with await instead of blocking:

import asyncio
from o6 import Client

async def main():
    client = Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840")
    await client.connect()
    try:
        print(client.connected)   # True
        # ... do work ...
    finally:
        await client.disconnect()

asyncio.run(main())

If the body of try raises, the finally block still runs await client.disconnect(), which is the same contract as the synchronous with form — just spelled out longhand.

items.title: async with — the async context manager
items.text:
Client is also an async context manager. The async with block calls await client.connect() on entry and await client.disconnect() on exit, including on exceptions. This is the recommended shape whenever you're inside an event loop and have more than one or two operations to perform:

import asyncio
from o6 import Client

async def main():
    async with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840") as client:
        print(client.connected)   # True
        # ... do work ...

    # disconnected automatically here, even if the body raised

asyncio.run(main())

items.title: Controlling the event loop
items.text: Client runs a worker thread that holds an asyncio event loop. Every synchronous call (client.read(...), client.write(...), client.monitor(...), …) dispatches onto that loop and blocks the caller until the result is ready. The choice of which loop the worker uses is made at construction time, and you have several options.

items.title: Let o6 create one for you — the default
items.text:
When no loop is passed, the client creates its own loop, owns it, and tears it down on disconnect(). This is the right choice for plain scripts, notebooks that do not use asyncio at all, and one-off REPL experiments.

from o6 import Client

client = Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840")
# o6 created a fresh loop behind the scenes; you do not interact with it.

IPython / Jupyter: the same Client(url) constructor automatically detects the IPython environment and gives the client its own loop, so synchronous client.read(...) calls do not interfere with the IPython kernel's loop.

items.title: Pass an external loop you manage yourself
items.text:
Useful for long-running services that own an event loop and want to share it across many subsystems. o6 will not start or stop this loop — driving it is your responsibility. In a service, that usually means running it on a thread you own, after which the synchronous calls work exactly as they do with the default loop:

import asyncio
import threading
from o6 import Client

loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()
runner = threading.Thread(target=loop.run_forever, daemon=True)
runner.start()

client = Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840", loop=loop)
client.connect()
print(client.read("ns=1;i=1201"))   # Status/State

# ... later, when shutting down the service:
client.disconnect()
loop.call_soon_threadsafe(loop.stop)
runner.join(timeout=5)
loop.close()

The loop has to actually run for callbacks to arrive

If you hand over a loop that nobody drives, o6 falls back to running each synchronous call inline (loop.run_until_complete(...)), so connect(), read() and write() still return values. Anything that arrives between your calls does not: subscription callbacks, event callbacks and state-change callbacks are only delivered while the loop is running. Start the loop — on its own thread as above, or via run_until_complete around your own coroutine as in the next section — before relying on any of them.

Note that connect() is a normal function that blocks in the synchronous case, so it must not be wrapped in run_until_complete: by the time loop.run_until_complete(client.connect()) is evaluated, connect() has already run to completion and returned None. Either call it synchronously, as above, or await it from inside a coroutine running on that loop.

items.title: Use the currently running loop
items.text:
When you're already inside a coroutine and want the client to share the loop you're running on, hand it asyncio.get_running_loop(). This is the cleanest pattern for async services that interleave OPC UA calls with other async work:

import asyncio
from o6 import Client

async def main():
    async with Client("opc.tcp://localhost:4840", loop=asyncio.get_running_loop()) as client:
        state = await client.read("ns=1;i=1201")   # Status/State
        print(state)

asyncio.run(main())

items.title: Server Tutorials
items.text:
These tutorials walk through the server side of o6 by building one server, one concept at a time. The Foundation band builds one continuous project — a small distillery exposing an object hierarchy, live variables, and methods — and that project is the same distillery the client tutorials ultimately connect to. Everything after Foundation applies the same domain, but as separate techniques you would reach for on a real deployment — Patterns, Composition, Behaviour, and Production are not folded back into that one running example.

The pages build on each other in ascending complexity. Each one introduces one concept and leaves the server runnable, so you can leave it running between pages and watch the address space grow.

Start from the first page

The project state at the top of each page is the project state at the bottom of the previous one. If you skip ahead, the imports and identifiers in the snippets will not match what you have.

items.title: Building a distillery server
items.text:
Throughout the tutorials we build, one concept at a time, the same automated distillery: a still driven by a background simulation, exposing its state under Objects/DistillingSystem and accepting two writes — Operating (run / park) and Setpoint (target kettle temperature). On the way there we:

  • start with the smallest possible server, then grow the address space by hand — that's the whole Foundation band, and it's the one continuous project;
  • then work through the same handful of patterns the server examples walk through — an external data source, an asyncio server, and the declare/implement split for a Variable and for an ObjectType — each as its own small, self-contained aside rather than a further extension of the running distillery;
  • take a detour through the declarative alternative in depth — the same shapes as @o6.objecttype/@o6.variabletype/@o6.datatype classes, and custom ReferenceTypes — as a technique worth knowing once a model gets bigger than a handful of nodes;
  • attach write handlers, method implementations, events and timers once the hand-built data model is worth reacting to;
  • then take a second detour through access control, authentication, security policies, monitoring and history — everything a server needs before it is hosted on a real network, but not things this particular small distillery turns on.

The very last page — The distillery server — points back at Set the stage, which describes the two-file runnable project the Foundation band builds up to, and says plainly which bands are and aren't part of it.

items.title: Topics
items.text: The tutorials are organised around what you typically build on a server, moving from the smallest runnable program to a fully modelled, secured endpoint. The first two bands track the same order as the server examples, one page per example; everything after that goes further than the examples do.

items.title: Foundation
items.text:
1. Creating a server — create a Server, bind an endpoint, start it, stop it.
  2. Add a hierarchy — group nodes into a small hierarchy under Objects/.
  3. Add a variable — drop the first values into the right slots.
  4. Add a method — register a callable method, return values and StatusCode.

items.title: Patterns
items.text:
The same shapes as the S07–S10 server examples, each as its own small aside rather than a further extension of the running distillery.

  1. Values from an external source — a Variable whose truth lives in a Python model, pushed in with server.write(...).
  2. Running on asyncio — async with server:, await asyncio.sleep(...), and asyncio.run(...).
  3. Declare and implement a Variable — declare a Variable as a contract, implement its read/write in a separate class.
  4. Declare and implement an ObjectType — the same declare/implement split, for a Method.

items.title: Composition
items.text:
1. Declare an object type — turn the hand-built hierarchy into a Python class with @o6.objecttype, define components, instantiate.
  2. Declare a variable type — @o6.variabletype for typed values with their own DataType, ValueRank, modelling rules.
  3. Declare a reference type — custom ReferenceTypes for relationships beyond HasComponent / HasProperty.
  4. Declare a data type — @o6.datatype for a custom Structure / Enum used by your variables and methods.

items.title: Behaviour
items.text:
The data model is now in place; the next band is what makes it do something — the instance-level counterpart to the declare/implement classes in Patterns.

  1. Method implementations — install callbacks with Server.implement(method, call=...), sync vs async, error mapping.
  2. Variables with sources — install read and write callbacks with Server.implement(variable, read=..., write=...), validate, mirror.
  3. Server callbacks — startup, shutdown, periodic timers, retention cleanup.
  4. Events — the distillery's writable "event log" pattern, firing on state transitions, and when to graduate to real BaseEventType / emitEvent notifications.
  5. Timers and async loops — long-running background work, asyncio integration, cooperative cancellation.

items.title: Production
items.text:
Take the distillery from "demo" to "ready for production".

  1. Access control — roles — Role / o6.roles, default-deny, granting reading / writing / calling per node, role mappings for built-in roles.
  2. Access control — authentication — session authentication, user token policies.
  3. Security policies and endpoints — SecurityPolicy selection, encrypted endpoints, certificate management.
  4. Subscribe monitoring on the server side — server-local monitored items for housekeeping.
  5. Historical data — historizing=True, server.config.setHistoryDatabase(...) + server._register_historizing(...), real HistoryRead against buffered values, and the allowHistoryUpdate / allowHistoryDelete hooks.

The distillery page that finishes the project — 500_distillery_server.md — defers to Set the stage, which is the same server in runnable form: the Foundation band, built incrementally, plus the plain write-loop pattern from Values from an external source. Patterns, Composition, Behaviour, and Production are separate techniques applied to the same distillery, not part of that one running file — 500_distillery_server.md says so explicitly.

items.title: Beyond the tutorials
items.text:
The server manual collects the same topics as long-form narrative:

  • Server manual — the full narrative.
    • Lifecycle & configuration
    • Building the address space
    • Declared types
    • Implementing behaviour
    • Server callbacks
    • Events, monitored items & timers
    • Access control & roles
    • Operations & interoperability
  • API Reference — every public method and its signature.

items.title: Creating a server
items.text:
This is the first page of a small project: building an OPC UA server for an automated distillery, one page at a time. By the end of the Foundation band we'll have a server that reports on a still — temperature, batch state, a couple of settings an operator can change — and every later page in these tutorials either extends that same server or applies the same ideas somewhere else. It starts here, with the one thing every server needs before anything else: something listening on the network.

In o6, that something is an o6.Server. This page covers constructing one, starting it, stopping it, and the couple of properties worth knowing before we start adding anything to it.

items.title: What is a server, before it does anything?
items.text:
A server is a process that listens on a TCP port and speaks the OPC UA protocol once something connects: it answers questions about its address space — the tree of nodes it exposes — reads and writes values on request, and runs whatever background work we give it. The address space is what the rest of these tutorials spend most of their time building.

A server that has just been constructed doesn't do any of that yet. It exists, but it isn't listening, and its address space is still just the handful of standard nodes every OPC UA server carries:

from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
print(server.running)        # False — not yet listening
print(server.endpointUrl)    # opc.tcp://localhost:4840

Constructing a Server only configures it — port=4840 says where it will listen once asked to. Nothing is actually happening on the network until start() is called.

items.title: Start it, and stop it again
items.text:
start() opens the listening socket; stop() closes it. Between the two, the server accepts connections at the address server.endpointUrl reports:

import time
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
server.start()

print(server.running)        # True
print(server.endpointUrl)    # opc.tcp://localhost:4840

# ... serve ...
server.stop()
print(server.running)        # False

port defaults to 4840 — the port these tutorials use throughout, and the one OPC UA reserves for exactly this — so Server() alone would bind the same address as Server(port=4840). The rest of a server's configuration — certificates, access control, the application URI — is covered in later pages, once there's a reason to need it. Nodes can be added to the address space either before or after start(), so there's no ordering to worry about yet.

Left as it is, the process would exit the moment start() returns. A server is meant to keep running, so the usual next step is a loop that just waits, until something — usually Ctrl+C — tells it to stop:

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

That's a complete, if empty, server: listening at opc.tcp://localhost:4840, ready for a client to connect to, with nothing yet in its address space worth looking at.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
server.start()

print(f"Server running at {server.endpointUrl}")
print("Press Ctrl+C to stop.")

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

items.title: Letting the server manage its own shutdown
items.text:
Calling stop() by hand works, but it's easy to forget on an exception, or on an early return. Server is also a context manager, so with takes care of both ends of the lifecycle — start() on entry, stop() on exit, even if the body raises:

from o6 import Server

with Server(port=4840) as server:
    print(server.running)        # True
    print(server.endpointUrl)    # opc.tcp://localhost:4840

# stopped automatically here, even if the body raised

The tutorials from here on use whichever form fits the example better; both end up doing the same thing. Timers and async loops covers the asynchronous form, async with, for a server that runs on an asyncio event loop instead of a background thread.

Info

Forgetting stop() entirely isn't fatal — the socket and session state are still released when the server is garbage-collected — but it isn't something to rely on. An explicit stop() (or a with block) drains the listener and tears down the worker thread in a predictable order; garbage collection doesn't promise either.

items.title: Checking whether it's listening
items.text:
server.running is the one property to check when something isn't behaving as expected: True once start() has run, False again after stop(). It's a direct read of the listening socket's state, not a separate health check that could disagree with reality.

with Server(port=4840) as server:
    assert server.running
    # ... build the address space, do work ...

This is the check the rest of these tutorials fall back on after each step: if something isn't working, the first question is whether the server is actually running.

items.title: Three addresses worth knowing before we build anything
items.text:
Before adding a single node of our own, it's worth knowing the three that already exist. They're o6.NodeId values — addresses into the tree, not the data itself — and everything we build over the next few pages hangs off one of them:

server.objectsNode    # i=85, the Objects folder — where our nodes go
server.typesNode      # i=86, the Types folder — for declared types, much later
server.serverNode     # i=2253, the Server object itself

For the distillery, server.objectsNode is the one that matters for now — it's the standard Objects folder every OPC UA server publishes, and it's the parent every node we add from here on hangs off, directly or through folders nested underneath it. typesNode doesn't come up until we declare our own types, much later in these tutorials.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The server is listening, but ask it about its address space and there's nothing under Objects/ yet — the distillery doesn't exist. The next page starts building it: a folder skeleton with a place for everything the later pages will fill in.

  • Add a hierarchy — group nodes into a small DistillingSystem folder with sub-objects.
  • Server manual — the full lifecycle and configuration story.

items.title: Add a hierarchy
items.text:
The server from Creating a server is listening, but its address space under Objects/ is empty — only the standard nodes every OPC UA server carries are there. Before adding anything to it, it's worth deciding what the distillery's address space should actually look like, rather than growing it one node at a time as an afterthought. This page builds that shape: a DistillingSystem folder with six sub-objects — Identification, Status, Kettle, Distillate, Actuators, and Events — each one waiting for the values the next few pages will put inside it.

By the end of this page the address space matches the layout every later tutorial assumes:

Objects/
└── DistillingSystem/
    ├── Identification/    Name, Manufacturer, ModelNumber
    ├── Status/            State, Cycle, Operating, Setpoint
    ├── Kettle/            Level, Temperature, WashStart
    ├── Distillate/        Level
    ├── Actuators/         FillValve, DrainValve, Heater
    ├── Events/            EventCount, LastEventTime, LastEventMessage, LastEventState
    ├── Start              (Method)
    └── Shutdown           (Method)

items.title: A folder is just another node: addObject
items.text:
Server.addObject() adds an Object node — in practice, a folder — to the address space. Like addVariable (the next page), the first two positional arguments are the name and the parent, and nodeId= pins the address:

from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")

# `sys` is now a parent for everything else — including further folders.
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")

That single line gives us a folder, and the second line gives us a folder inside it — status ends up nested two levels under Objects/, not directly beneath it, because its parent is sys rather than server.objectsNode. That's the whole idea behind a hierarchy: each addObject call decides where one more branch attaches, and the address space grows from there.

Neither sys nor status carries a value yet — they're folders, not Variables. Values are what the next page adds.

Info

Every node class attaches to its parent with a fixed reference type — Object and Variable with Organizes, Method with HasComponent — chosen automatically, not something addObject/addVariable take as an argument. A different kind of edge is possible, but it means creating the node first and adding the reference separately with Server.addReference — a technique its own later page covers.

items.title: Putting it all together — the smallest meaningful hierarchy
items.text:
import time
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)

# Top-level folder
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")

# Nested folders inside it
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")

server.start()

A read of Objects/ now sees:

DistillingSystem (Object, ns=1;i=1000)
├── Status (Object, ns=1;i=1200)
└── Kettle (Object, ns=1;i=1300)

That's the first two layers of the distillery. The rest of this page just repeats the same call a few more times.

items.title: Building the rest of the skeleton
items.text:
The full skeleton adds four more sub-objects next to Status and Kettle — Identification, Distillate, Actuators, Events — all still just as empty. Deciding the structure up front, before any value exists to put inside it, means every later page already knows exactly where its Variables and Methods belong:

from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")

ident = server.addObject("Identification", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1100")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
distillate = server.addObject("Distillate", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1400")
actuators = server.addObject("Actuators", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1500")
events = server.addObject("Events", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1600")

Every NodeId here is one every later page reuses without redefining it, so it's worth taking a moment to notice the pattern: each folder gets a round hundred (i=1100, i=1200, i=1300, ...), leaving room for the values that go inside each one to sit close by in the numbering.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
from o6 import Server


def build_address_space(server: Server):
    sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")

    ident = server.addObject("Identification", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1100")
    status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
    kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
    distillate = server.addObject("Distillate", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1400")
    actuators = server.addObject("Actuators", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1500")
    events = server.addObject("Events", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1600")

    return sys, ident, status, kettle, distillate, actuators, events


server = Server(port=4840)
build_address_space(server)
server.start()

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

The address space is now the right shape: every folder in place, every future leaf's parent already decided. Nothing in it has a value yet — that's deliberately the next page's job, not this one's.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
• Add a variable — drop the first writable Variable under Status/.
  • Add a method — register a callable method on the distillery.
  • Variables with sources — much later, install read and write callbacks with Server.implement(...) and connect this skeleton to a real simulation.

items.title: Add a variable
items.text:
Our distillery has a shape now — Add a hierarchy left us with Objects/DistillingSystem/ and its six sub-folders — but every one of those folders is still empty. A still that can't report its own temperature isn't very useful. This page is where that changes: we put our first real values inside those folders, starting with the two things an operator would actually want to change — a Setpoint and an Operating switch — and then round out Identification/ with a few descriptive facts about the machine.

Everything from here on reuses the same idea, so there's nothing to memorise: a Variable is a named slot with a value in it, hung off a parent node. Once that's clear, the rest of this page — and a good part of the tutorials that follow — is just applying it to different folders and different kinds of value.

items.title: Give Setpoint a home
items.text:
Server.addVariable() is how a slot gets created. It takes a name, the folder it lives in, and the value to start it off with, in that order:

from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")

setpoint = server.addVariable(
    "Setpoint",
    status,
    85.0,                   # the still should aim for 85 °C
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1204",
)
server.start()

Notice the parent is status, not server.objectsNode. Setpoint isn't a top-level thing; it belongs inside the Status folder built on the previous page, where a client browsing the distillery would expect to find it. That's the one decision to make each time a value is added: which folder does it belong in?

The nodeId= pins the address by hand, the same way every folder's address was pinned on the previous page, so Setpoint stays at ns=1;i=1204 across restarts, and every later page — and the client tutorials — can rely on it not moving.

o6 also picks the value's OPC UA type for us, from whatever Python value we pass in:

We write... The still gets a... 85.0 (a float) Double 1013 (an int) Int32 "idle" (a str) String True (a bool) Boolean

85.0 is a float, so Setpoint comes out as a Double. There's nothing to configure — write the kind of value you mean, and the wire type follows.

Info

The ns=1 in ns=1;i=1204 is a namespace — bookkeeping OPC UA uses to keep different vendors' NodeIds from colliding. 1 is the default for anything a server defines itself, which is all we're doing here, so it's the number every NodeId in these tutorials starts with.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")

setpoint = server.addVariable(
    "Setpoint",
    status,
    85.0,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1204",
)
server.start()

print(f"Server running at {server.endpointUrl}")
print("Press Ctrl+C to stop.")

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

Run that, and the distillery has something worth asking about for the first time. The simplest check is to read the value, write a new one, and read it back:

print(server.read("ns=1;i=1204"))   # 85.0
server.write("ns=1;i=1204", 90.0)
print(server.read("ns=1;i=1204"))   # 90.0

Read, write, read again. It's a small check, but it's the one we'll repeat throughout these tutorials every time a new value is added.

items.title: A shorter way to reach the same value
items.text:
Typing out the NodeId every time is tedious, so addVariable(...) returns something more convenient than the address alone: a live handle to the Variable itself. Call it with no arguments to read, call it with one argument to write:

print(setpoint())                 # 85.0  — read via the handle
setpoint(90.0)                    # write via the handle

That's the form used everywhere from here on — some_variable() to read, some_variable(new_value) to write — because it's shorter than spelling out server.read(...)/server.write(...) in a loop. It's still exactly the same operation underneath; the handle and server.read/server.write reach the same value, just through different syntax:

setpoint._value = 91.0            # a third form, doing the same thing
print(server.read("ns=1;i=1204")) # 91.0 — visible immediately, however it was set

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
setpoint = server.addVariable("Setpoint", status, 85.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1204")
server.start()

# Read and write from the server side
print(setpoint())           # 85.0
setpoint(90.0)
print(setpoint._value)      # 90.0
print(server.read("ns=1;i=1204"))  # 90.0

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

items.title: A second writable value: Operating
items.text:
A still an operator can retarget but never start or stop isn't much better. Operating is the second dial: a plain True/False flag, in the same Status/ folder, saying whether the distillery should be running a batch at all.

operating = server.addVariable("Operating", status, True, nodeId="ns=1;i=1203", writable=True)

Nothing new here — the same helper, the same folder, just a different kind of value (bool, so it becomes a Boolean). Once the Setpoint pattern is familiar, adding a second value is one line, not a new concept. writable=True is already the default; it's spelled out here because the next section is about turning it off.

items.title: Values that shouldn't be writable
items.text:
Two writable values — Setpoint and Operating — is the right number for this still. Everything else it reports should be readable but not writable, and OPC UA has a flag for exactly that: writable=False. Set it, and the value can still be read; an incoming write request is rejected instead of accepted.

Heater is the clearest example. It looks like something an operator should be able to switch — but the simulation drives it as part of the batch cycle, and a write from outside would just be overwritten again on the next tick. So it's locked down, and placed where it actually belongs: under Actuators/, not Status/.

actuators = server.addObject("Actuators", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1500")
heater = server.addVariable(
    "Heater",
    actuators,
    False,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1503",
    writable=False,
)

Info

writable=False clears a bit in the Variable's AccessLevel attribute — the field a client checks before it writes at all. From here on, the distillery's rule is simple: Setpoint and Operating are the only two values anyone outside the server may change. Everything else — kettle readings, valve and heater state, identification text — is read-only, because the simulation (or the machine's nameplate) is the one source of truth for it.

The same reasoning covers Identification/: three lines of descriptive text about the machine that nobody ever writes to.

ident = server.addObject("Identification", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1100")
server.addVariable("Name",         ident, "Distilling Demo Still", nodeId="ns=1;i=1101", writable=False)
server.addVariable("Manufacturer", ident, "o6 Tutorials",          nodeId="ns=1;i=1102", writable=False)
server.addVariable("ModelNumber",  ident, "DS-1000",               nodeId="ns=1;i=1103", writable=False)

Three calls, the same shape as everything above.

items.title: When the exact wire type matters
items.text:
The inference table further up covers every value the tutorials actually use — but it's worth knowing its limit: Python has only one int and one float, so it can't tell an Int32 from an Int64, or a Float from a Double. When that distinction matters, dataType= states it directly instead of leaving it to inference:

import o6

cycle = server.addVariable(
    "Cycle",
    status,
    0,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1202",
    dataType=o6.Int32,      # explicit, instead of leaving int → Int32 to inference
    writable=False,
)

Cycle is still a plain int on the Python side either way — dataType= only changes what goes out on the wire. It's worth remembering for later; most of what we build in these tutorials won't need it.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery now has Setpoint and Operating under Status/, three lines of Identification/ text, and a read-only Heater under Actuators/. It can already answer a read and accept a write. What it still can't do is act on a request — the next page gives it a first one of those: a Shutdown method a remote request can call.

  • Add a method — register a callable method, return values and StatusCode.
  • Server manual — every keyword argument on addVariable, including dataType=, valueRank, and historizing=.

items.title: Add a method
items.text:
Everything the distillery has exposed so far is a value: something a client reads, and in a couple of cases writes. That covers a lot of ground, but it doesn't cover actions — there's no way, yet, to tell the server to actually do something. This page adds the first one: a Shutdown method a client can call to stop the server.

A Method is a different kind of node from anything built so far — not a value that changes, but a function the server runs on request. By the end of this page the distillery exposes one Variable and one Method, both living under the DistillingSystem skeleton built on the hierarchy page.

items.title: Add a method with addMethod
items.text:
Server.addMethod() registers a callable on an Object node. The first two positional arguments are the name and the parent; the third is a Python function the server invokes when the Method is called.

import time
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")

setpoint = server.addVariable("Setpoint", status, 85.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1204")

def shutdown(node):
    """Stop the server when this method is invoked."""
    print(f"  [Method] Shutdown called from {node._nodeid}")
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)

shutdown_method = server.addMethod(
    "Shutdown",
    sys,
    shutdown,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=2002",
)
server.start()

The function receives the parent Object as its first argument (here, sys — the DistillingSystem object — because we hung the method directly under it, the same way the reference server does). It returns a one-tuple holding the StatusCode — Good accepts the call, anything else rejects it before the body even runs.

That is the entire pattern. A method is a node that points at a Python function; the server wires the function up when start() runs and routes the next call to it.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
setpoint = server.addVariable("Setpoint", status, 85.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1204")

def shutdown(node):
    print(f"  [Method] Shutdown called from {node._nodeid}")
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)

shutdown_method = server.addMethod("Shutdown", sys, shutdown, nodeId="ns=1;i=2002")
server.start()

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

That server has a Setpoint and a Shutdown method. addMethod handed back the Method node itself (shutdown_method), and calling it dispatches through the real Call service — the same path a client's Call request takes, just without the network round trip:

print(shutdown_method())   # ()  — no OutputArguments declared, so nothing comes back

A Bad status raises StatusCodeError instead of returning — shutdown_method() only returns normally once the callback has actually accepted the call. The node parameter is the right place to attach per-Object state to — the parent Object is always the first argument the server passes to the body.

items.title: Methods that need inputs and outputs
items.text:
Start and Shutdown take no inputs and return just a status. Real methods exchange arguments. addMethod takes optional inputArgs= and outputArgs= lists of ns0.datatypes.Argument descriptors — one entry per argument, in declaration order.

from o6.ns import ns0
from o6 import ValueRank

def set_setpoint(node, value):
    """Update the distillery setpoint."""
    setpoint(value)
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)

server.addMethod(
    "SetSetpoint",
    sys,
    set_setpoint,
    inputArgs=[
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(
            name="Value",
            dataType="i=11",                # Double
            valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR,
            description="New setpoint, °C",
        ),
    ],
    nodeId="ns=1;i=2003",
)

The callback signature now is (node, value) — node is the parent Object, value is the first input. The return value is still a (StatusCode,) tuple, because there are no outputs declared.

A method with outputs adds them to the return tuple, in declaration order:

def add(node, a, b):
    """Return the sum of two doubles."""
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, a + b)

server.addMethod(
    "Add",
    sys,
    add,
    inputArgs=[
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(name="A", dataType="i=11", valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR),
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(name="B", dataType="i=11", valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR),
    ],
    outputArgs=[
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(name="Sum", dataType="i=11", valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR),
    ],
    nodeId="ns=1;i=2010",
)

The first element is always StatusCode. A Bad status may stand alone — return (StatusCode.BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE,) — but a Good status must be followed by exactly the declared number of outputs.

Warning

valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR is not decoration. The default value rank is 0, which means array, and a scalar argument arriving at an array-typed parameter gets BAD_INVALID_ARGUMENT before the callback runs. This is the single most common cause of a method that "doesn't work".
