items.text:
import time
from o6.ns import ns0
from o6 import Server, StatusCode, ValueRank

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
setpoint = server.addVariable("Setpoint", status, 85.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1204")

def set_setpoint(node, value):
    setpoint(value)
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)

server.addMethod(
    "SetSetpoint",
    sys,
    set_setpoint,
    inputArgs=[
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(
            name="Value",
            dataType="i=11",
            valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR,
            description="New setpoint, °C",
        ),
    ],
    nodeId="ns=1;i=2003",
)

def add(node, a, b):
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, a + b)

server.addMethod(
    "Add",
    sys,
    add,
    inputArgs=[
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(name="A", dataType="i=11", valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR),
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(name="B", dataType="i=11", valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR),
    ],
    outputArgs=[
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(name="Sum", dataType="i=11", valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR),
    ],
    nodeId="ns=1;i=2010",
)

server.start()

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery has one Variable and one Method, both living under the DistillingSystem skeleton from the hierarchy page. The next pages move from "how do you add a node?" to "how does a value get its content?" — starting with values that come from somewhere other than a plain write.

  • Values from an external source — a Variable whose truth lives in a Python model instead of native storage.
  • Add a hierarchy — re-visit the folder skeleton any time you need to remind yourself of the layout.
  • Server manual — every keyword argument on addMethod, including inputArgs= and outputArgs=.

items.title: Values from an external source
items.text:
Every Variable built so far holds whatever was last written to it — an operator sets Setpoint, the server stores it, a read hands it back. That's the right shape for a setting, but not for a reading. The distillery's Kettle/Temperature doesn't work like Setpoint at all: nobody writes it, because there's nothing to write to it — the number comes from the still itself. This page is about that other shape: a value whose truth lives outside the address space, in a small Python model, and gets pushed in rather than stored.

This page is a short detour from the main build — it uses a fresh, throwaway server rather than continuing the exact one from the last few pages, so it's a good place to try the idea out without worrying about the rest of the distillery. The pattern it shows comes back for real once we reach Variables with sources, much later, where it's this same idea, wired directly into the running distillery.

items.title: Keep the real value outside the address space
items.text:
The pattern has two halves that stay deliberately separate: a plain Python object that is the process, and the OPC UA Variable that reports on it. Nothing about KettleModel below knows OPC UA exists — it just tracks a number and advances it:

class KettleModel:
    """Stands in for the kettle's actual temperature sensor."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._temperature = 20.0

    def tick(self) -> None:
        """Advance one simulated step, heating up a little."""
        self._temperature += 0.5

    def read_temperature(self) -> float:
        return self._temperature

Keeping the model this plain is worth the small extra step: it's trivial to test on its own, easy to swap for a real sensor driver later, and just as easy to reuse from a client-side script — none of which is true once OPC UA is mixed into the same class.

items.title: Seed the Variable, then push updates
items.text:
The Variable is created the same way as any other, except its initial value comes from the model instead of a literal:

import time
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")

model = KettleModel()
temperature = server.addVariable(
    "Temperature",
    kettle,
    model.read_temperature(),   # seed with the model's current value
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1302",
    writable=False,
)
server.start()

try:
    while True:
        model.tick()
        server.write(temperature, model.read_temperature())
        print(f"Kettle temperature = {server.read(temperature):.1f} °C")
        time.sleep(0.5)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

Every iteration does the same two things: advance the model, then server.write(...) the new reading into the Variable. Any client with a subscription open on Kettle/Temperature sees each of those writes as a data-change notification — from the outside, this looks exactly like a real sensor reporting in, even though nothing more than a Python loop is behind it.

Info

writable=False still matters here. The model, not an incoming write, is the only thing allowed to move this value — the read-only access level is what stops a client from overwriting the simulated reading with something else.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
from o6 import Server


class KettleModel:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._temperature = 20.0

    def tick(self) -> None:
        self._temperature += 0.5

    def read_temperature(self) -> float:
        return self._temperature


model = KettleModel()

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
temperature = server.addVariable(
    "Temperature", kettle, model.read_temperature(), nodeId="ns=1;i=1302", writable=False
)
server.start()

try:
    while True:
        model.tick()
        server.write(temperature, model.read_temperature())
        time.sleep(0.5)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

This is, in miniature, exactly what the real distillery server does: Set the stage's server.py runs a loop that ticks a much bigger simulation and mirrors its state into the address space with the same server.write(...) calls, just for every Variable under DistillingSystem instead of one.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
Explicit server.write(...) calls work, but they mean remembering to push every value on every tick, by hand, from whatever loop happens to own the model. Variables with sources shows the more automatic alternative, once we get there: installing a read callback so a read always consults the model directly, with no push step at all.

  • Running on asyncio — the same kind of update loop, running cooperatively instead of blocking a thread.
  • Variables with sources — the callback-based alternative to explicit server.write(...).
  • Server Data Source Updates — the runnable example this page is based on.

items.title: Running on asyncio
items.text:
Every server built so far runs on its own background thread: server.start() returns immediately, and the main thread is free to loop, sleep, and write values. That's the right shape for a script. It's the wrong shape once the distillery's update loop wants to await other things — an async database driver, an async sensor client — without a thread in the picture at all. This page runs the same kind of server cooperatively on a single asyncio event loop instead.

Like the previous page, this one is a short aside rather than a continuation of the exact running server — it builds its own small address space to demonstrate the idea cleanly. By the end, a Kettle/Temperature Variable updates once a second, driven entirely by await asyncio.sleep(...).

items.title: async with instead of start() / stop()
items.text:
Server is an async context manager as well as a sync one. async with server: calls start() on entry and stop() on exit — including on an exception — the same guarantee the sync with server: form makes, just on the event loop instead of a thread.

import asyncio
from o6 import Server

async def main():
    server = Server(port=4840)
    sys = await server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
    kettle = await server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
    temperature = await server.addVariable(
        "Temperature", kettle, 20.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1302", writable=False
    )

    async with server:
        print(f"Server running at {server.endpointUrl}")
        i = 0
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(1.0)
            i += 1
            await temperature(20.0 + i * 0.1)
            print(f"Kettle temperature = {await temperature():.1f} °C")


asyncio.run(main())

The same API builds the address space in either mode. Inside an async task, add await to creation, node calls, and dynamic child lookups, including operations that complete immediately. Use async with for lifecycle and await asyncio.sleep(...) to let other work progress.

Warning

time.sleep(...) still works inside an async def, but it blocks the entire event loop — no client request is served while it runs. await asyncio.sleep(...) hands control back to the loop instead, which is the entire point of running this way. Mixing the two defeats the purpose.

items.title: asyncio.run is the entry point
items.text:
asyncio.run(main()) creates the event loop, runs main() to completion, and tears the loop down afterward. It's the one call that starts everything — there is no separate "start the loop" step to remember.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        asyncio.run(main())
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("Server stopped.")

KeyboardInterrupt on the main thread cancels the running task; the async with server: block still runs server.stop() on the way out, so shutdown is just as clean as the synchronous version.

items.title: Repeated callbacks can be async def too
items.text:
server.addRepeatedCallback(...) — the timer API used later, in Server callbacks — accepts a coroutine function directly, and the server awaits it on its own loop:

async def tick():
    await temperature((await temperature()) + 0.1)

server.addRepeatedCallback(tick, 1000.0)   # every 1 s, as a coroutine

That's a second way to reach the same "do this periodically" goal as the while True: await asyncio.sleep(...) loop above — a registered timer instead of an explicit loop. Timers and async loops covers the deeper version of this: offloading genuinely blocking work to a thread pool, and cancelling cleanly on shutdown.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import asyncio
from o6 import Server


async def main():
    server = Server(port=4840)
    sys = await server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
    kettle = await server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
    temperature = await server.addVariable(
        "Temperature", kettle, 20.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1302", writable=False
    )

    async with server:
        print(f"Server running at {server.endpointUrl}")
        print("Press Ctrl+C to stop.")
        i = 0
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(1.0)
            i += 1
            await temperature(20.0 + i * 0.1)
            print(f"Kettle temperature = {await temperature():.1f} °C")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        asyncio.run(main())
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("Server stopped.")

The real distillery server (Set the stage) stays on the threaded form — its simulation already runs in a background thread, so there's no event loop to cooperate with. Reach for the async form when the code driving your updates is itself async: a database, an HTTP client, an async sensor SDK.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
• Declare and implement a Variable — the declared-type route to a Variable's read/write behaviour, in a separate implementer class.
  • Timers and async loops — cooperative cancellation, thread-pool offload, and the full async def callback story.
  • Server Async — the runnable example this page is based on.

items.title: Declare and implement a Variable
items.text:
So far, every Variable's behaviour has come from calling addVariable a particular way — writable=False here, a value there. That's fine for one still, but it doesn't scale to a plant with fifty of them: there's no single place that says "this is what a Setpoint looks like," only fifty separate addVariable calls that all happen to agree. This page is a first look at the alternative — declaring the shape once, as a reusable type, and writing its behaviour once too.

Concretely: the distillery's Setpoint clamps out-of-range writes to [0.0, 100.0] — Variables with sources, much later in these tutorials, builds exactly that by installing read=/write= callbacks on one already-built Variable node. This page reaches the same clamping behaviour a different way: declare a UA ObjectType that owns a Setpoint-shaped Variable, then implement its read and write behaviour in a separate Python class. Every object the server later builds from that type gets the behaviour for free — no per-instance callback wiring needed.

You don't need to have read the declared-types pages first — this page introduces just enough of @o6.objecttype to make the pattern work. Those pages go deep on the declaration side alone; this one is about pairing a declaration with an implementation.

items.title: The pattern has three parts
items.text:
1. Declare a UA ObjectType with a Variable child as a pure contract, with @o6.objecttype. The declaration carries no behaviour.
  2. Implement that contract in a separate subclass. @o6.read("<member>") and @o6.write("<member>") bind Python behaviour to the declared Variable, by its Python attribute name.
  3. Register the implementation with server.implement(Declaration, Impl) so the server uses it whenever it builds an instance of that type.

items.title: Declare the type
items.text:
A declared type needs a namespace to live in — register one shortname once, then reference it as ns="distillery" below. SetpointType declares one Variable child, setpoint, readable and writable (accessLevel=3), but with no behaviour attached yet:

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=6000", browseName="SetpointType")
class SetpointType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    """A setpoint object — declared only, implemented separately below."""

    setpoint: ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType(
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=6001",
            browseName="ns=distillery;Setpoint",
            dataType=o6.Double,
            accessLevel=3,       # CurrentRead | CurrentWrite
            userAccessLevel=3,
        )
    )

Nothing here says what a read or write of setpoint actually does — that's deliberate. A declaration on its own is metadata; instantiating it right now would give every instance the default, unclamped storage behaviour.

items.title: Implement read and write in a subclass
items.text:
Subclass the declaration and bind behaviour to setpoint by its Python attribute name — not by its BrowseName. The value lives in an ordinary instance attribute, self._value, so the write callback can validate before storing:

from typing import Any

class SetpointImpl(SetpointType):
    """Clamp writes to [0.0, 100.0] before storing them."""

    LOW, HIGH = 0.0, 100.0

    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self._value = 20.0

    @o6.read("setpoint")
    def _read_setpoint(self, **kwargs: Any) -> tuple[o6.StatusCode, o6.Double]:
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Double(self._value))

    @o6.write("setpoint")
    def _write_setpoint(self, value: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> tuple[o6.StatusCode]:
        clamped = max(self.LOW, min(self.HIGH, float(value.value)))
        self._value = clamped
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD,)

Both callbacks take keyword-only context (session, range, includeSourceTimestamp for reads) that this example ignores via **kwargs. The write callback returning a clamped value rather than rejecting the write outright is a choice — Variables with sources shows the alternative, rejecting out-of-range writes with BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE instead.

items.title: Register and instantiate
items.text:
server.implement(SetpointType, SetpointImpl) is the line the whole pattern is about: it wires SetpointImpl in as the class the server uses whenever it builds a SetpointType instance. From then on, addObject(typeDefinition=SetpointType, ...) hands back a live, fully-wired object — SetpointImpl is never named at the call site.

import sys
import time

server = o6.Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])
server.implement(SetpointType, SetpointImpl)

device = server.addObject(
    "Reflux",
    server.objectsNode,
    typeDefinition=SetpointType,
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=6100",
    ns=o6.ns.distillery.index,
)

server.start()
print(f"read            -> {server.read(device.setpoint)}")
server.write(device.setpoint, o6.Double(150.0))   # above range
print(f"read after 150  -> {server.read(device.setpoint)}")
server.write(device.setpoint, o6.Double(-5.0))    # below range
print(f"read after -5   -> {server.read(device.setpoint)}")

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

Warning

Pass server=server explicitly if a constructor call like this one runs from inside the same script that declared the namespace — o6 otherwise treats it as part of the declaration, not a live node. A namespace kept in its own importable module doesn't need this; only code in that module is affected.

server.read(device.setpoint) after the two out-of-range writes comes back 100.0 and 0.0 — the clamp lives entirely in SetpointImpl, and it fires whether the write comes from this script, another process on the server, or a remote OPC UA client.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The next page pairs the same declare/implement split with a Method instead of a Variable.

  • Declare and implement an ObjectType — the same pattern, for a Method's behaviour.
  • Declare a variable type — the full @o6.variabletype story: engineering units, ranges, and typed values.
  • Variables with sources — the instance-level alternative: Server.implement(variable, read=..., write=...) on one already-built Variable.
  • Server Variable Read/Write Override — the runnable example this page is based on.

items.title: Declare and implement an ObjectType
items.text: The previous page split a Variable into a declaration and a separate implementation. The same split applies to Methods, for the same reason: declare an ObjectType with a Method as a pure contract, implement its behaviour in a separate subclass, and register that class with server.implement(Declaration, Impl) so every instance the server builds dispatches to your code automatically. This page builds a CycleCounterType — the same idea behind the distillery's Status/Cycle, as a standalone reusable type.

items.title: The pattern, once more
items.text:
1. Declare the ObjectType and its Method with @o6.objecttype / o6.call(...). No behaviour yet.
  2. Implement the Method in a subclass, with @o6.call("<name>"). Ordinary instance attributes give each live node its own state.
  3. Register with server.implement(Declaration, Impl).

items.title: Declare the type
items.text:
CycleCounterType declares one Method, Increment, that takes an Int32 step and returns the running Int32 total. It reuses the same distillery namespace the rest of these tutorials register:

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=7000", browseName="CycleCounterType")
class CycleCounterType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    """A batch counter — declared only, implemented separately below."""

    increment: o6.node.MethodNode = o6.hasComponent(
        o6.call(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Increment",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=7001",
            inputArgs=[
                ns0.datatypes.Argument(
                    name="step",
                    dataType=o6.Int32,
                    valueRank=o6.ValueRank.SCALAR,
                    description="Batches to add",
                )
            ],
            outputArgs=[
                ns0.datatypes.Argument(
                    name="total",
                    dataType=o6.Int32,
                    valueRank=o6.ValueRank.SCALAR,
                    description="Cycle count after incrementing",
                )
            ],
        )
    )

Increment is declared, not implemented — the class body only says what the Method's signature is.

items.title: Implement the Method in a subclass
items.text:
Subclass the declaration and bind Python behaviour to Increment with @o6.call("Increment") — the bare local name resolves against the type's declared Methods, so the qualified ns=distillery;Increment doesn't need spelling out here. Every live node gets its own self._count:

from typing import Any

class CycleCounterImpl(CycleCounterType):
    """Track a running batch count per instance."""

    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self._count = 0

    @o6.call("Increment")
    def _increment(self, step: o6.Int32) -> tuple[o6.StatusCode, o6.Int32]:
        self._count += int(step)
        return (o6.StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Int32(self._count))

items.title: Register and dispatch
items.text:
import sys
import time

server = o6.Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])
server.implement(CycleCounterType, CycleCounterImpl)

counter = server.addObject(
    "BatchCounter",
    server.objectsNode,
    typeDefinition=CycleCounterType,
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=7100",
    ns=o6.ns.distillery.index,
)

# In-process: calling the Method attribute runs CycleCounterImpl directly.
print(counter.Increment(o6.Int32(1)))    # (StatusCode.GOOD, Int32(1))
print(counter.Increment(o6.Int32(1)))    # (StatusCode.GOOD, Int32(2))

server.start()
print(f"Server running at {server.endpointUrl}")

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

Both call paths — the in-process counter.Increment(...) above and a remote client's Call service request against the same Method — dispatch to CycleCounterImpl._increment and share the one instance's _count. addObject(typeDefinition=CycleCounterType, ...) hands back a fully-wired CycleCounterImpl instance; CycleCounterImpl itself is never named at the call site.

Add a second addObject(typeDefinition=CycleCounterType, ...) for a second still, and its counter starts independently at 0 — the shared behaviour lives on the type, the running count lives on each instance.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
Declaration and implementation are two separate concerns from here on. The next pages go deep on the declaration side alone, and the "beyond the examples" pages later on cover the instance-level alternative to what these two pages just built.

  • Declare an object type — every decorator, modelling rule, and composition option @o6.objecttype supports.
  • Method implementations — the instance-level alternative: Server.implement(method, call=...) on one already-built Method.
  • Server ObjectType Implementation — the runnable example this page is based on.

items.title: Declare an object type
items.text:
Every node in the distillery so far — the folders, the Setpoint, the Heater, the Shutdown method — was built by calling addObject or addVariable one at a time, by hand. That's been perfectly fine for one still. But picture the plant this server stands in for: not one still, but a dozen of them on the same floor, each with its own kettle, its own setpoint, its own sensors. Building each one by hand would mean repeating the same sequence of calls over and over, and trusting every copy stays in sync with the others. That's the problem a declared ObjectType solves: a Python class, written with @o6.objecttype, that describes the shape of a distillery once and lets the server produce as many instances of it as the plant needs.

This page builds that class — DistillingSystemType — as the same shape as the hand-built distillery, just described as a type instead of assembled call by call. It's worth being upfront about what this is: a parallel technique, not a continuation of the exact running server from the earlier pages. By the end, DistillingSystemType(...) produces a whole hierarchy from a single constructor call, but on a fresh server and namespace of its own.

Info

The reference server from Set the Stage (examples/tutorial-server/server.py) keeps building its address space imperatively — it doesn't switch to any of the declared types this page or the next three introduce. This band is a look at an alternative, more scalable way to model the same shape; the running example itself doesn't change.

items.title: Declare an ObjectType with @o6.objecttype
items.text:
@o6.objecttype declares a UA ObjectType whose instances are full subtrees. The declaration carries no behaviour — Declare and implement an ObjectType, earlier in these tutorials, pairs a declaration like this one with a separate implementer class. For now, the type describes what every DistillingSystem looks like.

A custom type needs a namespace to live in. o6.ns.namespace(...) registers a shortname once; that shortname is what the type's nodeId= references.

import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

# Register the distillery namespace once at module load
o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    """The complete distillery — one folder with six sub-objects."""

    identification: ns0.objtypes.FolderType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.objtypes.FolderType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Identification",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1100",
        )
    )

@o6.objecttype turns the class body into a UA ObjectType declaration. A child is declared in two parts: the instance (ns0.objtypes.FolderType(...)) describes the child node itself, and the linker (o6.hasComponent(...)) states the reference type that attaches it to the parent and returns the instance unchanged — which is why the class attribute can be annotated with the child's concrete type (identification: ns0.objtypes.FolderType). The BrowseName and NodeId are qualified with ns=distillery;..., which is what tells o6 to put the child into our namespace.

The declaration itself is just metadata: nothing is added to a server until you instantiate it or publish it on one.

Info

The decorators and their linkers are part of the declarative API — the same model-driven route the manual covers in depth, alongside Writing a Nodeset in Python. These tutorials use it alongside the imperative addX calls from earlier pages; the two mix freely on one server.

items.title: Add typed Variables and Methods
items.text:
A folder by itself doesn't get us far — the distillery still needs values inside it, and at least one thing it can be told to do. Children of an ObjectType use the same o6.hasComponent / o6.hasProperty linkers regardless of whether the child is a Property, a Variable, or a Method. For a leaf Variable or Property you construct the concrete VariableType directly with its initial value, DataType, and access level; for a Method, o6.call(...) describes the input and output argument shape.

@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    identification: ns0.objtypes.FolderType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.objtypes.FolderType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Identification",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1100",
        )
    )

    # Declared directly on the type for this tutorial; nesting it under
    # `identification` instead would use the same composition pattern —
    # a further ObjectType with its own `name` child, attached the same way.
    name: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Name",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1101",
            dataType=str,
            value="Distilling Demo Still",
            accessLevel=1,                   # read-only
        )
    )

value= seeds the child's initial value; dataType= takes the Python type directly (str, float, bool, or a declared @o6.datatype/@o6.enumtype class) and o6 resolves it to the matching UA DataType. Both accessLevel=1 (read-only) and accessLevel=3 (read-write) are accepted.

Every child declared this way is Mandatory by default — every instance of DistillingSystemType gets it. To make a child optional, annotate it with Optional[...] instead:

from typing import Optional

manufacturer: Optional[ns0.vartypes.PropertyType] = o6.hasProperty(
    ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(dataType=str)
)

Optionality belongs entirely to the annotation — Optional[T] gets the Optional ModellingRule, everything else is Mandatory. There is no separate keyword for it. Most distillery leaves are mandatory, so the plain (non-Optional) form is what the rest of this page uses.

A Method uses o6.call(...) for its declaration, with inputArgs and outputArgs lists of ns0.datatypes.Argument descriptors exactly as the imperative addMethod call uses them:

@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    # ... leaves as above ...

    shutdown: o6.node.MethodNode = o6.hasComponent(
        o6.call(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Shutdown",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=2002",
        )
    )

The Method is declared with o6.call(...) but left unimplemented here. Pairing a declaration like this one with a separate implementer class is the subject of Declare and implement an ObjectType, earlier in these tutorials — worth a look now if you skipped straight here.

items.title: Instantiate the type on a server
items.text:
The type is fully declared now — folder, values, an unimplemented method — but none of it exists on any server yet. Once a server has the namespace, constructing DistillingSystemType(parent=...) materialises the entire subtree:

import sys

server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])     # publish this module's namespace on this server

# One constructor call → the full hierarchy
system = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="MainStill", server=server)

server.start()

server.ns.append(...) takes a module object, never a string — sys.modules[__name__] is the running script itself, which is enough for a single-file tutorial. A real namespace is usually its own importable module (distillery_ns.py) so a client process can import distillery_ns and decode the types too; see Writing a Nodeset in Python.

DistillingSystemType(parent=..., browseName=...) instantiates the type and attaches it to the parent; the constructor takes care of every mandatory child node. The returned handle behaves like the imperative handle from the hierarchy page — system.name() reads a leaf variable, system.name(...) would write it if it were writable, attribute access browses children.

Warning

Pass server=server explicitly whenever the namespace module is the running script, as it is here. o6 treats any constructor call still running inside a module that declared a namespace as part of that declaration — even after server.start(), even from inside a function — so without an explicit server=, the call silently returns an inert declaration instead of a live node, and every later system.name()-style read fails with an AttributeError. A namespace kept in its own importable module doesn't need this: only code in that module is affected, so a separate driver script instantiating distillery.DistillingSystemType(...) gets a live node with no extra argument.

Info

The instance BrowseName and NodeId are not inherited from the type. The type declares the shape; the instance owns its own identity on the server. Pass browseName= (and optionally nodeId=) to the constructor to pin them.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import sys
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    name: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Name",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1101",
            dataType=str,
            value="Distilling Demo Still",
            accessLevel=1,
        )
    )

    operating: ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Operating",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1203",
            dataType=bool,
            value=True,
            accessLevel=3,                # read-write
        )
    )

    setpoint: ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Setpoint",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1204",
            dataType=float,
            value=85.0,
            accessLevel=3,
        )
    )

    shutdown: o6.node.MethodNode = o6.hasComponent(
        o6.call(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Shutdown",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=2002",
        )
    )


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])
system = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="MainStill", server=server)
server.start()

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

A read of Objects/ returns exactly the same tree the imperative version built — MainStill/Name, MainStill/Operating, MainStill/Setpoint, MainStill/Shutdown — but it was built by one constructor call rather than seven addX calls.

items.title: Multiple instances, same type
items.text:
The whole point of a declared type is reuse. The same DistillingSystemType(...) constructor can be called as many times as the plant has stills:

line_a = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="LineA", server=server)
line_b = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="LineB", server=server)
line_c = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="LineC", server=server)

Each call produces a complete, independent subtree. The shared shape lives in the type; the per-instance state (current Operating, current Setpoint, current cycle counter) lives on each instance. The three stills look identical from the outside — same hierarchy, same NodeId offsets within each instance — which is exactly what dashboards and recipes rely on.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import sys
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    name: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Name",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1101",
            dataType=str,
            value="Distilling Demo Still",
            accessLevel=1,
        )
    )
    operating: ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Operating",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1203",
            dataType=bool,
            value=True,
            accessLevel=3,
        )
    )
    setpoint: ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Setpoint",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1204",
            dataType=float,
            value=85.0,
            accessLevel=3,
        )
    )


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])
DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="LineA", server=server)
DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="LineB", server=server)
DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="LineC", server=server)
server.start()

A client connecting now sees three independent LineA, LineB, LineC objects under Objects/, each with the same shape — and adding a fourth means one extra constructor call.

items.title: Mix declared and imperative on the same server
items.text:
The two routes are not mutually exclusive. Imperative addObject calls and declared instances can sit next to each other on the same server, and clients cannot tell which is which:

import sys

server = Server(port=4840)

# Imperative
scratch = server.addObject("Scratch", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;s=Scratch")
server.addVariable("Counter", scratch, 0, nodeId="ns=1;s=Counter")

# Declarative
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])
DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="MainStill", server=server)

server.start()

Both end up in the same nodestore, browsable from the same Objects/. Most real servers mix the two: declarative types for the things the model captures (devices, sensors, methods), imperative helpers for one-off configurations and operational state.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery itself is now a typed class — something the server can produce on demand instead of assembling by hand, node by node. The same idea, that a type can carry shape and metadata once instead of repeating it on every instance, works just as well one level down, on a single value rather than a whole hierarchy.

  • Declare a variable type — @o6.variabletype for typed values with their own DataType and ValueRank.
  • Server manual — every decorator, in depth, with a complete reference model.

items.title: Declare a variable type
items.text:
The previous page gave the whole distillery a type of its own, so the server could produce as many identical stills as the plant ever needs. The same habit of thought works at a much smaller scale too — on a single value. Take Setpoint: it isn't really just a Double. It has units (degrees Celsius), a sensible operating range, an EngineeringUnits field — metadata that turns "a number" into "a temperature" an operator can actually trust. None of that context lives anywhere in the model yet; it would only ever live in a comment, or in whatever a client happens to assume. This page declares a custom VariableType and uses it as the type definition of a Setpoint-shaped Variable, so that metadata travels with the value instead of living outside it.

By the end of this page, a Setpoint is a typed Variable with engineering metadata carried on the type, not repeated on every instance.

Info

Looking for read/write behaviour on a declared Variable — validation, clamping — rather than metadata? Declare and implement a Variable, earlier in these tutorials, pairs a declared Variable with a separate implementer class using exactly the Setpoint-clamping example this page's Setpoint is named after.

items.title: Declare a VariableType with @o6.variabletype
items.text:
@o6.variabletype declares a UA VariableType — a template for Variables whose DataType, ValueRank, and other metadata come from the type rather than from each individual node.

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.variabletype(
    ns="distillery",
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=3000",
    browseName="TemperatureType",
    dataType=float,            # Double
    valueRank=o6.ValueRank.SCALAR,
)
class TemperatureType(ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType):
    """A temperature, in degrees Celsius, with an EngineeringUnits property."""

@o6.variabletype(...) declares a UA VariableType whose instances are scalar Doubles. The class body can declare further children — typically the EngineeringUnits and Range companion-spec properties that turn a Double into a real engineering value.

The declared class is the type. To get a typed instance, you construct TemperatureType(...) directly, or annotate a leaf inside another declared type with TemperatureType — either way o6 resolves the value's DataType, ValueRank and children from the class.

Info

VariableType and ObjectType declarations live in the same namespace table. The shortname distillery is registered once and reused.

items.title: Add EngineeringUnits and Range properties
items.text:
A "temperature" without units is just a number. The OPC UA companion specs define EUInformation and Range as the standard ways to attach units and an engineering range to a value. Declaring them on the type means every instance inherits them automatically.

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.variabletype(
    ns="distillery",
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=3000",
    browseName="TemperatureType",
    dataType=float,
    valueRank=o6.ValueRank.SCALAR,
)
class TemperatureType(ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType):
    """A temperature in degrees Celsius, with EUInformation and Range."""

    engineeringUnits: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;EngineeringUnits",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=3001",
            dataType="i=887",       # EUInformation
        )
    )

    instrumentRange: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;InstrumentRange",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=3002",
            dataType="i=884",       # Range
        )
    )

Two hasProperty children: EngineeringUnits (an EUInformation) and InstrumentRange (a Range). Both are declared as ns0.vartypes.PropertyType instances — a leaf Property is always constructed directly from the concrete VariableType it should be, never from a separate "variable" helper. They ride along on every instance of TemperatureType. The values are read by the same Value attribute path used for any other Variable, and a reader that knows the OPC UA companion specs can recognise "this is a Celsius temperature with a defined engineering range" by inspecting the EngineeringUnits value.

Info

The DataType identifiers — i=887 for EUInformation, i=884 for Range — come from the standard OPC UA namespace (ns0). They are part of the base types every server publishes, so no extra nodeset import is needed. dataType= accepts either a NodeId string like this or a Python type such as float; both resolve to the same UA DataType.

items.title: Use the type as a typeDefinition
items.text:
TemperatureType is fully declared now — DataType, EngineeringUnits, InstrumentRange, all in one place — but declaring it doesn't put anything on a server yet. With TemperatureType declared, a Variable can be constructed with TemperatureType as its type definition wherever the imperative addVariable would hold a bare Double. The declarative route constructs the class directly:

setpoint = TemperatureType(
    parent=server.objectsNode,
    browseName="Setpoint",
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1204",
    value=85.0,
    server=server,     # required when this script also declared the namespace — see the note on the ObjectType page
)

setpoint is now a Double Variable whose HasTypeDefinition points at TemperatureType — its EngineeringUnits and InstrumentRange properties come along automatically, because they are declared on the type. The instance still owns its own value (85.0).

The imperative equivalent uses addVariable(typeDefinition=...), passing the declared class itself as the type:

setpoint = server.addVariable(
    "Setpoint",
    server.objectsNode,
    85.0,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1204",
    typeDefinition=TemperatureType,
    writable=True,
)

typeDefinition= accepts the declared class directly (or the equivalent NodeId string, "ns=distillery;i=3000"). Either way, a browse that follows HasTypeDefinition from Setpoint lands on TemperatureType, reads EngineeringUnits from the type, and decodes the value's units and range without them being declared on every instance.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import sys
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.variabletype(
    ns="distillery",
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=3000",
    browseName="TemperatureType",
    dataType=float,
    valueRank=o6.ValueRank.SCALAR,
)
class TemperatureType(ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType):
    engineeringUnits: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;EngineeringUnits",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=3001",
            dataType="i=887",
        )
    )
    instrumentRange: ns0.vartypes.PropertyType = o6.hasProperty(
        ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;InstrumentRange",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=3002",
            dataType="i=884",
        )
    )


@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    setpoint: TemperatureType = o6.hasComponent(
        TemperatureType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Setpoint",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1204",
            value=85.0,
        )
    )


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])
system = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="MainStill", server=server)
server.start()

A read following HasTypeDefinition from Setpoint lands on TemperatureType, can read EngineeringUnits from there, and now has units, range, and value — three pieces of information carried on two nodes.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
Setpoint is no longer a bare Double — it's a typed value that carries its own engineering context with it, wherever it's used. Types have now shaped a whole object and a single value; the next page turns the same model-first habit toward something different again: not a node, but the relationship between two nodes. That's what custom ReferenceTypes are for.

  • Declare a reference type — custom ReferenceTypes for relationships beyond HasComponent / HasProperty.
  • Writing a Nodeset in Python — the full VariableType story, including valueRank= and array types.

items.title: Declare a reference type
items.text:
The last two pages put a name on the shape of things — a whole distillery, a single Setpoint. But not everything worth naming in an address space is a node; sometimes what matters most is how two nodes relate to each other, and HasComponent/HasProperty don't tell that whole story. Those two reference types carry most of the relationships in a typical OPC UA server — folders, sub-objects, variables under objects — because most relationships really are some form of "owns". A few aren't: a Sensor monitors a Kettle; a Valve controls a Conveyor; an Alarm reports on a Reading. Relationships like those deserve their own reference type, so the address space can say what's actually happening instead of forcing everything into an ownership shape it doesn't fit.

This page declares a Monitors reference type and uses it to attach a temperature sensor to the kettle — the still finally gets a sensor of its own, wired up with a reference that names exactly what it's doing there.

items.title: Why custom reference types?
items.text:
The default Organizes / HasComponent / HasProperty types are enough for "this folder contains this thing". A few situations want their own type:

  • Non-ownership edges. A Sensor is not part of the kettle — it reads from it. Monitors describes the edge more honestly than HasProperty, and a browse(reftype=Monitors) finds the temperature sensor that way.
  • Type-safe browsing. Knowing the distillery uses Monitors for sensor relationships lets you issue browse(reftype=Monitors) and get back exactly the sensors — no need to filter the entire hierarchy.
  • Semantic interoperability. A companion specification that defines a Controls or Supplies reference type gives every server that uses it the same vocabulary. Tools that understand the vocabulary can present the relationships meaningfully.

The distillery doesn't strictly need a custom reference type — every node fits the standard edges — but adding one is the natural way to express "this sensor watches this kettle".

items.title: Declare a reference type with @o6.referencetype
items.text:
With the motivation out of the way, the declaration itself is small. @o6.referencetype declares a UA ReferenceType and optionally names the inverse direction. Python inheritance is the HasSubtype chain — the base class you derive from is the reference type's parent, with no implicit fallback:

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.referencetype(
    ns="distillery",
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=4000",
    browseName="Monitors",
    inverseName="MonitoredBy",
)
class MonitorsType(ns0.reftypes.NonHierarchicalReferences):
    """A sensor that watches a piece of equipment."""

inverseName= is the name visible when the relationship is followed in the opposite direction — the kettle sees the sensor as MonitoredBy while the sensor sees the kettle as Monitors. OPC UA requires an InverseName for non-symmetric, non-abstract reference types. For symmetric references (symmetric=True), the type reads the same in both directions and no InverseName is needed.

Here MonitorsType derives from ns0.reftypes.NonHierarchicalReferences (the catch-all for "not strictly ownership"), which is what makes it MonitorsType's HasSubtype parent. Derive from ns0.reftypes.HasComponent or ns0.reftypes.HasProperty instead when the reference is a more specific kind of hierarchical edge — whatever Python base class you write becomes the parent, full stop.

A ReferenceType marker must have no annotated fields, and it is never instantiable.

items.title: Attach a reference with addReference
items.text:
Declaring MonitorsType doesn't connect anything on its own — a reference type only means something once it links two real nodes. The imperative route to adding an edge between two existing nodes is Server.addReference(source, reftype, target, ...), matching the client contract. The distillery builds its sensors imperatively and links them to the kettle with Monitors:

import sys
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.referencetype(
    ns="distillery",
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=4000",
    browseName="Monitors",
    inverseName="MonitoredBy",
)
class MonitorsType(ns0.reftypes.NonHierarchicalReferences):
    pass


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])

# Imperative skeleton
distilling_system = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", distilling_system, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
sensors = server.addObject("Sensors", distilling_system, nodeId="ns=1;i=1700")
sensor = server.addVariable("KettleTemp", sensors, 20.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1701")

# Custom reference: the sensor monitors the kettle
server.addReference(source=sensor, reftype=MonitorsType, target=kettle)

server.start()

addReference(source, reftype, target) attaches the edge. Both sides are existing nodes — the imperative call adds an edge between them, not a new node. MonitorsType here is the declared class itself; the equivalent NodeId string "ns=distillery;i=4000" works too.

browse(reftype=MonitorsType) from the kettle finds KettleTemp, and browse(reftype=MonitorsType, direction=INVERSE) from KettleTemp finds the kettle back as MonitoredBy.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import sys
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.referencetype(
    ns="distillery",
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=4000",
    browseName="Monitors",
    inverseName="MonitoredBy",
)
class MonitorsType(ns0.reftypes.NonHierarchicalReferences):
    pass


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])

distilling_system = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", distilling_system, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
sensors = server.addObject("Sensors", distilling_system, nodeId="ns=1;i=1700")
sensor = server.addVariable("KettleTemp", sensors, 20.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1701")

server.addReference(source=sensor, reftype=MonitorsType, target=kettle)

server.start()

items.title: Reference types on a declared type
items.text:
Custom references compose with the declarative route the same way they compose with the imperative one: declare the leaf as an ordinary HasComponent child so it materialises with every instance, then attach the extra, meaningful edge between the two live children once the instance exists — with server.addReference(...) or the equivalent three-argument o6.reference(source, SomeReferenceType, target):

@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    kettle: ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Kettle",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1300",
        )
    )
    kettleTemperature: ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;KettleTemperature",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1701",
            dataType=float,
            value=20.0,
        )
    )


system = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="MainStill", server=server)

# The sensor monitors the kettle — attached once both live nodes exist.
server.addReference(source=system.kettleTemperature, reftype=MonitorsType, target=system.kettle)

Both kettle and kettleTemperature are declared as ordinary HasComponent children, so every DistillingSystemType instance gets both. The Monitors edge between them is not part of the type's shape — it is added once, on the live instance, exactly as in the imperative section above. system.kettleTemperature and system.kettle are live node handles by then, so addReference (and a plain dot-access read like system.kettleTemperature()) both work on them directly.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import sys
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.referencetype(
    ns="distillery",
    nodeId="ns=distillery;i=4000",
    browseName="Monitors",
    inverseName="MonitoredBy",
)
class MonitorsType(ns0.reftypes.NonHierarchicalReferences):
    pass


@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    kettle: ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;Kettle",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1300",
        )
    )
    kettleTemperature: ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;KettleTemperature",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1701",
            dataType=float,
            value=20.0,
        )
    )


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])
system = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="MainStill", server=server)
server.addReference(source=system.kettleTemperature, reftype=MonitorsType, target=system.kettle)

The instance has MainStill/Kettle and MainStill/KettleTemperature both linked with HasComponent — that is the type's shape — plus a Monitors edge from KettleTemperature to Kettle added on this particular instance. A browse(reftype=MonitorsType, direction=INVERSE) from MainStill/Kettle finds KettleTemperature back as MonitoredBy.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The sensor now has a name for what it's doing to the kettle, not just a place in the tree. One piece is still missing from this tour of declaring things up front: a way to describe the values themselves, beyond the handful of numbers and strings OPC UA already knows.

  • Declare a data type — @o6.datatype for a custom Structure, and @o6.enumtype for a closed set of named values, used by your variables and methods.
  • Writing a Nodeset in Python — symmetric vs. asymmetric, abstract vs. concrete, and reference-type hierarchies.

items.title: Declare a data type
items.text:
Every value in the distillery so far has fit one of a handful of built-in types — strings, doubles, ints, booleans. That's plenty for a Setpoint or a Name, but it starts to strain on a value like the still's current State, which is really only ever one of five things: Idle, Filling, Heating, Distilling, Draining. Encoding that as a free-form string would work, technically, but it wouldn't say anything true about the value — a string field carries no declared set of legal values at all, so nothing in the model states what a valid State even is. The shape that actually fits is an Enum DataType: a named, closed set of values that the model, and any tooling reading it, can see explicitly.

This page declares a StillState enum and uses it as the DataType for the distillery's Status.State — the last stop in this tour of declaring things up front instead of building them by hand.

items.title: Why declare a data type?
items.text:
Two reasons:

  1. The wire format. Encoding "Distilling" as a 16-byte UTF-8 string every time is wasteful. Encoding it as an Int32 enum value is one byte. The DataType drives both the encoding and the visible shape of the value on the wire.
  2. A discoverable, closed set of values. Once StillState is a UA Enum DataType, a read of the data type node shows exactly the allowed values, instead of a free-form string field that documents nothing. The enum DataType is metadata the server publishes; it does not by itself stop a client from writing an out-of-range integer — enforcing that boundary at write time is application logic, the same Server.implement(variable, write=...) validation covered on the Variables with sources page.

The same shape works for Structure types — anything a vendor's spec calls a "complex data type" is a UA Structure DataType.

items.title: Declare an Enum with @o6.enumtype
items.text:
Start with State, since it's the value that motivated this page. Enumerations use @o6.enumtype, not @o6.datatype — @o6.datatype is for Structures, and raises TypeError on a bare class-body assignment like IDLE = 0. A decorated @o6.enumtype class becomes a real IntEnum; the class body just lists the values, and each becomes a member:

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.enumtype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=5000", browseName="StillState", description="The distillery's batch state machine")
class StillState:
    IDLE = 0
    FILLING = 1
    HEATING = 2
    DISTILLING = 3
    DRAINING = 4

The class body's assignments become the enum values — StillState.IDLE == 0, StillState.DISTILLING == 3, and so on. The server publishes the data type under ns=distillery;i=5000, and the values are read with the standard Value attribute path. o6.enumfield(value, description=..., displayName=..., name=...) adds per-member UA metadata when a bare integer isn't enough — the two forms mix freely in one class:

@o6.enumtype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=5000", browseName="StillState")
class StillState:
    IDLE = 0
    FILLING = o6.enumfield(1, description="tank is filling")
    HEATING = 2
    DISTILLING = 3
    DRAINING = 4

For an OPC UA enum, the integer values themselves are the wire encoding — StillState.DISTILLING is Int32(3) on the wire. The DataType node documents which integers are legal; it does not by itself make the server reject an out-of-range one. A read of an in-range value comes back as the Python enum member (StillState.IDLE), and enforcing the boundary on writes — rejecting 5 before it reaches the nodestore — is application logic, covered on the Variables with sources page.

items.title: Use the data type as a Variable's dataType
items.text:
Declared on its own, StillState is still just metadata sitting in the namespace — it needs to be attached to an actual Variable before it means anything for the distillery. The new type plugs into the dataType= keyword of addVariable, taking the declared class directly:

import sys
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.enumtype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=5000", browseName="StillState")
class StillState:
    IDLE = 0
    FILLING = 1
    HEATING = 2
    DISTILLING = 3
    DRAINING = 4


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])     # publish the enum's namespace before using it

distilling_system = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", distilling_system, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")

# `dataType=` takes the declared enum class directly
state = server.addVariable(
    "State",
    status,
    int(StillState.IDLE),      # initial value, as the underlying Int32
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1201",
    dataType=StillState,
    writable=False,
)

server.start()

server.ns.append(...) has to run before dataType=StillState is resolved — the DataType node only exists on a server once its namespace has been published there. The server publishes Status.State with the new data type, and the initial value 0 reads back as StillState.IDLE. As above, the DataType alone does not stop a write of an out-of-range integer — that validation is something a write callback adds explicitly.

Info

The same enum works as an input argument on a method: declare Argument(dataType=StillState, valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR) and o6 rejects an argument of the wrong UA DataType before the callback runs — the same structural check any other typed argument gets, not a bounds check against the enum's members.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import sys
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.enumtype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=5000", browseName="StillState")
class StillState:
    IDLE = 0
    FILLING = 1
    HEATING = 2
    DISTILLING = 3
    DRAINING = 4


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append(sys.modules[__name__])
distilling_system = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", distilling_system, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
server.addVariable(
    "State",
    status,
    int(StillState.IDLE),
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1201",
    dataType=StillState,
    writable=False,
)

server.start()

items.title: Declare a Structure DataType
items.text:
StillState covers a closed set of named values, but not every custom value is a choice among a handful of options — some are a small bundle of fields that belong together, like a summary of one finished batch. The same declarative pattern works for those compound types too, just with the other decorator: a Structure DataType has fields with names and types, and @o6.datatype reads a plain type annotation as the field's DataType — there is no separate field-declaration factory for the type itself. Extra metadata that the annotation can't express (a description, an optional field, a max string length) is layered on with o6.field(...):

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.datatype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=5010", browseName="BatchSummary", description="A summary of one completed batch")
class BatchSummary:
    cycle: int              # Int64 by default; use o6.UInt32 for the exact width
    yield_l: float           # litres
    duration_s: int          # seconds

BatchSummary is a three-field structure with cycle, yield_l, and duration_s — the annotation on each attribute is its DataType, the same way it is for a struct field anywhere else in o6. On the wire it is an ExtensionObject the server publishes under ns=distillery;i=5010.

To pin the exact integer width instead of the default Int64, annotate with one of the sized o6 aliases, and add o6.field(...) where a plain annotation isn't enough:

@o6.datatype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=5010", browseName="BatchSummary")
class BatchSummary:
    cycle: o6.UInt32
    yield_l: float = o6.field(description="litres produced")
    duration_s: o6.UInt32

Structure DataTypes are useful for the values a single Variable holds when a simple scalar isn't enough — readings with metadata, summaries, command payloads.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
That's the data type story done, and with it the last of these model-first pages. The distillery now has declared types for its objects, its variables, the relationships between them, and the values themselves. What's left is behaviour: reacting to writes, calling methods, and reading values that come from somewhere other than the nodestore — the subject the next pages turn to.

  • Method implementations — installing and swapping the Python callbacks that give Methods their behaviour.
  • Writing a Nodeset in Python — the full DataType story, including field metadata, inheritance, Unions, and (further down) enum value handling.

items.title: Method implementations
items.text:
The distillery's data model is complete now — Foundation gave it a hierarchy, Composition turned that same hierarchy into declared types a server can build instances from. None of that, on its own, makes the distillery act. Its Shutdown method, built back on the add a method page, only does anything because addMethod(name, parent, callback, ...) bound a callback to it at the moment it was created. That works fine while the method stays simple, but it stops covering the case once a Method needs to exchange arguments, return more than one output, or fail in a way its caller can actually tell apart from other failures.

This page is where methods start behaving like operations instead of fixed wiring. It centers on Server.implement(method, call=callback), the imperative way to attach a callback to a Method that already exists — built earlier, or shared with another server — rather than fixing it in at construction time. The validation, output, and error-mapping ideas are the same ones the add a method page introduced; what changes here is how the callback gets attached, and that it can be replaced later.

Info

This installs a callback on one already-built Method node. Declare and implement an ObjectType, earlier in these tutorials, covers the type-level equivalent — implement a Method once on a declared ObjectType, and every instance the server builds from that type gets the behaviour automatically.

items.title: Install a method callback with Server.implement(method, call=...)
items.text:
Server.implement(method, call=callback) installs a function on the call slot of an existing Method. From then on, the callback is the function the method routes to:

import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)

sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")

# Build the method without a callback at construction time — we will install one below.
shutdown_method = server.addMethod(
    "Shutdown",
    sys,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=2002",
)


def shutdown(node):
    """Stop the server when this Method is invoked."""
    print(f"  [Method] Shutdown called from {node.nodeId}")
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)


server.implement(shutdown_method, call=shutdown)
server.start()

The callback receives the parent Object as its first argument — here, the DistillingSystem folder at ns=1;i=1000. It returns a (StatusCode,) tuple; StatusCode.GOOD accepts, anything else rejects. For a no-output Method that is the whole result.

Info

Server.implement(method, call=None) clears the slot. Subsequent invocations return BadNotImplemented until a fresh callback is installed.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)

sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
shutdown_method = server.addMethod("Shutdown", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=2002")


def shutdown(node):
    print(f"  [Method] Shutdown called from {node.nodeId}")
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)


server.implement(shutdown_method, call=shutdown)
server.start()

# The method's Body is now the shutdown function — call it directly to verify.
print(shutdown(sys))   # (StatusCode.GOOD,)

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

The function is what the server invokes when the method is called. Calling it directly produces the same (StatusCode,) tuple the protocol would receive.

items.title: Methods with input and output arguments
items.text:
The next page, Variables with sources, adds a write handler that validates and rejects out-of-range writes to the distillery's Setpoint. Here, the same kind of logic is exposed as a Method instead: it takes an input argument, clamps it, and returns the clamped value:

import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode, ValueRank
from o6.ns import ns0

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")

set_setpoint = server.addMethod(
    "SetSetpoint",
    sys,
    inputArgs=[
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(
            name="Value",
            dataType="i=11",         # Double
            valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR,
            description="New setpoint, °C",
        ),
    ],
    outputArgs=[
        ns0.datatypes.Argument(
            name="Clamped",
            dataType="i=11",
            valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR,
            description="The setpoint value actually stored",
        ),
    ],
    nodeId="ns=1;i=2003",
)

LOW, HIGH = 0.0, 100.0


def set_setpoint_callback(node, value):
    """Clamp the incoming value and return what was actually stored."""
    clamped = max(LOW, min(HIGH, float(value.value)))
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Double(clamped))


server.implement(set_setpoint, call=set_setpoint_callback)
server.start()

The Method signature on the Python side mirrors the UA signature: input arguments are positional parameters in declaration order, the return tuple's first element is the StatusCode, and the remaining elements are the outputs in declaration order.

Argument(valueRank=ValueRank.SCALAR) is not decoration — the default rank 0 means array, and a scalar argument arriving at an array-typed parameter gets BAD_INVALID_ARGUMENT before the callback runs.
