An invocation of SetSetpoint with value=105.0 returns (StatusCode.GOOD, Double(100.0)) — the operation succeeded, and the clamped value is reported back. The whole point of the output is to echo the result: "I asked for 105, here's what I got".

items.title: Map failures to specific StatusCodes
items.text:
Clamping is one way to handle a bad input: quietly fix it, then report what was actually stored. It isn't always the right one — some failures need to be refused outright, with a StatusCode specific enough that the caller can tell what went wrong. A Method that can fail in multiple ways should pick the right StatusCode for each failure. The OPC UA spec lists the ones relevant to most control loops:

  • BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE — argument outside an accepted range
  • BAD_INVALID_ARGUMENT — argument type or count wrong (the spec usually catches this before the callback)
  • BAD_USER_ACCESS_DENIED — the caller has no permission for this operation
  • BAD_NOT_SUPPORTED — the server cannot do this operation right now
  • BAD_INVALID_STATE — the server is in a state where this operation is not allowed
def set_setpoint_callback(node, value):
    incoming = float(value.value)
    if not (LOW <= incoming <= HIGH):
        return (StatusCode.BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE,)
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Double(incoming))

A Bad status stands alone. A Good status must be followed by exactly the declared number of outputs — there is no way to return a partial result.

items.title: Async Method bodies
items.text:
Every callback so far has returned as soon as it ran, synchronously. Not every operation can finish that quickly — a shutdown that has to close valves in sequence, or a call that waits on real hardware, needs to await without blocking the rest of the server while it does. The Method callback may be async def. Synchronous and asynchronous callbacks have the same positional arguments and the same result-tuple semantics; the server drives the coroutine on its event loop and the resolved values are returned over the wire.

import asyncio

async def shutdown(node):
    """Stop the server after an ordered teardown."""
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    print("  [Method] Shutdown complete")
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)


server.implement(shutdown_method, call=shutdown)

Async Method execution is not guarded after the callback has returned its coroutine.

items.title: Replace or clear a callback
items.text:
Passing a fresh callback replaces the existing one, exactly like the Variable case on the Variables with sources page:

server.implement(set_setpoint, call=set_setpoint_callback_v2)

Server.implement(method, call=None) clears the slot. Subsequent invocations return BadNotImplemented until a fresh callback is installed:

server.implement(set_setpoint, call=None)
# set_setpoint() now returns BadNotImplemented.

The old callback is still a Python function (still in scope, still callable) but no longer bound to the Method.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
With Server.implement(method, call=...), the distillery's Methods can be wired, swapped, or cleared any time after they're built, not just at construction. That covers only half of what makes an address space active, though — Variables need the same kind of after-the-fact wiring for their own read and write behaviour, and that's exactly where the next page picks up.

  • Variables with sources — install read and write callbacks with Server.implement(...), validate, mirror to a simulation.
  • Server manual — the full Method callback signature, including node, session, and range keywords.

items.title: Variables with sources
items.text:
The previous page gave Methods a way to pick up new behaviour after they were built, rather than only at construction time. Variables need the same freedom, and for much the same reason. Right now, the distillery's Operating and Setpoint are passive Variables — the server stores the value, hands it back on read, and replaces it on write. The distillery's Kettle.Temperature, Kettle.Level, Distillate.Level, Actuators.Heater, Actuators.FillValve, and Actuators.DrainValve are the opposite: the server owns the value, and the value is published from a simulation running in the server process — never stored from incoming writes.

This page reuses the imperative Kettle/Temperature from the hierarchy page and installs a read callback with Server.implement(...). The callback reads from a Python object — the simulation state — and the simulation runs elsewhere in the process. By the end, every read of Kettle/Temperature returns the current simulation state, and the Python state is the source of truth.

A passive Variable accepts whatever is written, as long as the value's DataType matches. That's the right shape for sensor readings the server publishes — but for Setpoint, Operating, or any value the server uses to drive other state, the write needs server-side logic. That is what this page is about: turning a Variable into an active participant in the control loop by installing read= and write= callbacks.

Info

This installs callbacks on one already-built Variable node. Declare and implement a Variable, earlier in these tutorials, covers the type-level equivalent — implement a Variable's read/write once on a declared ObjectType, and every instance built from that type gets the behaviour automatically, with no per-instance Server.implement(...) call needed.

items.title: Install a read callback with Server.implement(variable, read=...)
items.text:
Server.implement(variable, read=callback) installs a function on the read slot of an existing Variable. From then on, the callback is called instead of returning the variable's stored value:

import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)

sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
kettle_temperature = server.addVariable(
    "Temperature",
    kettle,
    20.0,                              # initial value, used only as a seed
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1302",
    writable=False,
)

# Source of truth lives outside the Variables folder.
simulation_state = {"kettle_temp": 20.0}


def read_kettle_temperature(node, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Double(simulation_state["kettle_temp"]))


server.implement(kettle_temperature, read=read_kettle_temperature)
server.start()

The callback receives the Variable handle as its first argument and the keyword-only metadata range=, session=, and includeSourceTimestamp= (the distillery's callback ignores them). It returns (StatusCode.GOOD, value) — Bad statuses stand alone, Good ones must be followed by exactly one value.

simulation_state["kettle_temp"] is the source of truth. A background update loop (covered in the next server callbacks page) can poke that dict from a timer, and the next read sees the new value because the callback reads it on every read.

Warning

Once a Variable has a read callback, it owns the value. The initial value=20.0 is only the seed the callback receives on first invocation if it happens to read it; from then on the callback's return value is what is read. Server-side writes (simulation_state["kettle_temp"] = 25.0) bypass the callback and update the Python state directly.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)

sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
kettle = server.addObject("Kettle", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1300")
kettle_temperature = server.addVariable(
    "Temperature",
    kettle,
    20.0,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1302",
    writable=False,
)

simulation_state = {"kettle_temp": 20.0}


def read_kettle_temperature(node, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Double(simulation_state["kettle_temp"]))


server.implement(kettle_temperature, read=read_kettle_temperature)
server.start()

# Drive the temperature from a quick update loop
with server:
    for cycle in range(20):
        time.sleep(0.1)
        simulation_state["kettle_temp"] = 20.0 + cycle
        print(f"  cycle {cycle}: temperature = {server.read('ns=1;i=1302')}")

The temperature value never lands in native storage — the callback reads from a Python dict, and the dict is updated from a background loop. A read of Kettle/Temperature every 100 ms walks the value from 20.0 up to 39.0.

items.title: Read and write together
items.text:
Setpoint is the distillery's most useful example of a Variable with both halves: it is read (to display) and written (to change the target). Both slots need callbacks, and the read callback returns whatever the write callback last stored.

import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)

sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
setpoint = server.addVariable(
    "Setpoint",
    status,
    85.0,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1204",
    writable=True,
)

# Source of truth: a dict, updated by the write callback and read by the read callback.
setpoint_state = {"value": 85.0}
LOW, HIGH = 0.0, 100.0


def read_setpoint(node, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Double(setpoint_state["value"]))


def write_setpoint(node, value, *, range, session):
    incoming = float(value.value)
    if not (LOW <= incoming <= HIGH):
        return (StatusCode.BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE,)
    setpoint_state["value"] = incoming
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)


server.implement(setpoint, read=read_setpoint, write=write_setpoint)
server.start()

The two callbacks share setpoint_state["value"]. A read returns whatever the last write stored. There is no native storage involved — the Python dict is the source of truth, the read callback hands it out, the write callback accepts the new value (with validation).

Info

A read slot must exist before a write slot. open62541's callback value sources must be readable, so a write-only Variable is rejected. That fits the read-write pattern anyway — if a value can be written, it must also be able to be read back.

def write_setpoint(node, value, *, range, session):

The write validates the range before storing; the read returns whatever was stored. Two callbacks, one Python dict, no native storage.

items.title: Validate and reject with StatusCode
items.text:
A write callback returns (StatusCode.GOOD,) to accept, or (StatusCode.BAD_<something>,) to reject. The OPC UA spec lists the relevant codes — BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE, BAD_USER_ACCESS_DENIED, BAD_INVALID_ARGUMENT, BAD_NOT_SUPPORTED, etc. Pick the one that fits the failure; the rejection is reflected back on the wire.

LOW, HIGH = 0.0, 100.0


def write_setpoint(node, value, *, range, session):
    incoming = float(value.value)
    if not (LOW <= incoming <= HIGH):
        return (StatusCode.BAD_OUT_OF_RANGE,)
    setpoint_state["value"] = incoming
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)

This is the strict form: out-of-range is rejected outright, no clamping. Choose one or the other depending on the contract — the distillery's Setpoint Variable rejects here because the write should fail loudly when the operator asks for something out of range (the SetSetpoint Method on the method implementations page takes the opposite approach and clamps instead, echoing back what was actually stored); Operating accepts anything because it is a boolean and the only failure is the wrong type, which the type system catches before the callback runs.

items.title: Mirror a write to another node
items.text:
The most useful pattern is write A, react by writing B. The distillery's Operating=False should also clear the Cycle counter, so a new batch starts from 0:

import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")

operating = server.addVariable("Operating", status, True, nodeId="ns=1;i=1203", writable=True)
cycle = server.addVariable("Cycle", status, 0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1202", writable=False)

operating_state = {"value": True}


def read_operating(node, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Boolean(operating_state["value"]))


def write_operating(node, value, *, range, session):
    print(f"  [write] Operating = {value.value}")
    operating_state["value"] = bool(value.value)
    if not operating_state["value"]:
        # Parked: reset the cycle counter on the Status object.
        cycle(0)
    return (StatusCode.GOOD,)


server.implement(operating, read=read_operating, write=write_operating)
server.start()

cycle(0) is a server-side write that does not invoke the cycle's write slot (none is installed). The bypass is intentional — the server is the source of truth for the cycle counter.

Warning

Synchronous callback dispatch rejects recursion on the same node with BadInvalidState — a write callback cannot re-enter that same Variable's own read or write callback. Independent nodes are unaffected, which is why write_operating above can write cycle from inside its own write callback without issue. Still prefer triggering cross-node side-effects through a server-side update loop, a timer, or a queue when the logic grows more involved than a one-line reset.

For the distillery, the practical pattern is: write callbacks validate and log, the background timer reacts by reading the validated values and pushing state into other Variables.

items.title: Replace or clear a callback
items.text:
Server.implement(variable, read=None) clears the read slot. A read returns to the construction-time behaviour — the original stored value, with the initial value=... as the seed:

server.implement(setpoint, read=None, write=None)
# setpoint() now reads from native storage again, with the value it had when last written.

Passing a fresh callback replaces the existing one — Server.implement always wins on the concrete Variable:

def read_setpoint_v2(node, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
    return (StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Double(setpoint_state["value"] + 1.0))   # off-by-one variant

server.implement(setpoint, read=read_setpoint_v2)

The new callback is the one that runs from that point on. The old one is still a Python function (still in scope, still callable) but no longer bound to the Variable.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The Variables now have either a read callback (publishing from a Python source), a write callback (validating incoming writes), or both. The next page is about the glue that wires the whole thing together — periodic timers, startup hooks, and the long-running background loop that drives a simulation.

  • Server callbacks — startup, shutdown, periodic timers, retention cleanup.
  • Server manual — the full Variable callback signature, including range=, session=, and includeSourceTimestamp=.

items.title: Server callbacks
items.text:
A passive Variable holds whatever was last written. A callback-backed Variable holds whatever the read callback returns. The simulation is the thing in the middle — the long-running process that updates the kettle temperature, advances the state machine, and pushes values into the Variables.

This page wires a periodic update loop to the distillery. By the end, the server is running a 10 Hz tick that mirrors a simulated still into the address space.

items.title: Where do callbacks live?
items.text:
Two places:

  1. Per-node callbacks — Server.implement(variable, read=..., write=...) for Variables, Server.implement(method, call=...) for Methods. The previous pages and method implementations covered those. They run on the server's event loop.
  2. Server-wide timers — Server.addRepeatedCallback(...): These run on the loop too, but they are not bound to a node; they are scheduled work the server keeps firing.

The simulation's update loop is a server-wide timer. The Variable read callbacks are per-node callbacks that consult the simulation's state on every read.

items.title: addRepeatedCallback
items.text:
addRepeatedCallback(callback, intervalMs) registers callback to run every intervalMs milliseconds. The callback runs on the server's event loop — keep it short.

import time
import o6
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)

state = {"kettle_temperature": 20.0}


def tick():
    """Advance the simulated kettle temperature by 0.1 °C per tick."""
    state["kettle_temperature"] += 0.1


callback_id = server.addRepeatedCallback(tick, 100.0)   # 100 ms = 10 Hz

server.start()

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

tick() runs every 100 ms on the server's loop thread. It mutates a Python dict that read callbacks consult; a read of Kettle/Temperature sees the value walk up by 0.1 °C every tick.

changeRepeatedCallbackInterval(callback_id, newIntervalMs) adjusts the cadence without re-registering; removeCallback(callback_id) cancels it. The callback is removed automatically on shutdown, so a long-running server does not need to clean up at exit.

This section built the update loop with the same imperative Objects and Variables used throughout the tutorial so far. The next example wires the same read callback through a declared type instead — an @o6.objecttype with a Variable child and an @o6.read(...)-decorated method, resolved once when the Object is constructed rather than installed by hand with Server.implement(...). It is a second way to reach the same per-node callback slot, documented fully on the server manual's callbacks page.

items.title: Putting it all together — the distillery's 10 Hz update loop
items.text:
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode
from o6.ns import ns0

o6.ns.namespace(
    shortname="distillery",
    uri="http://o6-automation.com/UA/Distillery/",
    version="1.0",
)


@o6.objecttype(ns="distillery", nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1000", browseName="DistillingSystemType")
class DistillingSystemType(ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType):
    kettle_temperature: ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType = o6.hasComponent(
        ns0.vartypes.BaseDataVariableType(
            browseName="ns=distillery;KettleTemperature",
            nodeId="ns=distillery;i=1302",
            dataType="i=11",
            value=20.0,
            accessLevel=1,
        )
    )


class DistillingSystemImpl(DistillingSystemType):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self._kettle_temperature = 20.0

    @o6.read("kettle_temperature")
    def _read_kettle_temperature(self, *, range, session, includeSourceTimestamp):
        return (StatusCode.GOOD, o6.Double(self._kettle_temperature))


server = Server(port=4840)
server.ns.append("distillery")
server.implement(DistillingSystemType, DistillingSystemImpl)
system = DistillingSystemType(parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="MainStill")


def tick():
    system._kettle_temperature += 0.1


server.addRepeatedCallback(tick, 100.0)
server.start()

A read of MainStill/KettleTemperature repeatedly sees the value climb at 1 °C / second. The same read callback handles reads at any cadence.

items.title: Startup and shutdown hooks
items.text:
The server runs start() and stop() itself, but a project usually wants to do additional setup between them — open a database, build a simulation state, schedule retention cleanup. The cleanest place is a context manager (with server: ...) or explicit start/stop:

server = Server(port=4840)

# ... build the address space ...

server.addRepeatedCallback(tick, 100.0)
server.start()

# The server is now listening and the tick is firing.
# ... main work ...

server.stop()

For a project that wants hooks before/after start() runs, schedule them with server.addRepeatedCallback(...) on a one-shot timer — open62541's callback model treats one-shot and repeated the same, just stop the callback once it has run:

def start_of_day():
    print("Server is now serving")
    server.removeCallback(start_of_day_id)

start_of_day_id = server.addRepeatedCallback(start_of_day, 1.0)

A 1 ms one-shot is the standard pattern for "do this as soon as the loop is up".

Retention cleanup is the same idea applied on a slower, repeating cadence — a callback that trims an in-memory buffer instead of letting it grow forever:

batch_log = []   # appended elsewhere, one entry per completed batch
MAX_ENTRIES = 100


def trim_batch_log():
    """Keep only the most recent MAX_ENTRIES batches in memory."""
    del batch_log[:-MAX_ENTRIES]


server.addRepeatedCallback(trim_batch_log, 60_000.0)   # once a minute

trim_batch_log runs on the loop thread like any other repeated callback — it stays cheap because it only slices a list, never touches the network or disk.

items.title: Update loop discipline
items.text:
Three things matter once the loop is running:

  1. Keep callbacks short. Every callback runs on the loop thread. A 50 ms callback that blocks the loop for 50 ms means every other callback waits. Move slow work to a queue, a thread, or another process.
  2. Don't block the loop on I/O. Reading from a sensor or database should not stall incoming writes. Use asyncio for cooperative I/O on the loop, or a thread pool for blocking calls.
  3. Stop gracefully. When server.stop() is called, the loop drains in-flight callbacks before tearing down. Long-running callbacks should still respect cancellation — see the timers and async loops page.

Info

addRepeatedCallback(callback, intervalMs) does not guarantee the cadence — it guarantees the callback runs at least every intervalMs milliseconds. If a callback runs longer than the interval, the next invocation is scheduled immediately. The right mental model is "no sooner than this", not "exactly every".

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery's update loop is in place. The next page uses that loop to publish state transitions as events; the page after that covers scheduling work cooperatively and tying the whole thing to a real state machine.

  • Events — declaring an event type, making a source, and firing real events from the update loop with o6.Event / trigger().
  • Timers and async loops — long-running background work, asyncio integration, cooperative cancellation.
  • Server manual — every callback type, its signature, and the resolution order between callbacks.

items.title: Events
items.text:
You've been watching the Kettle values change continuously, and the update loop mirrors the simulation into the address space every tick. But the distillery also has events — discrete things that happen at specific moments (a batch starts, a batch ends, a state transition, a client changes the setpoint). A value change says "the temperature moved from 20.0 to 20.1"; an event says "the still just transitioned from Filling to Heating". This page wires that up.

By the end, the server emits a real BaseEventType notification — of its own DistilleryEventType — on every batch transition and every client write, and a client subscribed to the Server object or to DistillingSystem directly sees it land.

items.title: Emit one
items.text:
An event needs no setup at all. server.createEvent(...) fires one from the standard Server object, which every client can already subscribe to:

import o6
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
server.start()

server.createEvent(message=o6.LocalizedText("Server is up", "en"), severity=100)

That is a complete, valid BaseEventType notification. severity is 1..1000 and createEvent raises ValueError outside that range.

A message with a colon in it needs an explicit o6.LocalizedText(text, locale) rather than a bare string — a bare string is parsed as "locale:text", so "Batch started: filling kettle" would lose everything before the colon.

items.title: Add the fields you care about
items.text:
The distillery wants to say which batch and which state. Pass them as fields, keyed by the event-filter path a subscriber will select them with:

server.createEvent(
    message=o6.LocalizedText("Batch started: filling kettle with wash", "en"),
    severity=500,
    fields={"/1:Cycle": o6.Int32(1), "/1:State": "Filling"},
)

/1:Cycle means "the field named Cycle in namespace 1". Nothing has to be declared for this to work — the field travels with the notification, and a client that selects /1:Cycle receives it. See When you need more for what declaring it does buy.

items.title: Give it a source
items.text:
The Server object is a fine sender, but SourceName is more useful when it names the thing that actually happened. Any Object will do:

sys_obj = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode,
                           nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")

server.createEvent(source=sys_obj, message=o6.LocalizedText("Filling", "en"),
                 severity=500)

Events emitted from sys_obj still propagate up to the standard Server object on their own, so a client subscribed there sees them without knowing anything about the distillery.

items.title: Fire it repeatedly
items.text:
The distillery fires the same shape of event over and over, with only the message, severity, and two fields changing — which is what o6.Event(server, ...) is for. It builds a reusable draft without touching the address space, and trigger() re-reads whatever the draft currently holds:

draft = o6.Event(server, source=sys_obj)

draft["/1:Cycle"] = o6.Int32(1)
draft["/1:State"] = "Filling"
draft.message = o6.LocalizedText("Batch started: filling kettle with wash", "en")
draft.severity = 500
draft.trigger()

Event is a mutable mapping, which is why the fields are set with draft[...]. Build the draft once, then fire it as often as you like.

items.title: Wire it into the update loop
items.text:
The distillery's update loop already detects state and cycle changes on every tick. Emitting there is a small helper around the one draft:

def emit(draft, sim_state, message, severity):
    draft.message = o6.LocalizedText(message, "en")
    draft.severity = severity
    draft["/1:Cycle"] = o6.Int32(int(sim_state["cycle"]))
    draft["/1:State"] = sim_state["state"]
    draft.trigger()

Called on every state transition, with a severity that says how much the transition matters — 500 at a batch boundary, 200 for the steps between:

BATCH_BOUNDARIES = ("Filling", "Idle")

severity = 500 if sim_state["state"] in BATCH_BOUNDARIES else 200
emit(draft, sim_state, msg, severity)

And on a client write, so a subscriber hears about it immediately rather than at the next batch step:

if cur_setpoint != last_written_setpoint:
    sim_state["setpoint"] = float(cur_setpoint)
    emit(draft, sim_state, f"Setpoint set to {cur_setpoint:.1f} °C by a client", 400)

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
sys_obj = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode,
                           nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
draft = o6.Event(server, source=sys_obj)

server.start()

for cycle, state in ((1, "Filling"), (1, "Heating"), (2, "Filling")):
    draft["/1:Cycle"] = o6.Int32(cycle)
    draft["/1:State"] = state
    draft.message = o6.LocalizedText(f"Batch {cycle}: {state}", "en")
    draft.severity = 500 if state == "Filling" else 200
    draft.trigger()
    time.sleep(1)

server.stop()

items.title: When you need more
items.text:
Two things the simple path leaves out. Skip them until you want them.

A declared event type, so fields are discoverable. Passing fields works without declaring anything, but a client then has to know /1:Cycle in advance. Declaring the fields as Properties of an ObjectType lets a client find them by browsing, and makes "SELECT /1:Cycle, /1:State" a filter it can build from what it discovered:

event_type = server.addObjectType("DistilleryEventType",
                                  ns0.objtypes.BaseEventType,
                                  nodeId="ns=1;i=3000")
for name, initial, node_id in (("Cycle", 0, "ns=1;i=3001"),
                               ("State", "", "ns=1;i=3002")):
    ns0.vartypes.PropertyType(
        parent=event_type, browseName=f"1:{name}", displayName=name,
        nodeId=node_id, referenceType=ns0.reftypes.HasProperty,
        modellingRule="Mandatory", value=initial, server=server,
    )

Then name the type when you emit: server.createEvent("ns=1;i=3000", source=sys_obj), or prepare a draft with o6.Event(server, eventType="ns=1;i=3000", source=sys_obj). modellingRule="Mandatory" marks the fields as always present on an instance, matching the standard ones.

A source clients can subscribe to directly. Events already reach the Server object, so subscribing there always works. If you want a client to be able to point its subscription at DistillingSystem instead — and filter less — that node needs a non-zero EventNotifier, which addObject does not set. The declared form does:

sys_obj = ns0.objtypes.BaseObjectType(
    parent=server.objectsNode, browseName="1:DistillingSystem",
    displayName="DistillingSystem", nodeId="ns=1;i=1000",
    referenceType=ns0.reftypes.Organizes,
    eventNotifier=1,   # SubscribeToEvents
    server=server,
)
server.addReference(source=ns0.instances.server, reftype=ns0.reftypes.HasNotifier, target=sys_obj)

The HasNotifier reference is what makes that path browsable, so a client can discover it by walking the notifier hierarchy rather than being told the NodeId.

Both snippets need from o6.ns import ns0.

items.title: The mirror pattern, for polling clients
items.text:
Every event above is also written into four plain Variables under Events/:

Events/
├── EventCount       (Int32,    read-only)   (ns=1;i=1601)
├── LastEventTime    (DateTime, read-only)   (ns=1;i=1602)
├── LastEventMessage (String,   read-only)   (ns=1;i=1603)
└── LastEventState   (String,   read-only)   (ns=1;i=1604)

EventCount increments, and the other three carry the latest event's timestamp, message, and state. This is not a substitute for the real event — it is a second, simpler channel for the same information, useful for a client that already has a data-change subscription running and would rather not stand up a separate event subscription for one signal. A read of these Variables uses the standard data-change path: no EventFilter, no event notifier, just values that happen to move together.

The trade-off is shape: only the latest event is visible this way. There is no "last 100 events" or "all events in the last hour" without historical access on top — the real event, delivered as a BaseEventType notification, is the one a subscription actually pushes the moment it happens.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery's event story is real events now, with the writable log as a convenience alongside it. The next page covers asyncio integration, long-running background work, and cooperative cancellation for the update loop that drives both.

  • Timers and async loops — async def callbacks, thread-pool offload, cooperative cancellation on server.stop().
  • Listen to events — the client side: monitorEvent, reading the callback's fields, filtering with the SQL-like string syntax.
  • Server manual — the full createEvent / Event API, GeneratesEvent inference, and the << shorthand.

items.title: Timers and async loops
items.text:
The distillery's update loop runs at 10 Hz from Server.addRepeatedCallback(tick, 100.0). The same callbacks also accept async def — the server runs them on its asyncio event loop, and await inside them is cooperative: while the callback is waiting, the rest of the loop keeps running.

Running on asyncio, earlier in these tutorials, covers the basics — async with server:, await asyncio.sleep(...), asyncio.run(...). This page is the deeper version: long-running work that shouldn't block the loop, and cancelling cleanly on shutdown.

This page covers the three things you actually do with timers:

  • async def callbacks for cooperative I/O.
  • Long-running background work that should not block the loop.
  • Cooperative cancellation on server.stop().

items.title: Async callbacks
items.text:
addRepeatedCallback accepts a plain function or an async def. The two have the same result semantics; an async def callback can await other coroutines, run other tasks, or hand work to a worker pool.

import asyncio
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)


async def poll_sensor():
    """Read from an async sensor driver and push the value."""
    value = await read_sensor_async()      # cooperative I/O
    (await server.write("ns=1;i=1701", value)).check()


server.addRepeatedCallback(poll_sensor, 1000.0)   # every 1 s, as a coroutine
server.start()

poll_sensor runs on the server's event loop, and await read_sensor_async() yields control until the I/O completes. Other callbacks (variable reads, method calls, the listener socket) get their turn in the meantime.

Method, Variable read/write, and timer callbacks may all be async def. Await dual-mode API calls inside them. Synchronous callbacks retain immediate local results; a callback that needs pending work on the same loop must yield control by becoming asynchronous and awaiting that work.

The async with server block puts the server on the same loop as your asyncio.run(main()):

import asyncio
import o6
from o6 import Server

async def main():
    server = Server(port=4840)
    temperature = await server.addVariable("Temperature", server.objectsNode, 22.5)
    async with server:
        i = 0
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
            i += 1
            await temperature(22.5 + i * 0.1)


asyncio.run(main())

async with enters the loop-bound lifecycle. await asyncio.sleep(1) is non-blocking — the loop continues to run while the sleep is in flight.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import asyncio
import o6
from o6 import Server


async def main():
    server = Server(port=4840)
    temperature = await server.addVariable("Temperature", server.objectsNode, 22.5)

    async with server:
        i = 0
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
            i += 1
            await temperature(22.5 + i * 0.1)


try:
    asyncio.run(main())
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

asyncio.run is the entry point that drives the event loop and manages the lifecycle of the main task. KeyboardInterrupt on the main thread cancels the main task; the async with block runs server.stop() on exit.

items.title: Long-running work
items.text:
A callback that takes longer than the polling interval is a footgun. Two solutions:

  1. Cooperative I/O with asyncio. The right answer for I/O that has an async API — a database driver, a serial port, an HTTP client.
  2. Thread pool executor. The right answer for I/O that is intrinsically blocking — a legacy C library, a synchronous database driver.
import asyncio
import concurrent.futures
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
pool = concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)


def blocking_read():
    """Read from a synchronous driver."""
    return sensor.read()


async def poll():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    value = await loop.run_in_executor(pool, blocking_read)
    (await server.write("ns=1;i=1701", value)).check()


server.addRepeatedCallback(poll, 1000.0)

loop.run_in_executor(pool, fn) runs fn on the thread pool, returning a coroutine the loop awaits. The main loop stays responsive while the blocking call runs on a worker thread.

Warning

A plain time.sleep(1) inside a callback blocks the loop. Use await asyncio.sleep(1) (cooperative) or loop.run_in_executor(...) (offloaded to a thread). A pure synchronous callback that does I/O with no await will stall every other callback until it returns.

items.title: Cancellation on stop
items.text:
server.stop() drains in-flight callbacks before tearing down the loop. Plain def callbacks cannot be interrupted; async def callbacks can be cancelled. Wrap a long coroutine in try / except / finally if it has resources to release:

async def poll():
    try:
        while True:
            await read_sensor_async()
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        # server.stop() cancelled us — clean up
        await sensor.close()
        raise

The CancelledError propagates out of the coroutine; raising it lets the task machinery complete normally. Any cleanup that must run on shutdown goes in the finally branch.

For repeated callbacks, registration is the right place to attach cleanup hooks. server.removeCallback(callback_id) returns synchronously and removes the next invocation; the currently-running one continues until it returns.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery is now running on the server's event loop, with the update loop, and a clean shutdown path. The next pages move from behaviour to production: who is allowed to talk to the server, and over what kind of channel.

  • Access control — roles — Role / o6.roles, default-deny, granting reading / writing / calling per node, role mappings for built-in roles.
  • Server manual — every callback type, its signature, and the resolution order.

items.title: Access control — roles
items.text:
The distillery is running on an open channel — anyone who can reach opc.tcp://localhost:4840 can browse it, read the kettle values, write a new Setpoint, and call Shutdown. That's fine while you're poking at the sim on a laptop, but the moment the server is on a real network, it needs a role-based access control. Not "anyone", but "the control plane can write and the HMI dashboard can only read".

This page is the first half of that: defining what a role is, granting permissions to nodes by role, and using the well-known roles o6 ships with.

By the end of this page, an HMI dashboard session can browse and read but not write, and a control-plane session can do everything.

items.title: The shape of a role
items.text:
A role is a named identity the server can grant to a session. o6 ships the well-known OPC UA roles (Anonymous, AuthenticatedUser, Observer, Operator, Engineer, Supervisor, ConfigureAdmin, SecurityAdmin) as instances of o6.Role, available from the o6.roles singleton (o6.roles.anonymous, o6.roles.authenticated_user, o6.roles.observer, ..., o6.roles.configure_admin, o6.roles.security_admin). New roles can be added through server.roles.add(...) for site-specific identities (control plane, HMI dashboard, lab test rig).

Permissions are o6.Permission flags, combined with |. The four that matter for the distillery are:

Permission Meaning BROWSE Browse into the node. READ Read the Value attribute. WRITE Write the Value attribute. CALL Invoke Methods under the node.

A node's permissions are a dict from role to permission set. Permissions are inherited down the subtree unless a child overrides them.

items.title: Grant permissions to a node
items.text:
The node._permissions attribute holds a small object that supports the standard operations:

import o6
from o6 import Server, Permission

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")
status = server.addObject("Status", sys, nodeId="ns=1;i=1200")
setpoint = server.addVariable("Setpoint", status, 85.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1204", writable=True)


# Everyone can read; only Operator and Engineer can write.
setpoint._permissions.grant(
    o6.roles.observer,
    Permission.BROWSE | Permission.READ,
)
setpoint._permissions.grant(
    o6.roles.operator,
    Permission.BROWSE | Permission.READ | Permission.WRITE,
)

server.start()

The _permissions attribute is on every node handle (object, variable, method). It carries grant(...), revoke(...), clear(), and the bulk set(...) / get(). With recursive=True, a grant applies to the whole subtree, which is what you want for a top-level folder.

Warning

The leading underscore is part of the name. Every public helper on a node handle carries one, because unprefixed attribute access is reserved for browsing to child nodes by BrowseName. Assigning to node.permissions silently creates an ordinary Python attribute and changes no permissions at all.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import o6
from o6 import Permission, Server

server = Server(port=4840)
sys = server.addObject("DistillingSystem", server.objectsNode, nodeId="ns=1;i=1000")

# Read-only for everyone, write-on for operator+engineer, recursively
sys._permissions.grant(
    o6.roles.observer,
    Permission.BROWSE | Permission.READ,
    recursive=True,
)
sys._permissions.grant(
    o6.roles.operator,
    Permission.BROWSE | Permission.READ | Permission.WRITE | Permission.CALL,
    recursive=True,
)

server.start()

A client.browse(...) from a session that has only observer granted returns the hierarchy but every write attempt is rejected with BAD_USER_ACCESS_DENIED.

items.title: Read the current permissions
items.text:
_permissions.get() returns the dict-of-role-to-permissions for the node, keyed by the Role objects that were granted:

for role, permission in setpoint._permissions.get().items():
    print(role.name, permission)
# Observer  Permission.BROWSE|READ
# Operator  Permission.BROWSE|READ|WRITE|CALL

Permission is an IntFlag, so each combination is also an integer — Permission.BROWSE | Permission.READ is 33 (BROWSE=1, READ=32), not a small bitmask, because the enum reserves separate bits for role-permission and history operations further down the flag space. Compare with in (Permission.WRITE in permission) rather than assuming low bit positions.

set({role: perm, ...}) is the bulk form. clear() removes all role permissions on the node. The full set of helpers is in the server manual.

items.title: Default-deny
items.text:
A node with no role permissions is permissive by default — anyone can read and write. To switch a server to default-deny, set rbacForAnonymous=True on the Server(...) constructor, then explicitly grant permissions for each role you want to admit.

server = Server(port=4840, rbacForAnonymous=True)

Anonymous sessions then have no permissions unless a node explicitly grants them. The distillery's default is permissive — the constructor leaves rbacForAnonymous at False — so a client without authentication still sees the address space. The right pattern for a deployed distillery is rbacForAnonymous=True plus explicit grants on every node that should be reachable from a given role.

items.title: Grant per role, then assign roles to sessions
items.text:
Permissions are granted to roles, not to sessions. To give a session permissions, the session needs the role. The next page covers how a session ends up with the right role — through authentication, through identity mappings, or through explicit assignment on the server side. The role definitions and the per-node grants live here.

# The role itself — a site-specific "control plane" role, matched by the
# session's Application URI rather than by an identity-mapping rule.
control_plane = server.roles.add(
    o6.Role(
        "ControlPlane",
        applications=("urn:example:control-plane",),
    )
)

# The same role gets the permissions on the Setpoint
setpoint._permissions.grant(
    control_plane,
    Permission.BROWSE | Permission.READ | Permission.WRITE,
)

The role is registered once, then granted to it on whichever nodes the control plane should be able to write. Role.applications is a dedicated field for exactly this case — a tuple of Application URIs the role applies to (empty means "every application"); set applicationsExclude=True to treat it as a deny list instead. Sessions whose Application URI is in that tuple get the role and inherit its permissions, no IdentityMappingRuleType needed. Use identities=(...) instead when the mapping is based on user name, certificate thumbprint, or another IdentityCriteriaType — see the authentication page and the server manual for that story.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery now has a role-based access control story. The next page covers the other half: how sessions get roles — the authentication hooks that map user-name identities to roles.

  • Access control — authentication — session authentication and role assignment via activateSession.
  • Server manual — the full role story, including server.roles registry APIs.

items.title: Access control — authentication
items.text:
The roles page explained how to grant permissions to a node by role. This page is about how a session ends up with a role — the authentication hooks that map a client identity to a server-side role.

By the end, the distillery rejects anonymous clients and accepts two named users — hmi and control — with role assignments that match what each client is allowed to do.

items.title: The shape of an access control plugin
items.text:
o6.AccessControl is the base class for the server-side authentication plugin. Subclass it and override the hooks for the identity flows you want to support:

import o6
from o6.ns import ns0


class DistilleryAccessControl(o6.AccessControl):
    """Accept the distillery's two users; reject anonymous."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(anonymous=False, username=True)

    def activateSession(
        self,
        endpoint,
        remoteCertificate,
        session,
        userIdentityToken,
    ):
        if isinstance(userIdentityToken, ns0.datatypes.UserNameIdentityToken):
            user = userIdentityToken.userName
            pwd = bytes(userIdentityToken.password)
            if user == "hmi" and pwd == b"dashboard":
                return {"username": user, "role": "hmi"}
            if user == "control" and pwd == b"operator":
                return {"username": user, "role": "control"}
            raise o6.StatusCodeError(o6.StatusCode.BAD_USER_ACCESS_DENIED)
        raise o6.StatusCodeError(o6.StatusCode.BAD_USER_ACCESS_DENIED)


server = o6.Server(
    port=4840,
    accessControl=DistilleryAccessControl(),
)

__init__(anonymous=..., username=...) declares the identity-token types the server will advertise. anonymous=False removes the anonymous token policy — clients have to present a username and password.

activateSession(...) is called once per session. The server hands the hook the endpoint description, the remote certificate (or None for a None-policy endpoint), a Session proxy, and the user identity token. Returning a dict stores the dict as session.context; raising StatusCodeError(BAD_...) rejects the activation.

Warning

The hook names are lowerCamelCase — activateSession, closeSession, allowBrowseNode, and so on. A method named activate_session does not override anything: it is never called, the permissive/anonymous-only base implementation runs instead, and nothing warns you. If authentication seems to be ignored, check the spelling first.

items.title: Putting it all together — a minimal access control
items.text:
import o6
from o6.ns import ns0


class DistilleryAccessControl(o6.AccessControl):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(anonymous=False, username=True)

    def activateSession(self, endpoint, remoteCertificate, session, userIdentityToken):
        if isinstance(userIdentityToken, ns0.datatypes.UserNameIdentityToken):
            user = userIdentityToken.userName
            pwd = bytes(userIdentityToken.password)
            if user == "hmi" and pwd == b"dashboard":
                return {"username": user, "role": "hmi"}
            raise o6.StatusCodeError(o6.StatusCode.BAD_USER_ACCESS_DENIED)
        raise o6.StatusCodeError(o6.StatusCode.BAD_USER_ACCESS_DENIED)


server = o6.Server(
    port=4840,
    accessControl=DistilleryAccessControl(),
)

A client connecting with username="hmi", password="dashboard" activates successfully; anything else is rejected.

items.title: Assign roles from activateSession
items.text:
The activateSession hook can return a SessionActivation object instead of a bare context, attaching roles at the moment the session is born:

def activateSession(self, endpoint, remoteCertificate, session, userIdentityToken):
    if isinstance(userIdentityToken, ns0.datatypes.UserNameIdentityToken):
        user = userIdentityToken.userName
        if user == "hmi":
            return o6.SessionActivation(
                context={"username": user},
                roles=(o6.roles.observer,),
            )
        if user == "control":
            return o6.SessionActivation(
                context={"username": user},
                roles=(o6.roles.engineer,),
            )
    raise o6.StatusCodeError(o6.StatusCode.BAD_USER_ACCESS_DENIED)

The HMI session gets observer (read-only); the control-plane session gets engineer (read-write). The same Setpoint._permissions.grant(...) from the roles page then admits the right operations for each role.

items.title: The Session proxy
items.text:
The session argument to activateSession (and to authorization hooks like allowBrowseNode) is a Session proxy:

session.id                     # NodeId of the session
session.context                # whatever activateSession returned
session.set("shift", "night")  # server-side session attributes
session.get("shift")
session.delete("shift")        # a later get() raises BadNotFound
session.roles                  # tuple[Role, ...]
session.roles = (o6.roles.engineer,)
session.close()                # terminate the session

Attribute keys are QualifiedName values or plain strings, which are promoted to namespace 0. The proxy is a resolving wrapper — every operation validates the underlying session id, so using it after the remote session closes raises BadSessionIdInvalid safely.

session.close() does not lock the client out — a client with automatic reconnection simply activates a new one. It is the right way to log out a session that no longer needs to be alive (e.g. an inactive HMI tab).

items.title: allowBrowseNode and friends
items.text:
activateSession decides who the session belongs to. The rest of the access-control hooks decide what the session may do, on a per-operation basis:

  • closeSession — accept or reject a CloseSession request.
  • getUserRightsMask — combine into the per-session effective rights.
  • getUserAccessLevel — restrict a Variable's effective AccessLevel per session.
  • getUserExecutable / getUserExecutableOnObject — restrict a Method's effective executability per session.
  • allowAddNode / allowAddReference / allowDeleteNode / allowDeleteReference — gate the AddNodes / AddReferences / DeleteNodes / DeleteReferences services.
  • allowBrowseNode — gate the Browse service for a node.
  • allowCreateSubscription / allowTransferSubscription — gate subscription creation / transfer.
  • allowHistoryUpdate / allowHistoryDelete — gate history writes.

All have permissive defaults. Override only what the distillery actually needs:

class DistilleryAccessControl(o6.AccessControl):
    def allowBrowseNode(self, session, nodeId, context):
        # HMI may not browse Actuators (the wiring internals)
        if session.context and session.context.get("role") == "hmi":
            if nodeId.namespace == 1 and nodeId.id == 1500:
                return False
        return True

The hooks run on every operation that matches them. Override only when needed — the default behaviour is the right one for most calls.

Info

Inherited authorization hooks use native C defaults. Only hooks overridden by the concrete subclass cross into Python, so a plugin that overrides only activateSession and closeSession does not acquire the GIL for routine reads, writes, browses, or method calls.

items.title: allowNonePolicyPassword
items.text:
allowNonePolicyPassword=True permits UserNameIdentityToken authentication on an unencrypted endpoint. The flag is deliberately separate from access control, because it is a transport decision: without it the stack strips the username/password UserTokenPolicy from an insecure endpoint and logs a warning that the password would travel in the clear.

server = o6.Server(
    port=4840,
    accessControl=DistilleryAccessControl(),
    allowNonePolicyPassword=True,    # username/password allowed over plaintext
)

Enable it for local testing only. In production, run a secure endpoint and leave this flag at its default False.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery now authenticates sessions and assigns roles. The next page adds the encryption and integrity layer on top — security policies, certificates, and encrypted endpoints.

  • Security policies and endpoints — SecurityPolicy selection, encrypted endpoints, certificate management.
  • Server manual — the full authentication and authorization story, including session diagnostics.

items.title: Security policies and endpoints
items.text:
Authentication gets a session onto the distillery, but the bytes are still flying over the wire in cleartext. Without encryption, anyone who can sniff the network segment reads every value the operator writes, and tampers with messages on the way back. This page adds the encryption layer: certificates, security policies, and the encrypted endpoints that advertise them.

By the end, the distillery listens for None (anonymous, plaintext) and Basic256Sha256 (certificate + signed and encrypted), and a properly-configured client picks the secure one.

items.title: What does a security policy do?
items.text:
OPC UA separates the algorithm suite from the level of protection from the who are you? question:

  • Security policy — the cryptographic suite. o6.SecurityPolicy has six members: NONE, BASIC128RSA15, BASIC256, BASIC256SHA256, AES128_SHA256_RSAOAEP, AES256_SHA256_RSAPSS.

  • Security mode — what is applied to each message: None, Sign, SignAndEncrypt.

  • User identity token — Anonymous, UserName (username/password), Certificate (X.509).

The Server(...) constructor takes a certificate and private key that the server uses to identify itself; clients present certificates of their own that the server validates against the trust list. With both sides configured, the negotiated channel is encrypted end-to-end.

For the distillery, Basic256Sha256 is the safe default: well-supported, audited, and built on RSA-2048 / SHA-256. The newer Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss is preferred where it is supported — RSA-PSS signatures and AES-256 session keys.

items.title: Generate a self-signed certificate
items.text:
o6.util ships a helper that creates a self-signed pair:

from o6.util import createSelfSignedCertificate

srv_key, srv_cert = createSelfSignedCertificate(
    appUri="urn:example:distillery",
    commonName="DistilleryServer@localhost",
)

The return values are raw DER bytes. They can be passed directly to the Server(...) constructor or written to disk and loaded from a path:

from pathlib import Path

Path("server_key.der").write_bytes(srv_key)
Path("server_cert.der").write_bytes(srv_cert)

The applicationUri must match the URI the server advertises. Server(..., applicationUri="urn:example:distillery") is the right knob when the certificate is generated separately — there is no separate setter method, the constructor keyword argument is the only way to set it.

items.title: Configure encryption on the server
items.text:
Pass the certificate and key to the Server(...) constructor, along with the trust list of clients to accept:

import o6
from pathlib import Path
from o6.util import createSelfSignedCertificate

srv_key, srv_cert = createSelfSignedCertificate(
    appUri="urn:example:distillery",
    commonName="DistilleryServer@localhost",
)

# Load the client's certificate (issued out of band, or shared for local tests)
client_cert = Path("client_cert.der").read_bytes()

server = o6.Server(
    port=4840,
    certificate=srv_cert,
    privateKey=srv_key,
    trustList=[client_cert],
    applicationUri="urn:example:distillery",
)

With certificate= and privateKey= both set, the server enables the encrypting security policies for every cipher suite the build supports — typically Basic256Sha256, Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep, and Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss. The trust list decides which client certificates are accepted during the secure-channel handshake.

Info

Log lines such as Could not add SecurityPolicy#EccNistP256_AesGcm with error code BadCertificateInvalid on startup are expected with an RSA certificate: the elliptic-curve policies need an EC key and are skipped.

acceptAllCertificates=True accepts every client certificate without validation. It exists for development and interop testing, and it defeats the purpose of the trust list — do not ship it.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
from pathlib import Path

import o6
from o6.util import createSelfSignedCertificate

srv_key, srv_cert = createSelfSignedCertificate(
    appUri="urn:example:distillery",
    commonName="DistilleryServer@localhost",
)

server = o6.Server(
    port=4840,
    certificate=srv_cert,
    privateKey=srv_key,
    trustList=[Path("client_cert.der").read_bytes()],
    applicationUri="urn:example:distillery",
)

setpoint = server.addVariable("Setpoint", server.objectsNode, 85.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1204")
server.start()

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

server.stop()

A client connecting with a matching certificate and SecurityMode.SIGN_AND_ENCRYPT gets an encrypted session; clients without one still get the unencrypted None endpoint (because the server still advertises it for compatibility).

items.title: secureOnly
items.text:
secureOnly=True removes the None endpoint entirely. Clients have to negotiate a secure channel.

server = o6.Server(
    port=4840,
    certificate=srv_cert,
    privateKey=srv_key,
    secureOnly=True,
)

Warning

secureOnly=True removes the None endpoint entirely. In the current build no client can then connect — including a correctly configured secure o6.Client — because endpoint discovery is performed over the None endpoint before the secure channel is opened; every attempt fails with BadSecurityPolicyRejected. Leave secureOnly at its default and restrict access through access control instead until this is resolved.

items.title: What does a secure client look like?
items.text:
The matching o6.Client(...) carries the same shape:

from o6.util import createSelfSignedCertificate
from pathlib import Path
from o6 import Client, SecurityPolicy, SecurityMode

cli_key, cli_cert = createSelfSignedCertificate(
    appUri="urn:example:distillery-client",
    commonName="DistilleryClient@localhost",
)
Path("client_key.der").write_bytes(cli_key)
Path("client_cert.der").write_bytes(cli_cert)

client = Client(
    "opc.tcp://localhost:4840",
    certificate=cli_cert,
    privateKey=cli_key,
    trustList=[srv_cert],
    securityMode=SecurityMode.SIGN_AND_ENCRYPT,
    securityPolicy=SecurityPolicy.BASIC256SHA256,
    applicationUri="urn:example:distillery-client",
)

The same applicationUri must appear in both the certificate and the client constructor. The trust list contains the server's certificate, the security policy and mode are explicit, and the rest of the client API is unchanged.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
from pathlib import Path

from o6 import Client, SecurityPolicy, SecurityMode
from o6.util import createSelfSignedCertificate

# Generate both sides for a local round-trip
srv_key, srv_cert = createSelfSignedCertificate(
    appUri="urn:example:distillery",
    commonName="DistilleryServer@localhost",
)
cli_key, cli_cert = createSelfSignedCertificate(
    appUri="urn:example:distillery-client",
    commonName="DistilleryClient@localhost",
)

Path("server_key.der").write_bytes(srv_key)
Path("server_cert.der").write_bytes(srv_cert)
Path("client_key.der").write_bytes(cli_key)
Path("client_cert.der").write_bytes(cli_cert)

client = Client(
    "opc.tcp://localhost:4840",
    certificate=cli_cert,
    privateKey=cli_key,
    trustList=[srv_cert],
    securityMode=SecurityMode.SIGN_AND_ENCRYPT,
    securityPolicy=SecurityPolicy.BASIC256SHA256,
    applicationUri="urn:example:distillery-client",
)

with client:
    print(client.read("ns=1;i=1204"))

The connection is end-to-end encrypted. The same Client(...) constructor accepts username= / password= for an additional user-identity layer on top of the channel authentication; see the client security tutorial for the symmetric story.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery now speaks encrypted channels, has a role-based access story, and authenticates sessions. The next pages cover the housekeeping parts of a real server: server-side monitored items, internal retention, and historical data.

  • Subscribe monitoring on the server side — what the server sees when a client subscribes, internal monitored items for housekeeping.
  • Server manual — every security-related keyword on Server(...), including the issuer list, revocation list, and application URI.

items.title: Subscribe monitoring on the server side
items.text:
A subscription is the standard view of value changes — push notifications the server sends on its publishing interval. The same mechanism exists server-side: a server can register a monitored item on its own address space and react to value changes the same way, with no monitoring session in sight.

This page covers two patterns:

  • Internal monitored items. Drive housekeeping logic from value changes (Operating flips, Setpoint is rewritten, a batch boundary happens).
  • Server-side subscriptions to its own nodes. Useful for cross-instance reactions, audit trails, and trigger logic without polling.

items.title: Server-local data-change monitored items
items.text:
Server.createDataChangeMonitoredItem(...) registers a monitored item on a server-local Variable. The callback runs on the server's event loop on every value change.

import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)

setpoint = server.addVariable("Setpoint", server.objectsNode, 85.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1204")


def on_change(monitored_item_id, node_id, attribute_id, data_value, context):
    print(f"  [monitor] Setpoint changed to {data_value.value.value}")


server.createDataChangeMonitoredItem(
    "ns=1;i=1204",
    on_change,
    samplingInterval=100.0,            # 100 ms
    context={"label": "setpoint"},
)

The callback signature is (monitored_item_id, node_id, attribute_id, data_value, context). context is the dict the caller passed at registration, handed back unchanged on every notification — useful for tagging the callback with metadata rather than capturing it in a closure.

The returned object is an o6.subscription.MonitoredItem. Delete it with server.deleteMonitoredItem(item) or server.deleteMonitoredItem(item.id).

Info

Server-local monitored items exist for internal logic, not for shipping data across the network. The standard subscription path is unchanged. The two coexist on the same nodestore.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server, StatusCode

server = Server(port=4840)
setpoint = server.addVariable("Setpoint", server.objectsNode, 85.0, nodeId="ns=1;i=1204")


def on_change(item_id, node_id, attr_id, dv, ctx):
    print(f"  [monitor] {ctx['label']} = {dv.value.value}")


server.createDataChangeMonitoredItem(
    "ns=1;i=1204",
    on_change,
    samplingInterval=100.0,
    context={"label": "setpoint"},
)
server.start()

Incoming writes of 90.0 to Setpoint trigger both the server-side monitor and any other subscription. The server's monitor is the right place for internal reactions — audit logging, cross-instance triggers, derived values — without the cost of polling.

items.title: Event monitored items
items.text:
Event monitoring is the same shape, with an event-specific filter. The filter selects which fields of an event are delivered, plus an optional whereClause for content filtering.

from o6.ns import ns0


def on_event(item_id, fields, context):
    print(f"  [event] {fields}")


event_filter = ns0.datatypes.EventFilter.parse(
    "SELECT /Message, /Severity, /SourceName"
)

server.createEventMonitoredItem(
    server.serverNode,
    on_event,
    selectClauses=list(event_filter.selectClauses),
)

The EventFilter.parse(...) helper builds a valid filter from a query string — the same shape the client subscription filter tutorial uses. The callback receives (monitored_item_id, fields, context) where fields is a dict[str, Any] keyed by selected event-filter paths, such as "/Message" or "/ConditionName/Id". Read a selected field with fields["/Message"].

Info

An empty EventFilter is rejected with BadEventFilterInvalid. Always specify at least one select clause, or use EventFilter.parse(...) to build one for you.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
import time
import o6
from o6 import Server
from o6.ns import ns0

server = Server(port=4840)


def on_event(item_id, fields, context):
    print(f"  [event] {fields}")


event_filter = ns0.datatypes.EventFilter.parse(
    "SELECT /Message, /Severity, /SourceName"
)

server.createEventMonitoredItem(
    server.serverNode,
    on_event,
    selectClauses=list(event_filter.selectClauses),
)
server.start()

Server-local event monitors observe the same events an external subscription would. They are the right place for cross-instance logic: one still's Operating=False triggers another still's Operating=False, or a server-wide audit log captures every transition regardless of which session triggered it.

items.title: Driving housekeeping from a monitor
items.text:
The distillery's natural place for an internal monitor is Operating. When Operating=False, the simulation should park the still after the current batch:

def on_operating_change(item_id, node_id, attr_id, dv, ctx):
    new_value = bool(dv.value.value)
    if not new_value:
        print("  [housekeeping] Operating=False — will park after current batch")


server.createDataChangeMonitoredItem(
    "ns=1;i=1203",
    on_operating_change,
    samplingInterval=100.0,
    context={"label": "operating"},
)

The monitor fires on the loop thread the moment the value changes. The simulation's update loop sees the new value on its next tick and parks at the right boundary.

For cross-instance logic — a still finishing a batch triggers another still to start — event monitors on the source instance work the same way.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery has its full server-side behaviour: typed model, write handlers, method implementations, periodic timers, internal monitors. The next page finishes the production story with one last loose end.

  • Server callbacks — the addRepeatedCallback API that drives the update loop in lockstep with these monitors.
  • Server manual — the full server-local monitored item API, including createEventMonitoredItemEx for full control over an event filter (createDataChangeMonitoredItem has no Ex counterpart).

items.title: Historical data
items.text:
Historizing in the distillery: recording a Variable's values over time so a client can ask for a time range instead of only ever seeing the current value. It needs two things — a history database on the server, and a Variable marked as historizing — and once both are in place, recording and read-back are automatic.

The distillery already does this for Kettle/Temperature: Set the stage starts a server where that one Variable is historizing from the moment it comes up, so every value the simulation writes lands in the history and HistoryRead against ns=1;i=1302 returns real data.

items.title: Configuring the history database
items.text:
One call, before start(), gives the server somewhere to record:

server.config.setHistoryDatabase(maxNodes=10)

maxNodes sizes the initial node table — it grows on demand, so it isn't a hard ceiling on how many Variables can historize, just how much is pre-allocated. This has to run before start(); changing it afterwards raises.

items.title: Marking a Variable historizing
items.text:
Server.addVariable(...) accepts historizing= — either True for the defaults, or an o6.History(...) to size and tune the recording:

import o6
from o6 import Server

server = Server(port=4840)
server.config.setHistoryDatabase(maxNodes=10)

temperature = server.addVariable(
    "KettleTemperature",
    server.objectsNode,
    20.0,
    nodeId="ns=1;i=1302",
    historizing=True,
)
server.start()
Field Meaning Default capacity Samples kept per node — a ring buffer; the oldest sample is evicted once it fills. 100 strategy "on-write" (record every write), or "poll" (sample on a timer, independent of writes). "on-write" interval Poll period in seconds. Only meaningful with strategy="poll". 1.0

Variables created before startup register during start(), so setHistoryDatabase(...) may run before or after their creation. Startup raises if the database is missing or registration fails. Variables added after startup register immediately and require the database to be configured already.

A Variable your server didn't create — a nodeset node, a declared instance, or one a client added at runtime — can't take historizing= at construction time. server.historize(target, ...) is the equivalent for those: it takes effect immediately (the database has to already be configured), rather than waiting for start().

items.title: Reading it back
items.text:
Once a Variable is historizing, any client reads it back the normal OPC UA way:

data = client.historyRead("ns=1;i=1302", start, end)
for dv in data.dataValues:
    print(dv.sourceTimestamp, dv.value)

start/end are timezone-aware datetimes; end is exclusive. A large range comes back paged behind a continuation point sized by setHistoryDatabase(..., maxResponseSize=...) (default 100) — client.historyRead follows the first page only, so a full sweep over a big range needs serviceHistoryRead with the continuation point fed back in.

items.title: The allowHistoryUpdate / allowHistoryDelete hooks
items.text:
The o6.AccessControl base class exposes two authorization hooks for history, matching the HistoryUpdate and HistoryDelete service calls:

class DistilleryAccessControl(o6.AccessControl):
    def allowHistoryUpdate(self, session, nodeId, performUpdateType, value):
        """Decide whether this session may push history into the Variable."""
        return o6.roles.engineer in session.roles

    def allowHistoryDelete(self, session, nodeId, startTimestamp, endTimestamp, isDeleteModified):
        """Decide whether this session may delete history."""
        return False   # never let clients delete history

allowHistoryUpdate is consulted on every HistoryUpdate request, with performUpdateType (insert / replace / update / remove) and the DataValue being written. allowHistoryDelete is consulted on every HistoryDelete request, with the time range being deleted and whether modified values are included. Both default to permissive — the base class returns True — so an AccessControl subclass that does not override them allows any session to write or delete history.

The session.roles check mirrors where the authentication page leaves the reader: once activateSession returns SessionActivation(roles=(o6.roles.engineer,)) for the control-plane user, o6.roles.engineer in session.roles is True for that session and False for the HMI's observer session — roles live on session.roles, not folded into session.context.

items.title: What's next?
items.text:
The distillery's story is essentially complete. The last page in the tutorials assembles the core of it into the two files Set the stage distributes — the same server both the client and server tutorials talk to.

  • The distillery server — the address space and behaviour assembled into the runnable two-file project.
  • Server manual — the full history story, including ring sizing and the response-paging default.

items.title: The distillery server
items.text:
This is the server the tutorials build towards. The full runnable version — along with the simulation that drives it — is described in Set the stage: the page walks you through saving the two files (server.py and sim.py) and starting the server with python server.py. That is also the server the client tutorials connect to, so it is the one to keep running while you work through either set.

Why a separate simulation

We don't have a real distillery to drive, so the server is paired with sim.py: a small state machine that runs in a background thread and publishes the kettle level, temperature, valves, heater, state, cycle, and event log into the address space. The two-file split keeps the OPC UA side and the simulation side independently readable.

The address space in those two files is exactly what the earlier tutorials put together — the hierarchy from Add a hierarchy, the variables from Add a variable, and the methods from Add a method.

Getting values in and out is deliberately simpler than what Variables with sources and Server callbacks teach, though. Those pages install proper read/write callbacks with Server.implement(...) and a periodic tick with addRepeatedCallback — real, scalable mechanisms worth knowing for a bigger server. This particular server is small enough that it doesn't need either: server.py just keeps plain writable=True/False variables and runs a hand-rolled while loop (time.sleep(POLL_INTERVAL)) that polls the two writable variables for client-side changes and pushes values with call-syntax (some_var(new_value)). The event log follows the "writable event log" pattern from Events.

The declared-type band (200–230) and the production band (350, 400–440) are genuinely useful once a server needs typed models or is exposed on a real network — but neither is part of this particular reference server. It stays deliberately small, and deliberately insecure and unauthenticated: server.py's only flags are --port, --no-sim, --sim-speed, and --ui, with nothing security-related among them, matching what Set the stage hands you. The file also carries a bit of material no earlier tutorial covers at all — CLI argument parsing and the child-process/UI orchestration behind --ui — which exists to make the example pleasant to run, not to teach an o6 concept.

To run it, jump straight to Set the stage, save the two files, and run python server.py from that folder.
